content: うわさって、こわいものです。

content.content: A rumor is a scary thing.

content: 若いって、すばらしい。

content.content: Youth is wonderful.

content: 都会でひとりで暮らす（の）って、大変です。

content.content: Living alone in a large city is hard.

content: 反対する（の）って、勇気のいることです。

content.content: Disagreeing requires courage.

content: どちらかひとつに決める（の）って、むずかしい。

content.content: It’s difficult to decide on only one of them.
Used when raising something as a topic and describing its definition or meaning, or assessing it. Used in informal spoken language. When describing a definition or meaning, as in

content: , it is the spoken language equivalent of Nとは. When a verb is used in the phrase, as in
, it is the spoken language equivalent of Vのは...だ.

content.content: 3. ...って〈quotation〉a. ...って

content: かれはすぐ来るっていってますよ。

content.content: He’s saying he’ll come here soon.

content: それで、もうすこし待ってくれっていったんです。

content.content: That’s why I asked him to wait for a little longer.

content: A:お母さん、きょうは、いやだって。

content.content: Mother, I don’t want to go today.
B:じゃあ、いつならいいの。
So when will it be OK?

content: A:電話して聞いてみたけど、予約のキャンセルはできないって。

content.content: I called them and asked, but they said they can’t cancel the reservation.
B:ああ、そう。
Is that so?
The colloquial equivalent of とused for quoting sentences. Used widely except in formal conversation, regardless of whether the speaker is a man or a woman.

content: means “He’s saying he’ll be here soon.” Also used for conveying what the speaker has heard by abbreviating the latter half of the sentence, as in
and
A:これ、どこで買ったの。

content.content: Where did you buy this?
B:どこって、マニラだよ。
In Manila, of course.

content: A:もうこの辺でやめてほしいんだが。

content.content: I’d really like you to quit here.
B:やめろって、一体どういうことですか。
Quit here? What on earth are you talking about?
Used as a retort to question the listener by repeating what was said. Colloquial expression. ...というのはis often used as formal equivalent.
5. んだって〈hearsay〉［N／Na　なんだって］［A／V　んだって］

content: あの人、先生なんだって。

content.content: That person is a teacher apparently.

content: 山田さん、お酒、きらいなんだって。

content.content: Yamada-san apparently doesn’t like drinking.

content: あの店のケーキ、おいしいんだって。

content.content: They say the cakes at that bakery are really good.

content: 鈴木さんがあす田中さんに会うんだって。

content.content: Apparently Suzuki-san is meeting Tanaka-san tomorrow.

content: A:あの人、先生なんだって？

content.content: I hear he’s a teacher, right?
B:うん、英語の先生だよ。
Yes, an English teacher.

content: A:山田さん、お酒、きらいなんだって？

content.content: So I hear Yamada-san doesn’t like drinking?
B:ああ、そう言ってたよ。
Yes, he said so.

content: A:あの店のケーキ、おいしいんだって？

content.content: I hear the cake in that shop is really good, right?
B:いや、それほどでもないよ。
No, not especially.

content: A:鈴木さんがあす田中さんに会うんだって？

content.content: So Suzuki-san is meeting Tanaka-san tomorrow?
B:うん、約束してるんだって。
Yes, they have an appointment, apparently.
This is a combination of のだ／んだ and the quotation って. Expresses that something is information acquired by hearing it from someone else.

content: , with a rising tone at the end of the sentence, are expressions used for asking the listener to confirm what the speaker has heard. Both men and women use it in informal speech. なのだって／のだって are almost never used; they usually become んだって and んですって.

content.content: んですってis normally used by women. Note that in this case even though です is used, it cannot be used when speaking to a person of higher status. For example, あの人は先生なんだそうです should be used instead of ...先生なんですって.

content: そんなこと、したってむだだ。

content.content: It won’t work.

content: そんなこと、言ったって、いまからもどれないよ。

content.content: You say so, but I can’t go back now.

content: ここから呼んだって、聞こえないだろう。

content.content: He can’t hear us even if we call him from here.
【たって】
【ってば】

content: A:この字、間違ってるんじゃないか？

content.content: Isn’t this letter wrong?
B:あってるよ。
No, it’s right.
A:いや、絶対、間違ってるってば。
Nope, I’m sure it’s wrong.

content: A:宿題やったの？

content.content: Did you do your homework?
B:うん。
Yeah.
A:もう9時よ。
It’s already nine o’clock.
B:やったってば。
I said I did it!

content: A:お母さん

content.content: Mother?
A:お母さんってば。聞いてるの？
Mother! Are you listening?

Used to emphasize the speaker’s point in informal conversation between people who are close to each other, particularly when the speaker is a little irritated because his/her point is not communicated. Also used to attract someone’s attention, as in example
【っぽい】［Nっぽい］［Rっぽい］

content: 男は白っぽい服を着ていた。

content.content: The man was wearing whitish clothes.

content: あの人は忘れっぽくて困る。

content.content: It’s a problem because he can be forgetful.

content: 30にもなって、そんなことで怒るなんて子供っぽいね。

content.content: To be already thirty years old and get angry over something like that is really childish, isn’t it?

content: この牛乳水っぽくてまずいよ。

content.content: This milk is watery and tastes awful.

content: 死ぬだとか葬式だとか、湿っぽい話はもうやめよう。

content.content: Let’s quit talking about such depressing things like death and funerals.
Used with a noun or verb stem to form i-adjectives to express the meaning “feels that way” or “has the tendency to.”
Used with nouns that express colors, such as 赤(red), 白(white), 黒(black), 黄色(yellow), 茶色(brown), to express the meaning “has that color/characteristic” or “close to that color/characteristic,” as in

content: . Also used with verb stems such as 怒る(get angry)／ひがむ(have an inferiority complex) ／ぐちる(grumble) ／忘れる(forget) to express the characteristics of someone who “always does ...” or “often does ...,” as in
. Also used with 子供(child) ／女(woman) ／男(man) ／やくざ(the Japanese mafia) and so on, to express the meaning “like a child/yakuza” or “very manly (man-like)/womanly (woman-like),” as in

content.content: In addition, there are usages like 水っぽい (too watery and thin), 湿っぽい (seems damp, gloomy), and 熱っぽい (seems to have a temperature/feverish). 子供っぽい／水っぽいhave negative connotations. When expressing a positive feeling, 子供らしい／みずみずしい are used.
【つ...つ】［R-つR-つ］

content: 彼に会おうか会うまいかと悩んで、家の前を行きつ戻りつしていた。

content.content: I kept walking to and fro in front of his house, worrying over whether or not I should meet him.

content: お互い持ちつ持たれつで、助け合いましょう。

content.content: Let’s make it a give-and-take as we help each other.

content: 初詣の神社はものすごい人出で、押しつ押されつ、やっとのことで境内までたどり着いた。

content.content: The shrine for the first pilgrimage of the New Year was packed with people, and after pushing and being pushed, we finally made it into the inner grounds.

content: 久しぶりに友人とさしつさされつ酒を飲んで何時間もしゃべった。

content.content: For the first time in quite a while, I talked with a friend for many hours while we filled each other’s cup with sake.

Expresses that two actions alternate, by repeating verbs with opposite meaning (e.g. 行く(go)- 戻る(return)) or active and passive verbs (e.g. 押す(push)- 押される(being pushed)). Used in set expressions, such as 行きつ戻りつ or 持ちつ持たれつ, as in

content: and
respectively.

content.content: 【つい】

content: 太るとわかっていながら、あまりおいしそうなケーキだったので、つい食べてしまった。

content.content: I knew I would put weight on, but the cake looked so good that I ended up eating it all.

content: お酒はやめたはずだが、目の前にあると、つい手が出る。

content.content: I’m supposed to have given up alcohol, but when I see it in front of me, I just have to take some.

content: そのことは口止めされていたのに、つい口をすべらせて言ってしまった。

content.content: I was told not to say it to anyone, but it just slipped out.

content: おしゃべりが楽しくてつい遅くなってしまった。

content.content: It was so much fun visiting that I didn’t notice it had gotten late.

content: よく周りから声が大きいと苦情がでるので気をつけてはいるのだが、興奮するとつい声が高くなる。

content.content: People often complain that I have a loud voice. I am careful, but when I get excited, my voice starts booming.
Expresses the meaning that one can’t help doing something which one feels that one shouldn’t do or should try not to do. Often used together with V-てしまう.
【ついて】→
【について】
【ついては】

content: 《手紙》この秋に町民の大運動会を開催することになりました。ついては、皆様からの御寄付をいただきたく、お願い申し上げます。

content.content: 《in a letter》 It has been decided that we will hold a citizens’ Sports Day this fall. We would therefore be grateful for your kind donations.

content: 今の会長が来月任期満了で引退します。ついては、新しい会長を選ぶために候補者をあげることになりました。

content.content: The current chairperson will be retiring next month, as his term will come to an end. It has therefore been decided that we are to come up with candidates for selecting the new chairperson.
Means “for this reason.” Typical of written language, and is a euphemistic way of speaking. Often used when reporting to or asking something from the listener (or reader) in a formal way.
【ついでに】
1. ついでに

content: 図書館へ本を借りにいった。ついでに、近くに住んでいる友達のところへ行ってみた。

content.content: I went to the library to borrow a book. On my way, I dropped by a friend’s house in the neighborhood.

content: でかけるのなら、ついでに、この手紙を出して来てくれませんか。

content.content: If you’re going out, could you also mail this letter on your way?
Means “using the opportunity.” Used when doing something else in addition to what was originally intended.
2. ...ついで（に）［Nのついで］［Vついで］

content: 京都へ行くついでに、奈良を回ってみたい。

content.content: I’d also like to look around Nara when I go to Kyoto.

content: 洗濯機を直すついでに、ドアの取っ手も直してもらった。

content.content: In addition to fixing the washing machine, I also got them to fix the door handle.

content: 姉は実家に遊びに来たついでに、冷蔵庫の中のものをみんな持って帰った。

content.content: My big sister took everything in the fridge when visiting her family home.

content: 買い物のついでに、図書館へ行って本を借りて来た。

content.content: I went and borrowed a book from the library when I was out shopping.

content: 兄は出張のついでだといって、わたしの仕事場へ会いに来た。

content.content: My elder brother visited me in my office, saying that it was on his way to a business trip.
Used when doing something else in addition to what was originally intended. Nouns which express activity are used.
【ついに】
1. ついにV-た

content: 1995 年、トンネルはついに完成した。

content.content: The tunnel was finally completed in

content: 登山隊は、ついに頂上を征服した。

content.content: The mountaineering troop finally conquered the summit.

content: 待ちに待ったオリンピックがついに始まった。

content.content: The Olympic Games for which we have waited and waited have finally started.

content: 留学生の数は年々増え続け、ついに 10 万人を越えた。

content.content: The number of overseas students increased year by year, and finally exceeded 100,

content: 客は、一人去り二人去りして、ついに誰もいなくなった。

content.content: Customers left one after another, until finally no one was left.

content: 遭難して五日目、食糧も水もついに底をついた。

content.content: On the fifth day after taking refuge, both food and water ran out.

Expresses a situation where after various stages something is finally achieved. Often used when something is completed or succeeds after a long time or a period of hardship, or when some major matter starts or ends, as in

content: and
. Used also when reaching a large number which was a milestone or a target, as in
, or when a situation has gradually changed and reached the final stage which the speaker was expecting, as in
and

content.content: Places more emphasis on the matter that has occurred than the way in which it was reached. Example

content: below places emphasis on the result that has been completed. やっと in
, on the other hand, emphasizes the steps towards the result, meaning “it took a long time because of hard construction work.”

content.content: （例1）1995 年トンネルはついに完成した。
The tunnel was finally completed in
（例2）1995 年トンネルはやっと完成した。
At long last, the tunnel was completed in
やっと and とうとう are close expressions. See やっと (Usage 1) for more detail.
2. ついにV-なかった

content: 閉店時間まで待ったが、彼はついに姿を表さなかった。

content.content: I waited until the closing time, but he didn’t show up after all.

content: 彼の願いはついに実現しなかった。

content.content: Ultimately, his wish was never realized.

content: 彼はついに最後まで謝らなかった。

content.content: He didn’t apologize even to the end.

content: 犯人はついにわからずじまいだった。

content.content: We never found out who the culprit was.
Used when the speaker’s hope or wish didn’t come true, even in the end. とうとう can replace ついに in

content: , but やっと cannot.

content.content: 3. ついには

content: この病気は、次第に全身が衰弱し、ついには死亡するという恐ろしい病気だ。

content.content: This disease is horrible: the entire body gradually weakens and the ultimate result is death.

content: 血のにじむような練習に明け暮れて、ついには栄光の勝利を勝ち取った。

content.content: Punishing practice day in and day out eventually put a glorious victory in his grasp.
Expresses the situation of finally reaching a result after a long process. Used in written language.
【つきましては】

content: 《招待状》この度、新学生会館が完成いたしました。つきましては、次の通り落成式を挙行いたしますので、ご案内申し上げます。

content.content: 《an invitation card》 We are pleased to announce the completion of the new student hall. Please see the following details for the dedication ceremony to mark this occasion.

content: 先月の台風で当地は大きな被害を受けました。つきましては皆様にご支援いただきたくお願い致します。

content.content: Last month’s typhoon caused serious damage to this area. Therefore we would like to request your kind support (for reconstruction).
A polite form of ついては. Often used in formal letters.
【ついては】
【つつ】Used with a verb stem. Usually used in written language or formal conversation.
1. R-つつ〈simultaneity〉

content: 彼は、「春ももう終わりですね」と言いつつ、庭へ目をやった。

content.content: Saying “Spring is over, isn’t it,” he cast his eyes to the garden.

content: 静かな青い海を眺めつつ、良子は物思いにふけっていた。

content.content: Yoshiko was in deep thought while looking at the quiet blue sea.

content: この会議では、個々の問題点を検討しつつ、今後の発展の方向を探っていきたいと思います。

content.content: At this meeting, I hope that as we consider each problem point, we can explore ways to move forward for developing.

content: その選手はけがした足をかばいつつ、最後まで完走した。

content.content: Favoring his injured leg, the athlete ran the race to completion.
Expresses that the same subject does one action while also doing another. Has roughly the same meaning as ...ながら, but ...つつtends to be used in written language.
2. R-つつ〈adversative connective〉a. R-つつ

content: 夏休みの間、勉強しなければいけないと思いつつ、毎日遊んで過ごしてしまった。

content.content: I knew I had to study during the summer vacation, but I spent it having fun every day.

content: 早くたばこをやめなければいけないと思いつつ、いまだに禁煙に成功していない。

content.content: Even while thinking that I really ought to quit smoking right way, I still haven’t succeeded in giving it up.

content: その言い訳はうそと知りつつ、わたしは彼にお金を貸した。

content.content: I lent him money, all the while knowing that the pretext was a lie.

content: 青木さんは事業のパートナーを嫌いつつ、常に協力を惜しまなかった。

content.content: Aoki-san, even while disliking his project partner, never held back from cooperating with him.
Used to link two contrary matters. For example,

content: means “although I thought.” Close to the adversative use of のに or ながら. “All the while knowing it was a lie” in
is an often-used idiomatic expression.

content.content: b. R-つつも

content: 彼は、歯痛に悩まされつつも、走り続けた。

content.content: He continued running even while being bothered with a toothache.

content: 「健康のために働き過ぎはよくないのよ」と言いつつも、彼女は決して休暇をとらないのだ。

content.content: She keeps saying “Overwork is not good for your health,” yet never takes a vacation herself.

content: 医者に行かなければと思いつつも、忙しさに紛れて忘れてしまった。

content.content: All the while knowing I had to see a doctor, I was distracted by being busy and forgot all about it.

content: 設備の再調査が必要だと知りつつも無視したことが、今回の大事故につながったと思われる。

content.content: It is believed that this calamity is linked to the fact that, although (the responsible parties) were well aware of the necessity for a follow-up evaluation of the facilities, they ignored it.
Same as
【つつ】(Usage 2 a).
3. R-つつある

content: 地球は温暖化しつつある。

content.content: The planet is on its way to becoming warmer.

content: この会社は現在成長しつつある。

content.content: The company is currently growing.

content: この海底では長大なトンネルを掘りつつある。

content.content: A long tunnel is presently being dug below this sea bottom.

content: 手術以来、彼の体は順調に回復しつつある。

content.content: His health has been improving as hoped since the operation.

content: 若い人が都会へ出て行くため、五百年の伝統のある祭りの火がいまや消えつつある。

content.content: Because young people are leaving for the city, the 500-year-old tradition of having a fire at the festival is about to die out.

content: 彼は今自分が死につつあることを意識していた。

content.content: He was conscious of the fact that he was dying.

content: その時代は静かに終わりつつあった。

content.content: The era was quietly ending.
Used to express that an action or effect is moving in a certain direction. Often corresponds to ている, but there are also a few differences. つつある in

content: can be replaced by ている without changing the meaning very much, but when it is used with verbs which express instantaneous change, as in

, replacing it will alter the meaning of the sentence. When used with verbs which express such change, using つつある gives the meaning that a change has taken place and is heading in the direction of completion.ている, on the other hand, expresses that the situation after the change has been completed. Therefore if 死につつある(dying) in
is replaced with 死んでいる(dead), the sentence would not make sense.

content.content: In addition, つつある cannot be used with verbs which have no meaning of completion, so 彼女は泣きつつある cannot be used.
【つまり】
1. つまり〈restatement〉

content: 彼は、母の弟、つまり私の叔父である。

content.content: He is my mother’s younger brother, namely, my uncle.

content: 両親は、終戦の翌年、つまり1946 年に結婚した。

content.content: My parents married the year after the end of the war, that is, in

content: 相思相愛の仲とは、つまりお互いのことを心底愛し合っている関係のことである。

content.content: “Mutual loving relationship” means a relationship of deep love for each other.

content: A:この件については、ちょっと考えさせてください。

content.content: Please let me think about this matter a little.
B:つまり「引き受けていただけない」ということですね。
So you can’t agree to do it, is that it?
Used for replacing a phrase or sentence by a different expression that has the same meaning. For example, in

content: , following the listener’s statement, the speaker is replacing it using his own words. While close to すなわち, つまり is more like spoken language. Hence in conversation, like example
, replacing it with すなわち would be unnatural.

content.content: 2. つまり（は）〈conclusion〉

content: つまり、責任は自分にはないとおっしゃりたいのですね。

content.content: Thus, what you want to say is that you have no responsibility for this.

content: 子供の教育は、つまりは、家庭でのしつけの問題だ。

content.content: Children’s education is ultimately a question of discipline at home.

content: A:まあ、それほど忙しいというわけでもないんですけど…。

content.content: Well, it isn’t that I’m that busy, but....
B:つまり、君は何が言いたいんだ。
So what is it that you want to say?

content: 私の言いたいことは、つまり、この問題の責任は経営者側にあって…。そのつまり、社員はその犠牲者だということです。

content.content: What I want to say is that the responsibility for this problem is on the side of the management, and that in essence means the employees are the victims.
Used when describing a final conclusion without going into an explanation of the development leading to it. In

content: and
, it is used to confirm or facilitate the listener’s conclusion. Can also be used in the form つまりは. In
, つまり is used in spoken language conjunctively. Often replaced by 結局 or 要するに.

content.content: 【つもり】
1. V-るつもりa. V-る／V-ない　つもりだ

content: 来年はヨーロッパへ旅行するつもりだ。

content.content: I intend to travel to Europe next year.

content: 友達が来たら、東京を案内するつもりだ。

content.content: When my friend comes, I intend to guide him around Tokyo.

content: たばこは、もう決してすわないつもりだ。

content.content: I will never smoke again.

content: 山本さんも参加するつもりだったのですが、都合で来られなくなってしまいました。

content.content: Yamamoto-san was going to participate, too, but something came up that kept him from coming.

content: A:これから、美術館へいらっしゃいますか。

content.content: Will you be going to the art museum now?
B:ええ、そのつもりです。
Yes, that’s my plan.

Expresses will/intention. Can be used either for the speaker’s will or that of a third person. V-ないつもりだ expresses the intention of not doing a certain act. When omitting the verb,  その is attached, as in example

content: . はい、つもりです is an incorrect usage.

content.content: b. V-るつもりはない

content: この授業を聴講してみたい。続けて出るつもりはないけれど。

content.content: I want to try to attend this lecture. However, I don’t intend to continue attending (future lectures).

content: 趣味で描いていた絵が展覧会で入選して、売れたが、プロになるつもりはない。

content.content: The picture I drew for fun was selected for an exhibition and sold, but I have no intention of becoming a professional.

content: 今すぐ行くつもりはないが、アメリカのことを勉強しておきたい。

content.content: I don’t intend to go right away, but for now I’d like to study about the U.S.

content: この失敗であきらめるつもりはないけれど、やはりひどくショックなのには変わりがない。

content.content: I don’t intend to quit because of this failure, but that obviously doesn’t change the fact that I’m deeply shocked by it.

content: このけんかはあの人達が始めたことで、わたしにはそんなことをするつもりは全くなかったんです。

content.content: This fight was started by them, and I had no intention of doing anything like that at all.

content: A:この条件で何とか売っていただけないでしょうか。

content.content: Can’t you sell it to me on this condition?
B:いくらお金をもらっても、この土地を売るつもりはない。帰ってください。
I don’t want to sell this land no matter how much money I receive. Please go away.

Used to deny the speaker’s intention to do something. When using this sentence pattern, the speaker denies his intention to do what the listener is likely to predict or expect under a certain circumstance. In some cases, as in examples

content: and
, つもり is used when the speaker describes what the listener is likely to expect first, at the outset.

content.content: c. V-るつもりではない

content: すみません、あなたの邪魔をするつもりではなかったんです。

content.content: I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to disturb you.

content: A:彼はあなたが批判したといって気にしていましたよ。

content.content: He was concerned, saying that you criticized it.
B:あの、そんなつもりではなかったんです。
Oh, I didn’t mean to.

Denies the speaker’s intention to do something. Often used for explanation or self-defense when one’s action or attitude is likely to be misinterpreted, by expressing that one actually doesn’t or didn’t intend to do something. Can be replaced by つもりはない.
d. V-るつもりで

content: 今日限りでやめるつもりで、上司に話しに行った。

content.content: With the intent to quit this very day, I went to talk to my boss.

content: 彼女は彼と結婚するつもりでずっと待っていた。

content.content: Intending to marry him, she waited all the while.

content: 今回の試合には絶対負けないつもりで練習に励んで来た。

content.content: I have been practicing hard, definitely intending not to lose this match.
Means “with the intention or will to do....”
2. ...つもりだ［Nのつもりだ］［Na なつもりだ］［Aつもりだ］［V-た／V-ている　つもりだ］a. ...つもりだ〈conviction〉

content: ミスが多かったが、今日の試合は練習のつもりだったからそれほど気にしていない。

content.content: There were a lot of mistakes today, but I considered the match today to be practice, so I’m not too concerned.

content: まだまだ元気なつもりだったけど、あの程度のハイキングでこんなに疲れてしまうとはねえ。もう年かなあ。

content.content: I thought I was still in good shape, but to be this exhausted after only that much of a hike...I must be getting old.

content: まだまだ気は若いつもりだよ。

content.content: I still consider myself young in spirit.

content: よく調べて書いたつもりですが、まだ間違いがあるかもしれません。

content.content: I believe I have carefully checked everything I wrote, but there may still be some errors.

content: A:君の仕事ぶり、評判いいよ。

content.content: I have good feedback on the way you work.
B:そうですか。ありがとうございます。お客様にご満足いただけるよう、毎日ベストをつくしているつもりです。
Is that so? Thank you. I have been doing my best in order to have our customers be satisfied.
When the subject is in first person, this expresses the meaning that the speaker thinks so or believes so, regardless of whether this is contrary to what other persons may think.
b. ...つもりだ〈counter-factual〉

content: なによ、あの人、女王のつもりかしら。

content.content: Who does she think she is—a queen?

content: あの人は自分では有能なつもりだが、その仕事ぶりに対する周囲の評価は低い。

content.content: He thinks he’s capable, but the people around him don’t think very much of his work.

content: 彼女のあの人を小ばかにしたような態度は好きじゃないな。自分ではよほど賢いつもりなんだろうけどね。

content.content: I don’t like her attitude of belittling him. She may consider herself to be rather clever, but...

content: 君はちゃんと説明したつもりかもしれないが、先方は聞いてないといっているよ。

content.content: You may have thought that you had explained it clearly, but they say they weren’t aware of it.

content: 彼女はすべてを知っているつもりだが、本当は何も知らない。

content.content: She thinks she knows it all, but in fact she doesn’t know anything.
When the subject is in the second or third person, this is used to mean that the person’s belief differs from what the speaker or others perceive to be the fact.
c. V-たつもりはない

content: 私はそんなことを言ったつもりはない。

content.content: That’s not what I meant to say.

content: あの人、怒ってるの？　からかったつもりはないんだけどねえ。

content.content: Is he angry? I didn’t mean to make fun of him, you know.

content: A:彼、あなたに服をほめられたって喜んでたわよ。

content.content: He was pleased, saying that you complimented him on his outfit.
B:こまったな。ほめたつもりはないんだけどな。
Oh, dear. I didn’t think I was complimenting him, but...
Used for denying one’s perception or judgment about the other’s action. The sentence in

content: can be replaced by そんなつもりはないんだけどな.

content.content: 3. V-たつもりで

content: 旅行したつもりで、お金は貯金することにした。

content.content: I decided to save money, telling myself that I had spent it traveling.

content: 学生たちはプロのモデルになったつもりで、いろいろなポーズをとった。

content.content: With the idea that they were professional models, the students struck all sorts of poses.

content: 昔にもどったつもりで、もう一度一からやり直してみます。

content.content: I intend to go back into the past and start over again from the beginning.

content: 完成までまだ一週間かかるのに、もう終わったつもりで、飲みに行った。

content.content: It will still take a week for completion, and yet he’s gone drinking as if it were completed.

content: 死んだつもりで頑張ればできないことはない。

content.content: There’s nothing you can’t do if you’re ready to give it your all (lit. lay down your life) to try it.

Expresses the meaning of provisionally imagining something as a prerequisite for an action, and can be replaced by したと見なして, したと考えて or したと仮定して. 死んだつもりで is an idiomatic expression for showing a strong determination to do something.
【つれて】→
【につれて】

【て】［N／Na　で］［A-くて］［V-て］で is attached to nouns and na-adjectives. In the case of i-adjectives, it takes the form くて. ない has two forms: なくて and ないで. In the case of verbs, で is used for those whose dictionary form ends in グ, ヌ, ブ and ム, while all others take て.

content: 朝ご飯を作って、子供を起こした。

content.content: I cooked breakfast and then woke my children up.

content: しっかり安全を点検して、それからかぎをかけた。

content.content: I checked that everything was safe and then locked up.

content: まず、買い物をして、それから、映画を見て、帰って来た。

content.content: I went shopping first, then watched a film, and then came home.

content: 電話をかけて、面会の約束をとりつけて、会いに行った。

content.content: I called them, made an appointment for an interview, and then went to see them.

content: 山田さんがやめて、高田さんが入った。

content.content: Yamada-san quit, and then Takada-san joined.

content: びっくりして、口もきけなかった。

content.content: I was so surprised that I couldn’t speak.

content: 着物を着て、出掛けた。

content.content: I put on a kimono and went out.

content: 地下鉄ははやくて安全だ。

content.content: The subway is fast and safe.

content: 外が真っ暗でこわかった。

content.content: Outside was dark and scary.

content: めずらしい人から手紙をもらってうれしかった。

content.content: I was happy to receive a letter from someone who rarely writes me.
Used for loosely linking two clauses. ...て can be used twice, as in

content: and

content.content: By linking sentences which express actions, this describes matters that take place in sequence, as in

content: and
. Also used to express contrast, a possible reason, a means of action, or circumstances related to such, depending on the context.

content.content: In sentences expressing an attribute or state by the use of adjectives, this is sometimes used to list two attributes or to mention a possible reason. When an adjectival clause or description of a characteristic follows an expression of activity, as in

content: , it often expresses a possible reason for something.

content.content: When several actions or situations alternate, or when one is describing something unrelated to a time sequence, たりis used instead of て.
【て...て】［Na で Na で］［A-くて A-くて］［V-て V-て］

content: 連絡がいつまで待っても来ないので、不安で不安で仕方がなかった。

content.content: Because no contact came no matter how long I waited, I was beside myself with worries.

content: お土産を買い過ぎたので、トランクが重くて重くて腕がしびれそうだった。

content.content: I bought too many gifts, so the suitcase was so heavy that my arm nearly become numb.

content: はじめて着物を着たら、帯がきつくてきつくて何も食べられなかった。

content.content: I wore a kimono for the first time, and I couldn’t eat anything because the obi sash was so tight.

content: 走って走ってやっと間に合った。

content.content: I ran and ran and managed to get there in time.

content: 一晩中飲んで飲んで、飲みまくった。

content.content: I drank and drank all night.
Used for emphasizing degree by repeating the same verb or adjective. Usually used in conversation.
【てあげる】
1. V-てあげる

content: おばあさんが横断歩道で困っていたので、手を引いてあげた。

content.content: An elderly woman was having trouble at the crosswalk, so I took her hand to guide her.

content: 妹は母の誕生日に家中の掃除をしてケーキを焼いてあげたらしい。

content.content: It seems that my little sister cleaned the whole house and baked a cake for my mother’s birthday.

content: この暖かいひざかけ、お母さんに一枚買ってあげたら喜ばれますよ。

content.content: Your mother will be pleased if you buy her one of these lap blankets.

content: せっかくみんなの写真を撮ってあげようと思ったのに、カメラを忘れてきてしまった。

content.content: Here I thought I would take pictures for everyone, but I forgot the camera!

content: A:何を書いているの。

content.content: What are you writing?
B:できたら、読ませてあげる。
I’ll let you read it when it’s finished.

content: A:ごはん、もうできた？

content.content: Is the rice cooked?
B:まだ。できたら呼んであげるから、もう少し待ってて。
Not yet. I’ll call you when it’s ready, so just wait a little more.

Expresses that the speaker (or someone on the side of the speaker) is doing something for someone else. When the listener is the one receiving the favor, unless the listener and the speaker are socially equal as well as close, as in

content: , it will sound rude. In spoken language, the form is often changed to V-たげる, as in 話してあげる→話したげる or 読んであげる→読んだげる.

content.content: ...にV-てあげる cannot be used when the action relates to someone’s body parts or belongings, or when speaking directly to someone.
（×）おばあさんに手を引いてあげた。
I took the elderly woman’s hand and guided for her.
（○）おばあさんの手を引いてあげた。
I took the elderly woman’s hand and guided her.
（×）友達に荷物を持ってあげた。
I carried luggage for a friend.
（○）友達の荷物を持ってあげた。
I carried my friend’s luggage for him.
（×）キムさんに手伝ってあげた。
I helped for Kim-san.
（○）キムさんを手伝ってあげた。
I helped Kim-san.
2. V-てあげてくれ（ないか）V-てあげてください

content: ケーキを作りすぎたので、おばあさんに持っていってあげて下さい。

content.content: I baked too much cake, so please take some to your grandmother.

content: 太郎くん、今度の日曜日、暇だったら花子さんの引っ越しを手伝ってあげてくれない？　私、用事があってどうしても行けないのよ。

content.content: Taro-kun, if you’re free next Sunday, could you help Hanako-san move? I have something to do so there’s no way I can go.
Used when requesting someone to do something which will be beneficial to a third person. If the third person is someone whom the speaker represents, it is more natural to use ...てやってくれ／くれないか／ください.
【てある】［V-てある］

content: テーブルの上には花が飾ってある。

content.content: Flowers have been arranged on the tabletops.

content: A:辞書どこ？

content.content: Where is the dictionary?
B:辞書なら机の上においてあるだろ。
The dictionary? It should be on the desk.

content: 黒板に英語でGoodbye！と書いてあった。

content.content: It said “Good-bye” in English on the blackboard.

content: 窓が開けてあるのは空気を入れかえるためだ。

content.content: The window’s been left open to air out the room.

content: あしたの授業の予習はしてあるが、持っていくものはまだ確かめていない。

content.content: I have prepped for tomorrow’s class, but I haven’t checked what I have to take.

content: 起きてみると、もう朝食が作ってあった。

content.content: Breakfast had already been cooked when I got up.

content: 推薦状は準備してあるから、いつでも好きなときにとりにきてください。

content.content: The letter of recommendation is ready, so please come anytime to get it.

content: 電車の中に忘れたかさは、事務所に届けてあった。

content.content: The umbrella which I left on the train had been delivered to the business office.

content: ホテルの手配は、もうしてあるので心配ありません。

content.content: The hotel’s already been reserved, so there’s no worry.

content: パスポートはとってあったので、安心していたら、ビザも必要だということが分かった。

content.content: Because I had already gotten a passport, I felt relieved, but then I found out that I needed a visa, too.

content: その手紙は、カウンターにおかれてあった。

content.content: The letter was lying on the counter.

Uses a transitive verb to express that a situation exists as a result of someone’s action. In some cases, depending on the context, it can have the meaning “do something in preparation for the future.”

In this pattern, the semantic object of the verb becomes the subject and the person who has taken the action is often not expressed, but the existence of that person is implied. There is an expression 窓があいている, similar to 窓があけてある, but the former doesn’t imply an agent. In あけてある, the existence of the agent is felt even though it is not expressed, while this is not felt in あいている. In addition, when the passive is used, as in

content: , the existence of the agent is felt more strongly. Refer to

content.content: 【ておく】for the difference between てある and ておく.
【ていい】［N／Na　でいい］［A-くていい］［V-ていい］

content: この部屋にあるものは自由に使っていい。

content.content: Help yourself to anything in this room.

content: ちょっとこの辞書借りていいかしら。

content.content: May I borrow this dictionary?

content: 3000 円でいいから、貸してくれないか。

content.content: Can you lend me just 3,000 yen?
Expresses permission or concession. It is the same as ...てもいい (Usages 1 and 4), but ...ていい is used exclusively in spoken language.
【てもいい】1、
【てもいい】4
【ていく】
1. V-ていく〈manner at time of movement〉

content: 学校まで走っていこう。

content.content: Let’s run (all the way) to school.

content: 重いタイヤを転がしていった。

content.content: I rolled a heavy tire.

content: 時間がないからタクシーに乗って行きましょう。

content.content: We have no time, so let’s go by taxi.

content: トラックは急な坂道をゆっくり登っていった。

content.content: The truck climbed slowly up the steep road.
Expresses the method of going or what action is taken while going.
【てくる】
2. V-ていく〈movement away from something〉

content: あの子は、友達とけんかして、泣きながら帰っていった。

content.content: That kid had a fight with his friend and went home crying.

content: ブーメランは大きな弧を描いて彼のもとに戻って行きました。

content.content: The boomerang traced a large circle and returned to where he was.

content: 船はどんどん遠くに離れて行く。

content.content: The ship is going farther and farther away.
Expresses that something is going or moving away from the speaker.
3. V-ていく〈successive events〉

content: あと少しだからこの仕事をすませていきます。

content.content: There’s just a little more left to do, so I’ll finish this job and then go.

content: A:じゃ、失礼します。

content.content: I’ll leave now.
B:そんなこと言わないで、ぜひうちでご飯を食べていって下さいよ。
Don’t say that. Please eat with us and then leave.

content: 疲れたからここで休んで行くことにしましょう。

content.content: I’m tired, so let’s rest here and then go on.

content: 叔母の誕生日だから、途中でプレゼントに花を買って行きました。

content.content: Because it’s my aunt’s birthday, I bought some flowers on my way.
Means “going somewhere after doing a certain action.” Expresses a certain action done with the assumption of going somewhere, but the action has more weight than the subsequent act of going.
4. V-ていく〈duration〉

content: 結婚してからも仕事は続けていくつもりです。

content.content: I intend to continue working after I get married.

content: 今後もわが社の発展のために努力していくつもりだ。

content.content: We intend to continue making efforts for the development of our company.

content: 日本ではさらに子供の数が減少していくことが予想される。

content.content: It is expected that in Japan the number of children is going to decrease even more.

content: 見ている間にもどんどん雪がつもっていく。

content.content: The snow is accumulating more and more even as I watch it.

content: その映画で評判になって以来、彼女の人気は日増しに高まっていった。

content.content: Since becoming famous for that film, her popularity was increasing by the day.

content: 当分この土地で生活して行こうと思っている。

content.content: I’m thinking of living in this place for some time to come.
Expresses that a change is progressing or that an action is continuing beyond a certain point in time.
5. V-ていく〈disappearance〉

content: この学校では、毎年五百名の学生が卒業していく。

content.content: Five hundred students graduate from this school every year.

content: 見てごらん、虹がどんどん消えていくよ。

content.content: Look, the rainbow is disappearing little by little.

content: 小さいボートは木の葉のように渦の中に沈んでいった。

content.content: The small boat sank like a leaf into the whirlpool.

content: 毎日交通事故で多くの人が死んでいく。

content.content: Many people die in traffic accidents every day.

content: 仕事についても3ヶ月ぐらいで辞めていく人が多いので困っている。

content.content: It’s a problem because a lot of people quit work after only about three months.

content: 英語の単語を覚えようとしているが、覚えたはしから忘れていく。

content.content: I’m trying to memorize English vocabulary, but I forget it as soon as I learn it.
Expresses that something that existed has disappeared or become more distant from the speaker.
【ていけない】［V-ていけない］

content: この音楽を聞くたびに、別れた恋人のことが思い出されていけない。

content.content: Every time I listen to this music I can’t keep from remembering the girlfriend that I broke up with.

content: こんな光景を見ると涙がでていけない。

content.content: When I see such a scene, it makes me cry.

content: 最近若い人の言葉使いが気になっていけない。

content.content: I’ve just bothers me how young people use language recently.
Expresses that a certain feeling naturally occurs repeatedly but cannot be helped. A slightly old-fashioned expression, similar to ...てしかたがない in meaning.
【ていただく】This is a form in which いただく is attached to the verb te-form. おR-いただく and ごNいただく are similar but more polite expressions.
1. V-ていただく〈benefit〉

content: 友達のお父さんに、駅まで車で送っていただきました。

content.content: My friend’s father kindly drove me to the station.

content: 高野さんに教えていただいたんですが、この近くにいいマッサージ師がいるそうですね。

content.content: I was told by Takano-san that there is a good masseur in this area.

content: 会議の日程は、もう、山下さんから教えていただきました。

content.content: Yamashita-san has already explained to me the agenda for the meeting.

content: 《手紙》珍しいものをたくさんお送りいただき本当にありがとうございました。

content.content: 《in a letter》 Thank you so very much for sending many unusual things.

The humble form of ...てもらう. Expresses the meaning that someone does an action for the speaker or someone on the listener’s side. Usually implies that the recipient is aware of receiving a favor or benefit. に is normally used for the person who does the favor, but から may also be used if a transfer of information or things is being expressed.
2. V-ていただく〈instructions〉

content: まず、1階で受け付けをすませていただきます。それから3階の方にいらして下さい。

content.content: First of all, please complete the registration on the first floor, and then continue up to the third floor.

content: この書類に名前を書いていただきます。そして、ここに印鑑を押していただきます。

content.content: We will first ask you to write your name here. Then please stamp your seal here.
Used when giving polite instructions. Can only be used by the person giving instructions. Instead of V-ていただく, it often takes the form お／ご...いただく, as follows.
（例）3才以下のお子様はコンサート会場への入場をご遠慮いただきます。
We ask that children under three refrain from entering the concert venue.
（例）クレジットカードはご利用いただけません。
I’m afraid credit cards cannot be used.
3. V-ていただきたい

content: A:この次からは、間違えないでいただきたいですね。

content.content: After this, I should hope there won’t be any more mistakes.
B:はい、申し訳ございませんでした。
Yes, I’m terribly sorry.

content: この忙しいときにすみません、あした休ませていただきたいんですが...。

content.content: I’m sorry to ask at this busy time, but I’d like to have tomorrow off if I could.

content: すみません、もう少し席をつめていただきたいんですが。

content.content: Excuse me, could you put the chairs a little closer to each other?

A humble expression corresponding to ...てもらいたい. Used when describing something that one wants the listener to do. If used in the ...ていただきたい form, often expresses a strong demand, although the form itself is polite. The form ...ていただきたいのですが, where the sentence is not finished, is used when making a hesitant request.
4. V-ていただける〈request〉

content: A:ご注文のお品ですが、取り寄せますので、3日ほど待っていただけますか。

content.content: The goods you ordered need to be sent for, so could you wait for three days or so?
B:ええ、かまいません。
Yes, that’s no problem.

content: これ、贈り物にしたいんですが、包んでいただけますか。

content.content: I want to make this a gift—could you wrap it for me?

content: A:わたしも手伝いに来ますよ。

content.content: I’ll come and help, too.
B:そうですか。じゃあ、日曜日のお昼頃来ていただけますか。
Is that so? Well, could you come around lunchtime on Sunday?

content: タクシーがまだ来ませんので、あと5分ぐらい待っていただけませんか。

content.content: The taxi hasn’t arrived yet, so could you wait for five more minutes?

content: 先生、論文ができたんですが、ちょっと見ていただけませんか。

content.content: Sensei (Professor), my paper is finished, so may I ask you to look at it for me?

content: そのことはぜひ知りたいんです。もし何か詳しいことがわかったら、連絡していただけませんか。

content.content: I would really like to know about this. May I ask you to contact me if you learn of any details?

content: 5分ほど待っていただける？

content.content: Could you wait for five minutes or so?

content: こちらにいらしていただけない？

content.content: Would you come this way?

Expresses a polite request by using いただける, the potential form of いただく. いただけませんか is a somewhat more hesitant expression than いただけますか, and it is often used when you don’t think the listener would necessarily agree to the request. Examples

content: and
are used when a woman makes a friendly request in a refined manner of someone of the same status or below. お／ご...いただける, an even politer form, is also often used.

content.content: （例）修理に少し時間がかかっています。すみませんが、もう少々お待ちいただけないでしょうか。
The repairs are taking a little time. I’m sorry, but could you wait a little longer?
5. V-ていただけるとありがたいV-ていただけるとうれしい

content: A:私がやりましょう。

content.content: I’ll do it.
B:そうですか。そうしていただけると助かります。
Can you? That would be very helpful.

content: 一人では心細いんで、いっしょに行っていただけるとうれしいんですけれど。

content.content: It would be lonely by myself, so I’d be happy if you could go with me.

content: 《手紙》お返事がいただければ幸いです。

content.content: 《in a letter》 We would appreciate a reply.

Used with suppositional expressions such as ...ば, ...たら, ...と and describes a situation which will be favorable to the speaker if the listener takes the action. The speaker’s reaction is expressed by such phrases as ありがたい (grateful),うれしい (pleased), or 助かる (be saved trouble).
【ていはしまいか】［V-ていはしまいか］

content: 環境保護の運動が盛んになってきたが、本質的な問題を忘れていはしまいか。

content.content: There’s a lot of action on behalf of protecting the environment, but I wonder if people have forgotten the basic issues.

content: 娘はひとりで旅行にでかけたが、今頃言葉のわからない外国で苦労していはしまいかと気になる。

content.content: My daughter went on a trip by herself, and I’m worried that she might be having trouble now in a country where she doesn’t know the language.

content: 幼い子供は両親の家に預けてきたが、寂しくなって泣いていはしまいかと心配だ。

content.content: I left my young children at my parents’, but I’m worried they might be feeling lonely and crying.

content: はじめて報告レポートを書いたときは思わぬ間違いをしていはしまいかと、何度も見直したものである。

content.content: When I first wrote a report, I kept checking it, thinking I might have made an unexpected mistake.

content: 彼は、自分の書いた批評が彼女をおこらせていはしまいかと、おそるおそる挨拶した。

content.content: He greeted her with great hesitation, thinking that the review he had written might have angered her.
まい is a written expression for indicating negative supposition, and しまい is equivalent to しないだろう. The sentence as whole is more or less the same as ていないだろうか. For example,

content: expresses that the speaker thinks that his daughter is probably having a hard time abroad.

content.content: 【ている】In spoken Japanese, V-ている is often shortened to V-てる.
1. V-ている〈duration〉

content: 雨がざあざあ降っている。

content.content: It’s raining hard.

content: わたしは、手紙の来るのを待っている。

content.content: I’m waiting for a letter to arrive.

content: 子供たちが走っている。

content.content: Some children are running.

content: A:今、何してるの。

content.content: What are you doing right now?
B:お茶飲んでるところ。
I’m just having a cup of tea.

content: 五年前から、日本語を勉強している。

content.content: I’ve been studying Japanese for five years.

content: このテーマはもう三年も研究しているのに、まだ結果が出ない。

content.content: I’ve been researching this topic for three years already, but I still haven’t gotten any results.
With verbs that express an action or effect, ている indicates that the action/effect is in progress.

content: and

express actions that continue into the present from a point in the past. Note, however, that not all verbs indicate continuation of an action when used with ている. For example, in the sentence 彼はアメリカに行っている, 行く does not mean “He is on his way to the U.S.” but rather “He is now in the U.S.” See Usage

content.content: 2. V-ている〈result〉

content: 授業はもう始まっている。

content.content: The class has already started.

content: せんたくものはもう乾いている。

content.content: The laundry is already dry.

content: 彼女が着ている着物は高価なものだった。

content.content: The kimono she’s wearing was an expensive one.

content: その集まりには彼も来ていたそうだ。

content.content: I heard that he came to the meeting, too.

content: A:お母さんはいらっしゃいますか。

content.content: Is your mother home?
B:母はまだ帰っていません。
She’s not back yet.

content: 今5時だから、銀行は、もうしまっている。

content.content: It’s five o’clock now, so the bank is already closed.

content: 電灯のまわりで、たくさん虫が死んでいた。

content.content: There were a lot of dead bugs around the light.

content: A:あそこにいる人の名前を知っていますか。

content.content: Do you know the name of that person over there?
B:さあ、知りません。
Hmm, no, I don't.

content: 疲れていたので、そこで会った人のことはよく覚えていません。

content.content: I was tired, so I don't really remember much about the people I met there.

content: わたしが新聞を読むのはたいてい電車に乗っているときだ。

content.content: It’s when I’m riding the train that I usually read a newspaper.

content: 今はアパートに住んでいるが、いずれは一軒家に住みたいと思っている。

content.content: I live in an apartment now, but I think I’d like to live in a house someday.

content: このプリントを持っていない人は手を上げてください。

content.content: Anyone who doesn’t have this handout, please raise your hand.

content: 彼は今はあんなにふとっているが、若いころは、やせていたのだ。

content.content: He’s gotten that heavy now, but when he was young he used to be slim.

content: その家の有り様はひどいものだった。ドアは壊れているし、ガラスは全部割れているし、ゆかはあちこち穴があいていた。

content.content: The house was in terrible condition. The door was damaged, the windows were all broken, and there were holes in the floor everywhere.

Expresses a state that is the result of an action or effect. Verbs that express a change of state, such as 始まる(begin), 乾く(dry), あく(open/become empty), and 閉まる(close), have this meaning when used with ている, as do 行く(go), 来る(come), and 帰る(return). Verbs such as 知る(know), 持つ(have), and 住む(live) also express a state when followed by ている. These verbs do not usually express actions in progress. However, they can be used to express repetition, as in Usage
3. Some verbs, like 着る(wear), can be used to express either an action in progress or a resulting state, depending on the context.
3. V-ている〈repetition〉a. V-ている

content: 毎年、交通事故で多くの人が死んでいる。

content.content: Many people die in traffic accidents every year.

content: いま週に一回、エアロビクスのクラスに通っている。

content.content: I go to an aerobics class once a week now.

content: この病院 では毎日二十人の赤ちゃんが生まれている。

content.content: Twenty babies are born in this hospital every day.

content: いつもここで本を注文している。

content.content: I always order books here.

content: 戸田さんはデパートで働きながら、大学の夜間部へ行っているそうだ。

content.content: I heard that Toda-san goes to night classes at the university while working at a department store during the day.
Expresses that an action is repeated. There are cases when a person or a group of people repeats the same action many times, and cases when many people perform the same action one after another.
b. Nをしている

content: 彼は、トラックの運転手をしている。

content.content: He’s a truck driver.

content: わたしの父は、本屋をしている。

content.content: My father runs a bookstore.

content: 彼女は、以前、新聞記者をしていたが、今は主婦をしている。

content.content: She used to be a newspaper reporter, but now she’s a homemaker.

content: A:お仕事はなにをしていらっしゃいますか。

content.content: What sort of work do you do?
B:コンピューター関係の会社につとめています。
I work at a computer company.
When をしている follows a noun that describes an occupation, it indicates someone’s current job. Nをしていた indicates someone’s previous job.
4. V-ている〈experience〉

content: 調べてみると、彼はその会社を三か月前にやめていることがわかった。

content.content: When we checked, we found out that he had left the company three months earlier.

content: わたしは、十年前に一度ブラジルのこの町を訪れている。だから、この町を知らないわけではない。

content.content: I once visited this town in Brazil ten years ago. That’s why it’s not like I don’t know this town.

content: 記録をみると、彼は過去の大会で優勝している。

content.content: According to the records, he has won a tournament in the past.

content: 北海道にはもう3度行っている。

content.content: I’ve been to Hokkaido three times already.
Expresses recollection of a past event. Used when the past event is thought to be relevant to the present in some way.
5. V-ている〈completion〉a. V-ている

content: 子供が大学に入るころには、父親はもう定年退職しているだろう。

content.content: By the time the children go to college, their father will probably already have retired.

content: 遅刻した高田が会場に着いたときにはもう披露宴が始まっていた。

content.content: By the time Takada-san—who was running late—got to the venue, the wedding reception had already started.

content: 彼女が気づいたとき、彼はもう彼女の写真をとっていた。

content.content: By the time she noticed, he’d already taken her picture.
ている expresses a matter which will have been completed at a certain point in the future, and ていた expresses a matter that has already been completed in the past.
b. V-ていない

content: A:もう終わりましたか。

content.content: Have you finished it?
B:いいえ、まだ終わっていません。
No, not yet.

content: A:試験の結果を聞きましたか。

content.content: Have you heard the results of the examination?
B:いや、まだ聞いていません。
No, not yet.
C:わたしは、もう聞きました。
I have already heard them.

content: 卒業後の進路についてはまだはっきりとは決めていない。

content.content: I haven’t decided for sure what I’ll do after graduating.
Expresses that a movement or action has not yet come about. May be replaced in some cases by the まだV-ない form, as in まだ来ません, but such verbs are limited. More natural to use the form まだV-ていない.
6. V-ている〈state〉

content: ここから道はくねくね曲がっている。

content.content: The road curves a lot from here onwards.

content: 北のほうに高い山がそびえている。

content.content: A high mountain towers to the north.

content: 日本と大陸はかつてつながっていた。

content.content: Japan and the continent used to be linked.

content: 先がとがっている。

content.content: The tip is sharp.

content: 母と娘はよく似ている。

content.content: The mother and her daughter look very similar.

Expresses an unchanging situation. Verbs such as そびえる(rise/tower) and 似る(resemble) are usually only used in ている and ていた forms. When these verbs are followed by a noun, it is more natural to say, for example, 曲がった道 rather than 曲がっている道.
【ておく】［V-ておく］

content: このワインは冷たい方がいいから、飲むときまで冷蔵庫に入れておこう。

content.content: This wine is better chilled, so let’s keep it in the fridge until we’re ready to drink it.

content: 帰るとき窓は開けておいてください。

content.content: Please leave the window open when you leave.

content: その書類はあとで見ますから、そこに置いておいて下さい。

content.content: I’ll look at the document later, so please leave it there.

content: A:岡田教授にお目にかかりたいんですが。

content.content: I would like to see Professor Okada.
B:じゃあ、電話しておくよ。向こうの都合がつけば、来週にでも会えると思うよ。
Then I’ll call her. If she’s available, I think you can see her as soon as next week.

content: インドネシアへ行く前にインドネシア語を習っておくつもりだ。

content.content: Before I go to Indonesia, I intend to learn Indonesian.

content: よし子が遅れて来てもわかるように、伝言板に地図を書いておいた。

content.content: So that Yoshiko will know, even if she arrives late, I drew a map on the notice board.

ておく has the meaning of “taking an action and maintaining the situation which has come about as a result of such action.” Depending on the context, it can mean either a temporary measure or preparation for the future. ...てある also expresses preparation for the future. Apart from the structural difference,  ...ておく differs from ...てある in that the former expresses that the preparation has to take place while the latter expresses that the preparation has already been done. In spoken language, ...ておく becomes ...とく.
（例）お母さんに話しとくね。
I’ll let Mom know.
（例）ビール冷やしといてね。
Please chill the beer ahead of time.
【てから】
1. V-てから

content: 先に風呂に入ってから食事にしよう。

content.content: Let’s take a bath first and then have dinner.

content: 遊びに行くのは仕事が終わってからだ。

content.content: I go out to have fun after work finishes.

content: 日本に来てから経済の勉強を始めた。

content.content: I started studying economics after arriving in Japan.

content: 夏休みになってから一度も学校に行っていない。

content.content: I haven’t been to school even once since summer vacation started.

content: 今は昼休みですので、1時になってから来て下さい。

content.content: It’s the lunch break now, so please come after one o’clock.
Expresses that X is done before Y. In

content: , for example, it expresses the time sequence where 風呂に入る is done before 食事をする.

content.content: 2. V-てからでないとa. V-てからでないとV-ない

content: A:いっしょに帰ろうよ。

content.content: Let’s go back together.
B:この仕事が終わってからでないと帰れないんだ。
I can’t leave until I finish this job.

content: わが社では、社長の許可をもらってからでなければ何もできない。

content.content: In our company, we can’t do anything unless we first get permission from the president.

content: まずボタンを押して、次にレバーを引いて下さい。ボタンを押してからでなければ、レバーはうごきません。

content.content: Please push the button first, then pull the lever. The lever won’t move unless you push the button.

Patterns such as Xてからでないと／なければ／なかったらY express a condition X which has to be fulfilled in order to realize something Y. This means that Y can only be done after X is done. In some cases, expressions of time are used with it, as in the following examples.
（例）3日からでないとその仕事にはかかれない。
I can’t start the job unless it’s from the 3rd.
（例）1時からでなければ会議に出席できない。
I can’t attend the meeting unless it starts at one o’clock.
b. V-てからでないとV-る

content: A:あした、うちへ泊まりにおいでよ。

content.content: Come and stay over at my house tomorrow.
B:後で返事するよ。お母さんに聞いてからでないとおこられるから。
I’ll let you know later. If I don’t ask my mother first, she’ll get angry with me.

content: きちんと確かめてからでないと失敗するよ。

content.content: You will fail if you don’t check it properly first.
Patterns such as Xてからでないと／なければ／なかったら Y express that “if X is not done, then Y will happen.” Situation Y is usually something negative.
3. V-てからというもの（は）

content: 彼女は、学生時代には、なんとなくたよりない感じだったが、就職してからというもの見違えるようにしっかりした女性になった。

content.content: She gave the feeling of being unreliable in her student days, but now it’s hard to recognize her as the very dependable woman she’s become since she started working.

content: 彼は、その人に出会ってからというもの、人が変わったようにまじめになった。

content.content: Ever since he met that person, he has become very serious, as if his personality changed.

content: 70 才を過ぎても元気だったのに、去年つれあいをなくしてからというものは、別人のようになってしまった。

content.content: Here he was hale and hearty even after seventy, but after losing his better half last year, he’s become like a different person.
Means “triggered by an incident.” Used when expressing that a substantial change has taken place since such an incident. Has the feel of written language.
【てください】［V-てください］

content: 今週中に履歴書を出してください。

content.content: Please submit your CV by the end of this week.

content: 来週までにこの本を読んでおいてくださいね。

content.content: Please read this book by the end of next week, OK?

content: この薬は1日3回、毎食後に飲んでください。

content.content: Please take this medicine after each meal three times a day.

content: 授業はできるだけ遅刻しないでください。

content.content: Please make every effort not to be late for class.

content: 頼むから、邪魔しないでくださいよ。

content.content: I beg you not to disturb me.
Expresses requests or orders that something be done for the benefit of the speaker (or someone associated with the speaker).
This is more formal than V-てくれ but is only used when it is natural or expected for the listener to do the action. Used when addressing someone equal or junior in position or age.
【てくださる】くださる is attached to a verb te-form. There are other expressions that are even more polite, such as おR-くださる and ごNくださる.
1. V-てくださる〈benefit〉

content: 先生が論文をコピーしてくださった。

content.content: My teacher kindly photocopied the thesis for me.

content: 明日山田さんがわざわざうちまで来てくださることになった。

content.content: It was decided that Yamada-san would kindly come to my house tomorrow.

content: どうも今日はわざわざおいで下さってありがとうございました。

content.content: Thank you for coming all the way to see me today.

content: せっかくいろいろ計画して下さったのに、だめになってしまって申し訳ありません。

content.content: With all the trouble you took to make all sorts of plans, I am so sorry that they didn’t work out.

This is an expression which makes the person doing an action the subject, and it is used for expressing that the person does something for the benefit of the speaker or someone associated with the speaker. Used when the person doing the action is senior or not close to the speaker. The honorific form of V-てくれる.
2. V-てくださる〈request〉

content: ちょっとここで待っていてくださる？

content.content: (a woman speaking) Would you wait for me here for a moment?

content: いっしょに行ってくださらない？

content.content: (a woman speaking) Would you come with me?

content: ついでにこの手紙も出しておいて下さいますか。

content.content: Could you also mail this letter for me?

content: ちょっとこの書類、ミスがないかどうかチェックして下さいませんか。

content.content: Could I ask you to check that there is no mistake in this document?

This is an expression used to request someone to do something for the speaker or someone associated with the speaker. ...てくださいますか and ...てくださいませんか are even more polite than ...てください.  ...てくださる and ...てくださらない in

content: and
are used by women to make a request of someone subordinate or equal in a friendly and refined way.

content.content: 【てくる】
1. V-てくる〈manner at time of movement〉

content: ここまで走ってきた。

content.content: I ran all the way here.

content: 歩いて来たので汗をかいた。

content.content: I walked here, so I sweated.

content: バスは時間がかかるから、タクシーに乗って来て下さい。

content.content: The bus will take some time, so please come by taxi.
Expresses a method of traveling and an action undertaken while traveling.
2. V-てくる〈movement toward something or someone〉

content: 先月日本に帰ってきました。

content.content: I came back to Japan last month.

content: 頂上から戻ってくるのに1時間かかった。

content.content: It took an hour to come down from the summit.

content: 船はゆっくりとこちらに向かって来ます。

content.content: The ship is slowly approaching.

content: その物体はどんどん近づいて来た。

content.content: The object steadily drew near.
Expresses a situation in which a person or thing far away is approaching the speaker’s location.
3. V-てくる〈successive events〉

content: ちょっと切符を買ってきます。ここで待っていて下さい。

content.content: I’ll go and buy the ticket. Please wait here.

content: A:小川さんいらっしゃいますか。

content.content: Is Ogawa-san here?
B:隣の部屋です。すぐ呼んできますから、中に入ってお待ち下さい。
He’s in the next room. I’ll call him right away, so please wait inside.

content: A:どこに行くの？

content.content: Where are you going?
B:ちょっと友達のうちに遊びに行ってくる。
I’m going to visit a friend for a little while.

content: おそくなってごめんなさい。途中で本屋に寄ってきたものだから。

content.content: Sorry to be late. I popped into a bookshop on my way.

content: A:かさはどうしたの？

content.content: What happened to your umbrella?
B:あ、電車の中に忘れて来ちゃった。
Oh, dear. I’ve left it on the train.
Expresses doing an action before arriving somewhere.

content: to
mean “depart from the place where one is, conduct an action, and then return to the original location.”
and

mean “I’ve come to where I am, having conducted an action in another place.” Both can be expressed without using てくる, but てくる is used more often than not. This expression is used for linking what happened in another place to where the conversation is taking place.

content.content: 4. V-てくる〈duration〉

content: この伝統は5百年も続いてきたのだ。

content.content: This tradition has continued for five hundred years.

content: 17 歳のときからずっとこの店で働いてきました。

content.content: I have worked in this shop straight through since I was seventeen.

content: 今まで一生懸命頑張ってきたんだから、絶対に大丈夫だ。

content.content: You’ve been giving it your very best until now, so I’m sure you’ll be all right.

content: これまで先祖伝来の土地を守り続けてきたが、事業に失敗して手放さなければならなくなった。

content.content: I had watched over the land inherited from my ancestors until now, but I was forced to let it go because of a business failure.
Expresses that a change or an action has been continuing from the past to the present.
5. V-てくる〈emergence〉

content: 少しずつ霧が晴れて、山が見えてきた。

content.content: The fog is slowly clearing, and I can see the mountain now.

content: 雲の間から月が出てきた。

content.content: The moon appeared between the clouds.

content: 赤ちゃんの歯が生えてきた。

content.content: The baby’s teeth have started to come in.

content: 春になって木々が芽吹いてきた。

content.content: Spring has come and the leaves on the trees are coming out.
Expresses that something that didn’t exist or couldn’t be seen before has emerged. Conversely, ...ていく is used when the thing in question is disappearing.
6. V-てくる〈inception〉

content: 雨が降ってきた。

content.content: It’s starting to rain.

content: 最近少し太ってきた。

content.content: I’ve put on a little weight recently.

content: ずいぶん寒くなってきましたね。

content.content: It’s really gotten cold, hasn’t it?

content: このあいだ買ってあげたばかりのくつが、もうきつくなってきた。

content.content: Those shoes I bought you just the other day are already starting to pinch.

content: 問題がむずかしくて、頭が混乱してきた。

content.content: The question is so hard that I’m getting confused.
Expresses that a change is taking place.
7. V-てくる〈action directed toward speaker〉

content: 友達が結婚式の日取りを知らせてきた。

content.content: My friend let me know the date of the wedding.

content: 化粧品を買った客が苦情を言ってきた。

content.content: A customer who bought some cosmetics has made a complaint.

content: 急に犬がとびかかってきた。

content.content: A dog suddenly jumped on me.

content: 歩いていたら、知らない人が話しかけてきました。

content.content: I was walking when a stranger spoke to me.

content: 息子は勝手にスーツを買って、請求書を送りつけてきた。

content.content: My son bought a suit without asking, and then he sent me the bill.

This expresses that an action is conducted for the speaker or someone the speaker is focusing on. ...が is used for the person conducting the action, and ...に is used for the person on the receiving end of the action.
（例）山田さんが父に電話をかけてきた。
Yamada-san called my father.
When the agent of the action is an organization, such as a company, rather than an individual, ...から is sometimes used.
（例）会社から調査を依頼してきた。
The company has requested an investigation.
Some of these sentences may be rephrased in a passive sense, where the action happens to the subject, as in the following examples.
（例）山田さんから父に電話がかかってきた。
Father was called by Yamada-san.
（例）国の家族から衣類や食料が送られてきた。
I was sent things like clothes and food by my family back home.
In this case, ...から is used for the person conducting an action and ...に for the person on the receiving end of the action.
【てくれ】
1. V-てくれ

content: もう帰ってくれ。

content.content: Just leave, will you?

content: いいかげんにしてくれ。

content.content: Quit that right now!

content: 人前でそんなこと言うのはやめてくれよ。

content.content: Stop saying such things in front of other people.

content: こんなものは、どこかに捨ててきてくれ。

content.content: Just throw these things away somewhere.

This is a strong expression which is used to order someone to do an action for the speaker or someone associated with the speaker. Used when speaking to someone equal or junior. Women seldom use this expression.
2. V-ないでくれ

content: 冗談は言わないでくれよ。

content.content: Are you kidding me?

content: ここではたばこを吸わないでください。

content.content: Please don’t smoke here.

content: 見ないで！

content.content: Don’t look!

content: このことは絶対に外にはもらさないでいただけませんか。

content.content: Can I ask that you never let any of this matter out to anyone else?
Used in patterns such as V-ないでくれ, V-ないでもらえないか, and V-ないでください to request someone not to do the action indicated by V. Constructed by changing the V-て part of the V-てくれ form to a negative te-form.
Used in informal spoken language. Sometimes the latter half of the sentence is omitted, as in example

content: . V-ないでください（ませんか）／いただけませんか／いただけないでしょうか are the polite forms of the same expression. V-ないでほしい is also used.

content.content: 【てくれる】
1. V-てくれる〈benefit〉

content: 鈴木さんが自転車を修理してくれた。

content.content: Suzuki-san repaired the bicycle for me.

content: 誰もそのことを（私に）教えてくれなかった。

content.content: No one told me about it.

content: 母がイタリアを旅行したとき案内してくれたガイドさんは、日本語がとても上手だったらしい。

content.content: The tour conductor who guided my mother when she traveled  around Italy was apparently very fluent in Japanese.

content: 自転車がパンクして困っていたら、知らない人が手伝ってくれて、本当に助かった。

content.content: Just when I was in trouble as my bicycle got a flat tire, a stranger generously lent me a hand. That really helped me!

content: せっかく迎えに来てくれたのに、すれ違いになってしまってごめんなさい。

content.content: You took the trouble to come meet me and then we just missed each other—I’m sorry!

This is an expression which makes the person doing an action the subject, and it is used for expressing that the person does something for the benefit of the speaker or someone associated with the speaker. Used when the person conducts the action voluntarily. V-てもらうis often used if the action is conducted at the request of the speaker.

If only the verb is used instead of V-てくれる, the sentence will mean that the action was done for someone other than the speaker or someone associated with the speaker, so care is needed. For example, 鈴木さんが自転車を修理した means that Suzuki-san fixed a bicycle, and 鈴木さんが自転車を修理してくれた means “Suzuki-san fixed a bicycle for me.” If the speaker does not use the V-てくれる form, despite the fact that the action was done for his/her benefit, the sentence will sound odd.
（×）誰もそのことを私に教えなかった。
No one told me about it.
（○）誰もそのことを私に教えてくれなかった。
No one told me about it.
（×）おいしいリンゴを送って、ありがとう。
Sent delicious apples, thank you.
（○）おいしいリンゴを送ってくれて、ありがとう。
Thank you very much for sending me delicious apples.
This expression may also be used sarcastically, when a certain action causes the speaker an inconvenience or problem, as seen in the following example.
（例）大事な書類をどこかに置き忘れるなんて、まったく困ったことをしてくれたな。
You’ve certainly given me a lot of trouble by misplacing an important document somewhere!
2. V-てくれる〈request〉

content: この本、そこの棚に入れてくれる？

content.content: Can you put these books on the shelf there?

content: ちょっとこの荷物運んでくれないか？

content.content: (a man speaking) Hey, can you carry this luggage for me?

content: すみませんけど、ちょっと静かにしてくれませんか。今大事な用事で電話してるんです。

content.content: Sorry, could you be quiet? I’m in the middle of an important phone call.

content: もしよかったら、うちの子に英語を教えてくれないか？

content.content: Is there a chance you could teach my child English?

This is an expression to request an action for the speaker or someone associated with the speaker. The plain form is used towards a subordinate or someone equal and close. ...てくれないか  is used by men. ...てくれませんか creates a politer impression than ...てくれますか. Used when cautioning someone, as in example
3. V-てやってくれないか

content: 息子にもう少し勉強するように言ってやってくれ。

content.content: Can you tell my son to study a bit more?

content: 山田君に何か食べるものを作ってやってくれないか。

content.content: Can you maybe make something for Yamada-kun to eat?

Used when requesting the listener to conduct an action for a third person (someone other than the speaker and the listener). Used when the speaker, the listener, and the third person in question are close to one another and all are somehow associated with the speaker.
【てこそ】［V-てこそ］

content: 一人でやってこそ身につくのだから、むずかしくてもがんばってやりなさい。

content.content: Keep working on it, even if it’s hard, because it’s only by doing it yourself that you will learn.

content: この木は雨の少ない地方に植えてこそ価値がある。

content.content: It’s only worth planting this tree in areas with little rain.

content: 互いに助け合ってこそ本当の家族といえるのではないだろうか。

content.content: Isn’t it only by helping each other that you can be called a real family?

content: この問題は皆で話し合ってこそ意味がある。規則だけ急いで決めてしまうというやり方には反対だ。

content.content: This issue has meaning only if everyone discusses it together. I’m opposed to rushing to make decisions only about rules.

content: 今あなたがこうして普通に暮らせるのは、あの時のご両親の援助があってこそですよ。

content.content: The reason you can live normally now is only because of your parents’ support at that time.

In this expression, こそ is attached to the verb te-form for emphasis. A positive expression follows V-てこそ to express the meaning “only by doing ... does it become meaningful and render a good result.” When it expresses the reason for the positive result, as in example

content: , こそ can be replaced by ばこそ.

content.content: （例）ご両親の援助があればこそです。
It is completely owing to your parents’ support.
【てさしあげる】［V-てさしあげる］

content: 昨日は社長を車で家まで送ってさしあげた。

content.content: I took the president home by car yesterday.

content: A:あなた、お客様を駅までお見送りしてさしあげたら？

content.content: 《wife speaking to husband》Why don’t you take our guests to the station to see them off?
B:うん、そうだな。
OK, I’ll do that.

content: 田中さんをご存じないのなら、私の方から連絡してさしあげましょうか。

content.content: If you do not know Tanaka-san, shall I contact him for you?

Expresses that the speaker (or someone on the side of the speaker) does an action for other people. Often used when the person receiving the action is superior or equal to, but not close to, the speaker. sed to express, in a humble way, that the speaker does something for someone who is having problems or cannot do the action which the speaker can do. However, it can also give the impression of forcing something upon someone.
Thus, it is strange to use this form when directly addressing a higher-status person. When one does use it, it will sound impolite unless one avoids using the forms V-てさしあげます／ましょう, as in

content: , in order to soften the impression of forcing something upon someone. In polite speech, humble forms such as お送りした and ご連絡しましょうか are usually used.

content.content: 【てしかたがない】［Na でしかたがない］［A-くてしかたがない］［V-てしかたがない］

content: 公園で出会って以来、彼女のことが気になってしかたがない。

content.content: Ever since I met her in the park, I just can’t get her out of my mind.

content: この映画はみるたびに、涙が出てしかたがない。

content.content: I just can’t help tearing up every time I watch this movie.

content: 何とか仕事に集中しようとしているのだが、気が散ってしかたがない。

content.content: No matter how much I try to concentrate on my work, I just can’t keep my mind from wandering.

content: 毎日ひまでしかたがない。

content.content: I have too much time on my hands every day.

content: 試験に合格したので、うれしくてしかたがない。

content.content: I couldn’t contain myself after passing the examination.

content: 台風のせいで、あの山に登れなかったのが、今でも残念でしかたがない。

content.content: I still regret that I couldn’t climb that mountain because of a typhoon.

content: わたしが転職したのは、前の会社で働くのがいやでしかたがなかったからだ。

content.content: The reason I changed jobs was that I just couldn’t stand working at my previous company.

content: 田中さんは孫が可愛くて仕方がないらしい。

content.content: Apparently Tanaka-san dotes shamelessly on her grandchild.

Expresses an emotion or feeling arising naturally from a source beyond the control of the speaker. Often used to express an irrepressibly strong emotion. Usually preceded by an expression of emotion, feeling, or desire; use of words denoting an attribute or evaluation leads to awkward constructions.
（×）歌が下手で仕方がない。
Her singing can’t help but be poor.
（○）歌がとても下手だ。
Her singing is really poor.
In addition to directly expressing emotion or feeling, this construction can also be used in cases when a situation lies beyond the control of the speaker and results in problems or annoyance.
（例）最近うちの息子は口答えをしてしかたがないんです。
Recently our son has taken to talking back to us and we don’t know what to do.
（例）年のせいか物忘れをしてしかたがない。
It might just be age, but I’m getting awfully forgetful.
At times が is omitted, resulting in the construction ...てしかたない. In casual conversation, the form ...てしょうがない is also used. For the difference in meaning from てならない, refer to that section.
【てしまう】In casual spoken language, this often takes the form ...ちゃう, as in 言っちゃう and 来ちゃう.
1. V-てしまう〈completion〉

content: この本はもう読んでしまったから、あげます。

content.content: I’ve already finished reading this book, so I’ll give it to you.

content: A:でかけますよ。

content.content: I’m leaving.
B:ちょっと、この手紙を書いてしまうから、待ってください。
Umm, give me a little time to finish writing this letter.

content: この宿題をしてしまったら、遊びにいける。

content.content: I can go out and play after I’m finished this homework.

content: 仕事は、もう全部完成してしまった。

content.content: I’ve already finished all my work.

content: あの車は売ってしまったので、もうここにはない。

content.content: We’ve sold that car, so it’s not here anymore.

content: 雨の中を歩いて、かぜをひいてしまった。

content.content: I caught a cold from walking in the rain.

content: 朝早くから働いていたので、もうすっかり疲れてしまって、動けない。

content.content: I’ve been working since early this morning, so I’m completely exhausted and can’t move an inch.
Expresses completion of an action that is a process. When used with a verb that expresses a continuing action, as in

content: , its meaning is close to that of the R-おわる form. Depending on the meaning of the verb, V-てしまう may also express “ending up in a certain condition” (
and
means “was in the condition of having a cold.”

content.content: 2. V-てしまう〈strong feeling〉

content: 酔っ払って、ばかな事を言ってしまったと後悔している。

content.content: I regret saying something stupid when I was drunk.

content: 新しいカメラをうっかり水の中に落としてしまった。

content.content: I accidentally dropped my new camera into the water.

content: 電車の中にかさを忘れて来てしまった。

content.content: I forgot my umbrella on the train.

content: だまっているのはつらいから、本当のことを話してしまいたい。

content.content: It’s hard to keep quiet, so I want to tell the whole truth.

content: 知ってはいけないことを知ってしまった。

content.content: I found out something I had no business knowing.

content: 彼は、友達に嫌われてしまったと言う。

content.content: He says he is thoroughly disliked by his friends.

content: アルバイトの学生にやめられてしまって、困っている。

content.content: I’m in a real fix because my part-time student went and quit on me.
Used to express a variety of strong feelings, such as remorse and regret, depending on the context. Sometimes conveys the nuance of an irrevocable result.

content: and
show the usage of てしまう with the passive voice.

content.content: 3. V-てしまっていた

content: わたしが電話したときには、彼女はもう家を出てしまっていた。

content.content: When I telephoned, she had already left home.

content: 友達が手伝いに来たときには、ほとんどの荷造りは終わってしまっていた。

content.content: We were just about finished packing by the time my friend came to help.

content: 警察がかけつけたときには、犯人の乗った飛行機は離陸してしまっていた。

content.content: By the time the police arrived, the plane the criminal was on had already taken off.

Expresses the completion of an action at a point in the past. While ...ていた can be used, ...てしまっていた emphasizes the completed aspect of the action (i.e. “completely finished”) and/or conveys the nuance of an irrevocable result.
【てしょうがない】［A-くてしようがない］［V-てしょうがない］

content: 赤ちゃんが朝から泣いてしょうがない。

content.content: The baby has been crying his eyes out since morning.

content: このところ、疲れがたまっているのか、眠くてしょうがない。

content.content: It might be just tiredness, but I have been so sleepy these days.

content: バレーボールを始めたら、毎日おなかがすいてしょうがない。

content.content: I have been famished every day since starting volleyball.

content: 可愛いがっていた猫が死んで、悲しくてしょうがない。

content.content: I have been beside myself with grief since my beloved pet cat died.

content: 二度も、自転車を盗まれた。腹がたってしょうがない。

content.content: I’ve had my bicycle stolen twice. I am really seeing red!

content: うちの子は先生にほめられたのがうれしくてしょうがない様子だ。

content.content: Our child seems absolutely ecstatic after being commended by her teacher.
This is a casual, spoken-language form of ...てしかたがない, as well as a reduced form of ...てしようがない.
【てしかたがない】
【てたまらない】［Na でたまらない］［A-くてたまらない］

content: 今日は暑くてたまらない。

content.content: Today is so hot I can’t stand it.

content: この仕事はやめたくてたまらないが、事情があってやめられないのだ。

content.content: I want to quit this job more than anything, but there are reasons I just can’t.

content: 彼女に会いたくてたまらない。

content.content: I can’t wait to see her.

content: ショーウィンドーに飾ってあった帽子がほしくてたまらなかったから、もう一度その店に行ったんです。

content.content: There was a hat in the show window that I really wanted, so I went back to that store one more time.

content: はじめての海外旅行が中止になってしまった。残念でたまらない。

content.content: My first overseas trip has been canceled. I am so disappointed.

content: うちの子供は試合に負けたのがくやしくてたまらないようです。

content.content: It seems our child just can’t get over losing the game.
Expresses a strong feeling, sensation, or want on the part of the speaker. For example,

content: is similar to “It is really hot.” Has approximately the same meaning as てしかたがない. Comments concerning the condition of a third person are accompanied by ようだ, そうだ, or らしい, as in

content.content: 【てちょうだい】［V-てちょうだい］

content: 伸子さん、ちょっとここへ来てちょうだい。

content.content: Nobuko-san, come here for a minute, OK?

content: 彼女は「和雄さん、ちょっと見てちょうだい」と言って、わたしを窓のところへ連れて行った。

content.content: She said, “Kazuo-san, please just take a look,” and led me over to the window.

content: 「お願いだから、オートバイを乗り回すのはやめてちょうだい」と母に言われた。

content.content: My mother told me, “I just want you to stop riding around on your motorcycle.”

Used to make a request of someone. Usually used by women or children to people with whom they have a close relationship. Although it is not a rough or impolite expression, it is not used in formal situations.
【てっきり...とおもう】

content: 彼女がいろいろな結婚式場のパンフレットを持っているので、これはてっきり結婚するんだと思ってしまったんです。

content.content: She had all sorts of brochures of places for wedding receptions, so I was convinced she was going to get married.

content: 人が倒れていたので、てっきり事故だと思って駅員に知らせたんです。

content.content: I saw someone lying on the floor and was sure there had been an accident, so I went to tell the station staff.

content: 窓ガラスが割れていたので、これはてっきり泥棒だと思ったんです。

content.content: I saw the broken window and was sure there had been a robber.

content: てっきり怒られるものと思っていたが、反対にほめられたので、驚いた。

content.content: I expected him to be angry at me, so I was surprised to be praised instead.

Used to explain, after the fact, that the speaker believed something was really true, based on an assumption s/he had made on the grounds of a piece of evidence or reason. てっきり emphasizes the strength of the conviction. Often the assumption is actually mistaken. Can only be used for assumptions made in the past.
（×）てっきり帰ったと思っています。
I feel sure you had gone home.
（○）てっきり帰ったと思いました。
I felt sure you had gone home.
【てでも】［V-てでも］

content: どうしても留学したい。家を売ってでも行きたいと思った。

content.content: I was set on studying abroad. I even considered selling my house and going.

content: 彼女がもしいやだと言えば、引きずってでも病院へ連れて行くつもりだ。

content.content: If she were to refuse, I was ready to drag her to the hospital with me.

content: いざとなれば、会社をやめてでも、裁判で争うつもりだ。

content.content: Were the day to come, even if I quit my company, I still plan to fight it out in court.

content: 由起子はまだ熱が下がらないが、この試合だけは、這ってでも出たいと言っている。

content.content: Though Yukiko still had a temperature, she insisted that this was the one match she would play even if she had to crawl to it.

Used to indicate tough measures for dealing with a situation. Accompanied by expressions of strong intent or desire, it conveys a determination to accomplish something even by employing extreme measures.
【てならない】［Na でならない］［A-くてならない］［V-てならない］

content: 卒業できるかどうか、心配でならない。

content.content: I am beside myself with worry about whether or not I’ll be able to graduate.

content: 将来がどうなるか、不安でならない。

content.content: Thinking about the future gives me great concern.

content: 子供のころニンジンを食べるのがいやでならなかった。

content.content: When I was a child, having to eat carrots repulsed me.

content: あのコンサートに行き損ねたのが今でも残念でならない。

content.content: I will never stop regretting that we missed going to that concert.

content: 住み慣れたこの土地を離れるのがつらくてならない。

content.content: It is really painful for us to leave this place that has been our home for such a long time.

content: だまされてお金をとられたのがくやしくてならない。

content.content: I am so ticked off at getting cheated out of my money.

content: 青春時代を過ごした北海道の山々が思い出されてならない。

content.content: I can’t help recalling the mountains of Hokkaido, where I spent my youth.

content: きのうの英語の試験の結果が気になってならない。

content.content: The results of yesterday’s English exam are really bothering me.

content: 大切な試験に失敗してしまった。なぜもっと早くから勉強しておかなかったのかと悔やまれてならない。

content.content: I failed an important exam. I am filled with regret that I didn’t start studying sooner.

Expresses a feeling or state of emotion that is the natural outcome of a situation and beyond the control of the speaker. Often used to indicate a state of mind that cannot be suppressed, resulting in a highly emotional condition. てならない is preceded by words denoting emotion or feeling or desire. If words that refer to characteristics or evaluation are used, an awkward construction results.
（×）この本はつまらなくてならない。
This book can’t be anything but boring.
（○）この本はすごくつまらない。
This book is really boring.
Has essentially the same meaning as てしかたがない. One difference is that てならない is difficult to use with words that do not indicate emotion, feeling, or desire.
（×）赤ちゃんが朝から泣いてならない。
The baby has had to be crying since morning.
（○）赤ちゃんが朝から泣いてしかたがない。
The baby has been crying his eyes out since morning.
A somewhat old-fashioned expression that is most often used in written language.
【てのこと】［V-てのこと］

content: 彼が6年も留学できたのは、親の援助があってのことだ。

content.content: It is thanks to his parents’ support that he was able to study abroad for six years.

content: 彼は来年から喫茶店を経営するつもりだ。しかし、それも資金調達がうまく行ってのことだ。
