Also, when いただく and くださる are attached to honorific expressions such as おいでになる (to come/to be here) or Sino-Japanese verbs such as 来店する (to come to a shop), になって and して are usually omitted and the forms おいでいただけませんか／くださいませんか and ご来店いただけませんか／くださいませんか are used.
V-てくれないか forms are often pronounced with a rising intonation, and か can be omitted. In polite language, these forms can also be replaced by ...願えないか (lit. “can’t/couldn’t I ask...?”), as shown below.
（例）もう一度ご来店願えないでしょうか。
Could we ask you to come to our shop again?
3. V-ないか〈imperative〉

content: おい、待たないか。

content.content: Hey, can’t you wait?

content: だまらないか。

content.content: Can’t you shut up?

content: いい加減でやめないか。

content.content: It’s about time you stopped.

content: 早く起きないか。

content.content: Why don’t you get up now?

content: さっさと出かけないか。

content.content: Why don’t you hurry up and get going?
Used to order an interlocutor to take action immediately when s/he does not seem to be doing so. For instance,

content: means “Wait!” and
“Shut up.”

content.content: These expressions are similar to imperatives. However, because they are used in situations where an interlocutor is reluctant to take immediate action, they often convey the sense that the speaker is irritated or upset. V-ないか is pronounced with falling intonation in a demanding tone and does not have a polite form. It is used by male speakers.
4. ...ない（か）〈confirmation〉［N／Na　ではないか］［A-くないか］［V-ないか］

content: A:彼が犯人じゃないですか。

content.content: Isn’t he guilty?
B:そうかな。
We’ll see.

content: A:子供には無理じゃないですか。

content.content: Isn’t this impossible for a child?
B:大丈夫ですよ。
It should be all right.

content: A:君にはちょっと難しくない？

content.content: Isn’t this a bit difficult for you?
B:ええ、でもやってみます。
Yes, but I’ll try.

content: A:この部屋、変な匂いがしない？

content.content: Doesn’t this room smell strange?
B:うん、なんだかちょっと。
Yeah, a bit....

content: A:ちょっと駅から遠すぎませんか。

content.content: Isn’t it a little too far from the station?
B:そうですか。歩いて 15 分ぐらいですけど。
Do you think so? But it’s only about a fifteen-minute walk.

content: 彼の様子、ちょっと変だと思いませんか。

content.content: Don’t you think something about him looks a bit strange?

Used to ask the listener to confirm whether or not what the speaker is thinking is correct. Even though this pattern takes negative forms such as Xじゃないか (isn’t it X?), what the speaker wants to confirm is a positive state of affairs, Xである (it is X). When the listener agrees with what the speaker says, s/he responds with はい／うん、そうだ, and when the listener disagrees, s/he uses いいえ／いや、そうではない. When the speaker wants to confirm an event that has apparently already taken place, s/he uses the ta-form, as below.
（例）A:何か物音がしなかったか。
Didn’t you hear a noise?
B:いや、僕には何も聞こえなかったけど。
No, I didn’t hear anything.
（例）A:私に電話かかって来ませんでしたか。
Wasn’t there a phone call for me?
B:いいえ。
No, there wasn’t.
5. ...ない（か）〈mild assertion〉［N／Na　ではないか］［A-くないか］［V-ないか］

content: 彼が、東大に合格したなんて何かの間違いではないか。

content.content: Wasn’t it some kind of mistake that he passed the entrance exam for Tokyo University?

content: 最近の彼の言動はちょっと変じゃないか。

content.content: Don’t you think that lately he’s been behaving a little strangely?

content: このスープ、ちょっと、塩味が薄くない？

content.content: Doesn’t this soup need a little more salt?

content: やめといたほうがよくないか。

content.content: Wouldn’t it be better if you just let it drop?

content: そんなに働いたら病気にならないか。

content.content: Don’t you think that working so hard will make you sick?

Used to make a mild assertion of personal opinion. Conveys the speaker’s feeling that “I think this might be so” and is used to make an inconclusive statement that leaves room for a little doubt. As shown in

content: , the use of ...ないか often implies the speaker’s anxiety or concern.

content.content: ...ないか is often replaced by expressions implying conjecture or doubt, such as (の)ではないか, (の)ではないだろうか／(の)ではなかろうか／(の)ではあるまいか or ないかしら／ないかな. When talking about a past event, (では)なかったか is used, as illustrated below.
（例）昨日見かけた人、山田さんの奥さんじゃなかったか。
Wasn’t the person we saw yesterday Yamada-san’s wife?
In spoken Japanese, when ...ではないか attaches to a noun or a na-adjective it is usually replaced by じゃないか.
6. ...じゃないか→
【じゃないか1】、
【じゃないか2】
7. ...ではないか→
【ではないか1】、
【ではないか2】

【ないかしら】The ないかしら pattern consists of the negative form of an inflected word combined with かしら, which expresses a sense of uncertainty on the part of the speaker. It is used for both self-addressed questions and questions addressed to an interlocutor. In the past, ないかしら was conventionally used by female speakers. However, now it is infrequent, and ないかな is used instead.
1. ...ないかしら〈wish, desire〉［V-ない／V-れない  かしら］［V-てくれないかしら］

content: またあの人から手紙が来ないかしら。

content.content: I do hope I will receive a letter from him again.

content: お金持ちと結婚できないかしら。

content.content: I wish I could marry a rich man.

content: バス、すぐに来てくれないかしら。

content.content: I do hope the bus comes soon.

content: ちょっと手伝ってくれないかしら。

content.content: I wonder if you could help me for a moment.
When ないかしら is used with the negative form of an action verb, the negative form of the potential V-れる, or the pattern V-てくれない, it expresses the speaker’s hope or desire. When a sentence like

content: is directly addressed to a listener, it can be understood as a request from the speaker.

content.content: 2. ...ないかしら〈conjecture, concern〉［N／Na　ではないかしら］［A-くないかしら］［V-ないかしら］

content: 向こうからくる人、鈴木さんじゃないかしら。

content.content: Could that be Suzuki-san over there, walking this way?

content: この着物、私にはちょっと派手じゃないかしら。

content.content: I wonder if this kimono is a little too showy for me.

content: このご飯、ちょっとかたくないかしら。

content.content: I wonder if this rice isn’t a bit undercooked.

content: あんなに乱暴に扱ったらこわれないかしら。

content.content: I wonder if it might not break if it’s handled so roughly.

Expresses a conjecture, as in “I’m not absolutely sure, but it just might be so,” or a feeling of anxiety or concern, as in “I have the sense that/I’m worried about....” If the speaker is talking to him/herself, ないかしら functions as a self-addressed question, but if this expression is used to address a listener, it means “Don’t you think so?” and functions as an appeal for the listener’s judgment.

【ないかな】...ないかな consists of the negative form of an inflected word combined with かな, which expresses uncertainty on the part of the speaker. It is used for both self-addressed questions and questions addressed to others. Unlike かしら, ないかな can be used by both male and female speakers. However, since this expression is not polite language, when it is used to address others it should be used only with interlocutors who have a close relationship to the speaker.
1. ...かな（あ）〈wish, desire〉［V-ない／V-れない　かなあ］［V-てくれないかなあ］

content: 早く夏休みにならないかなあ。

content.content: I can’t wait for summer vacation.

content: 今夜いい夢が見られないかな。

content.content: I hope I’ll have a good dream tonight.

content: 息子が一流大学に入ってくれないかな。

content.content: I wish my son would enter a top-class university.

When ないかな takes the negative form of a verb referring to an action, a change of state, or existence, or the negative form of the potential V-れる, it means “I hope so” or “I wish it would happen.” Expresses the speaker’s hope, wish, or desire.
2. ...かな（あ）〈conjecture, concern〉［N／Na　ではないかなあ］［A-くないかなあ］［V-ないかなあ］

content: あの人、森田さんの奥さんじゃないかな。

content.content: I wonder if that person isn’t Morita-san’s wife.

content: 彼だったら大丈夫じゃないかな。

content.content: If it’s him, I guess he’ll be fine with it.

content: こっちのほうがよくないか。

content.content: Isn’t it better this way?

content: 子供にはちょっと難しすぎないかな。

content.content: Isn’t this a little bit too difficult for a child?

content: この靴、ちょっと小さくないかな。

content.content: I wonder if these shoes aren’t a bit small.

content: あんなことを言って、彼女怒っていないかな。

content.content: I wonder if she’s upset because I said such a thing to her.

When used with the negative form of a predicate, ...かな(あ) expresses a conjecture, like “I’m not completely sure, but it just might be so,” or a feeling of anxiety or concern, like “I’m concerned/I have the sense that....” If the speaker is talking to him/herself, ...かな(あ) functions as a self-addressed question, but if this expression is addressed to a listener, it means “don’t you think so?” and functions as an inquiry regarding the listener’s judgment.
【ないことはない】［V-ないことはない］

content: A:とても明日までには終わりそうにないんですけど...。

content.content: There doesn’t seem to be any way for me to finish this by tomorrow....
B:いや、やる気があればできないことはありませんよ。
Well, if you are motivated enough, it’s not impossible.

content: A:彼女は来ないんじゃないか。

content.content: She isn’t coming, is she?
B:来ないことはないと思うよ。遅れても必ず来ると言っていたから。
I don’t think she’s not coming. She said she’d come for sure, although she might be late.

content: A:1週間でできますか。

content.content: Can you do this in a week?
B:できないことはないですが、かなり頑張らないと難しいですね。
It’s not totally impossible, but unless I try really hard, it’ll be difficult.

content: A:行きたくないの？

content.content: Don’t you want to go?
B:行きたくないことはないけど、あまり気がすすまないんだ。
It’s not that I don’t want to go, but I can’t say I’m very enthusiastic about it.

ないことはない is used in response to a statement an interlocutor has made, either to deny the statement completely, with the meaning “that is not at all the case,” or to defer making a firm judgment, with the meaning “that is partly true/possible, but not necessarily 100% so.”

content: and
are instances of the former use, and
and
of the latter.

content.content: More precisely, in

content: B responds to A’s negative statement, which means “I can’t do this,” by saying, “it’s not impossible for you to do it,” implying that B thinks A actually can do it. On the other hand, in
, B’s response means “I can do it, but I won’t guarantee it,” which implies “there is a possibility that I can’t do it.”

content.content: The latter usage of ないことはない (above) can be rephrased as ないこともない. However, this is not possible for the former usage.
【ないこともない】［V-ないこともない］

content: よく考えてみれば、彼の言うことももっともだと思えないこともない。

content.content: If I think about it carefully, I can see that what he said wasn’t totally without reason.

content: 言われてみれば、確かにあのときの彼は様子がおかしかったという気がしないこともない。

content.content: Now that you mention it, I can’t deny that his behavior at the time seemed somewhat strange.

content: この会社は社長一人の意見で動いていると言えないこともない。

content.content: It wouldn’t be completely wrong to say that this company operates solely according to the opinion of the president.

ないこともない is a double negative expression that conveys the affirmative meaning  “there is such an aspect/possibility.” Means that although something is not completely X, it is possible to say that some aspect of it is X. Used when the speaker wants to withhold a firm judgment. Related expressions such as 言えなくもない (it wouldn’t be impossible to say...) and 気がしなくもない (not be without the sense that...) are often used.
【ないで】ないで is the te-form of a negated verb. It indicates the manner, situation, or circumstances in which the action or state referred to after ないで is realized.
1. V-ないで〈attendant circumstances〉

content: 息子は今朝もご飯を食べないで出かけた。

content.content: My son left the house again this morning without eating breakfast.

content: 彼女は一生結婚しないで独身を通した。

content.content: She didn’t marry, she remained single for her entire life.

content: 傘を持たないで出かけて雨に降られてしまった。

content.content: I went out without an umbrella and got rained on.

content: 予約しないで行ったら、満席で入れなかった。

content.content: I went without making a reservation, so I couldn’t get in because every seat was taken.

content: 歯を磨かないで寝てはいけません。

content.content: Don’t go to bed without brushing your teeth.
Followed by a main verb clause X, V-ないでhas the meaning of “do X without doing Y.” In written language, ...ずに is also used. Cannot be replaced by V-なくて.
2. V-ないで〈instead of〉

content: 親が来ないで子供が来た。

content.content: The child came, but not the parents.

content: ロンドンには行かないでパリとローマに行った。

content.content: Instead of London, I went to Paris and Rome.

content: 運動してもちっともやせないで、かえって体重が少し増えた。

content.content: Even though I’m working out, I’m not losing weight at all—instead I’ve gained a little.

content: 頑張っているのに成績はちっともよくならないで、むしろ下がってきている。

content.content: Even though I’m trying my best, my marks aren’t getting any better—if anything, they’re getting worse.

V-ないで is used to make a contrastive statement about two things. Means “do such-and-such instead of doing something else,” or “such-and-such happens instead of something else.” Often implies that what follows V-ないで is a result that contradicts the speaker’s expectation or anticipation. In written language, ...ずに is also used.

It is not impossible to replace V-ないで with V-なくて. However, なくて does not convey the contrastive meaning of 代わりに (instead of). Rather, it means that two situations or states of affairs have been realized at virtually the same time. Thus, when the speaker wants to express contrastive meaning, ないで must be used.
3. V-ないで〈cause〉

content: 子供がちっとも勉強しないで困っています。

content.content: I don’t know what to do, because my child isn’t studying at all.

content: やつが来ないで助かった。

content.content: I was relieved that the guy didn’t come.

content: 試験にパスできないでがっかりした。

content.content: I was disappointed because I couldn’t pass the exam.

content: 朝起きられないで授業に遅れた。

content.content: I was late for class because I couldn’t get up in the morning.

content: 大事故にならないでよかった。

content.content: I’m glad it didn’t turn into a big accident.
Means “because someone does not do X” or “because something does not happen.” Often followed by expressions that indicate an emotion or evaluation, such as 困った (didn’t know what to do) in

content: and 助かった (was relieved) in
, or expressions that present a chronological relationship between situations or events, as in
. In this usage, ないで can be replaced relatively freely by なくて.

content.content: 【ないである】［V-ないである］

content: 手紙は書いたけれど出さないである。

content.content: Although I wrote a letter, it still hasn’t been sent.

content: 頂き物のメロンがまだ手をつけないであるから、召し上がれ。

content.content: This melon, which we received as a gift, hasn’t been touched yet, so have some.

content: このことはまだ誰にも知らせないである。

content.content: I haven’t told this to anyone yet.

ないである means “leave something as it is, without doing X.” It is used in cases when people deliberately continue not to do something. The transitive verb in “transitive verb + てある” patterns such as 手紙はもう出してある (The letter has already been sent) is used in the negative form. The expression (せ)ずにある is more common than ないである.
【ないでいる】［V-ないでいる］

content: 昨日から何も食べないでいる。

content.content: I haven’t eaten anything since yesterday.

content: このことは夫にも話さないでいる。

content.content: I haven’t told this even to my husband.

content: 雨の日曜日は部屋から一歩も出ないでいた。

content.content: I didn’t set foot outside all day Sunday because it was raining.

content: 祖母は自分一人では起き上がることもできないでいる。

content.content: My grandmother is unable to get up by herself.

ないでいる means “remain in the same state, without doing (being able to do) X.” It can be replaced by ...(せ)ずにいる. The subject of a sentence with ないでいる must be a person or animal with feelings and/or intentions, so expressions such as the following are not acceptable:
（×）雨が降らないでいる。
The rain is still not falling.
【ないでおく】［V-ないでおく］

content: 時間がないので昼ご飯は食べないでおこう。

content.content: We’re running out of time, so let’s skip lunch.

content: 十分に残っているのでまだ注文しないでおいた。

content.content: We still have plenty, so I haven’t placed another order yet.

content: 他人がさわると分からなくなると思ったので、机の上は掃除しないでおきました。

content.content: I didn’t clean the desk because I thought you wouldn’t be able to find things if someone else moved them.
Means “intentionally leaving something as it is, without doing X,” for some sort of reason or purpose. It is also possible to say ...せずにおく.
【ないでくれ】

content: 危険なことはしないでくれよ。

content.content: Don’t do anything dangerous.

content: ここではたばこを吸わないでくれ。

content.content: Don’t smoke here.
【てくれ】2
【ないですむ】［V-ないですむ］

content: 道がすいていたので遅刻しないですんだ。

content.content: I wasn’t late, because there wasn’t much traffic on the road.

content: 電話で話が着いたので行かないですんだ。

content.content: I didn’t have to go, because we reached an agreement over the phone.

Means “it turns out to be all right not to do something that was previously planned,” or “something that was predicted can be avoided.” Used when an unfavorable situation or circumstance can be averted.
【ないではいられない】［V-ないではいられない］

content: こんな悲しい話を聞いたら、泣かないではいられない。

content.content: I can’t help but cry when I hear such a tragic story.

content: 言わないほうがよいことは分かっているが、話さないではいられなかった。

content.content: I know I shouldn’t have said anything, but I couldn’t help talking about it.

content: あの映画を見たら、誰だって感動しないではいられないだろう。

content.content: Anyone who sees that movie can’t help but be impressed by it.

content: 子供のことでは、日々悩まされないではいられない。

content.content: I can’t stop worrying about my child every single day.

This pattern attaches to the negative form of a verb and expresses the meaning that the subject cannot control him/herself by force of will but rather does something spontaneously, in spite of him/herself. Verbs that refer to a person’s actions or a change in someone’s thoughts or feelings are used, such as 泣く (cry), 思う (think) and 感動する (be impressed/moved by). This pattern implies that the speaker views the spontaneous response as natural. In written language, ...せずにはいられない can be used instead.
【ないではおかない】［V-ないではおかない］

content: この作品は読む者の胸を打たないではおかないだろう。

content.content: This piece cannot but move the reader’s heart.

content: 彼女の言動はどこか私を苛立たせないではおかないものがある。

content.content: There is something in her behavior that cannot but irritate me.

content: 彼女とのこと、白状させないではおかないぞ。

content.content: I’m not going to let you get off without confiding in me about your girlfriend.

Used after the negative form of a transitive verb or the negative causative form of an intransitive verb (V-させない). Expresses that a certain state or action will be brought about by a strong external force, regardless of the intention of the person concerned. Since this is essentially a written expression, it usually takes the form せずにはおかない.
【ないではすまない】［V-ないではすまない］

content: 知り合いに借りたキャンプ用のテントをひどく破ってしまった。新しいのを買って返さないではすまないだろう。

content.content: The camping tent I had borrowed from an acquaintance got badly torn. I’m not going to get away without buying a new one to replace it.

content: こんなひどいことをしたんでは、お母さんにしかられないではすまないよ。

content.content: You’re not going to get off without a talking-to from your mother, after doing such a terrible thing.

content: 罪もない人々にこのような過酷な運命を強いてしまった。いつの日にかその報いを受けないではすまないであろう。

content.content: I have forced a cruel fate on innocent people. There’s no way that I can avoid getting my just reward for this someday.
Used with the negative form of a verb, ないではすまない means that one has no choice but to take (or undergo) some action. For instance,

content: means that the speaker must buy a new tent, since s/he cannot return the torn one. ないではすまない usually conveys a negative evaluation of the situation in question and is a formal expression.

content.content: 【ないでもない】Used with the negative form of a verb or the negative adjective ない, ないでもない means that it isn’t possible to say that something never happens; on the contrary, there are times that it does occur or exist. ないこともない and なくもない are also used.
1. V-ないでもない

content: A:納豆はお好きですか。

content.content: Do you like nattoo (fermented soybeans)?
B:食べないでもないですが、あまり好きじゃありません。
It’s not that I avoid eating it, but I don’t like it very much.

content: A:ねえ、行きましょうよ。

content.content: Come on, let’s go.
B:そんなに言うなら行かないでもないけど。
If you’re going to insist, I guess I might go.

content: 自分にも悪い点があったことは認めないでもない。

content.content: I admit that I was wrong too, in some respects.

content: 考えてみれば、彼の意見ももっともだという気がしないでもない。

content.content: When I think about it, I can’t say that his opinion was completely without reason.

ないでもない is used with the negative form of a verb and means that a certain action or perception is to some extent possible. When used with verbs of thought or perception, such as 言う (say), 考える (think/consider), 思う (think), 認める (acknowledge), 感じる (feel), and 気がする (have the sense that), it means “to somehow have a feeling (that).”
2. Nがないでもない

content: 時には一人になりたいと思うことがないでもない。

content.content: I sometimes want to be alone.

content: 娘は、見合いで結婚するつもりがないでもないらしい。

content.content: It seems that my daughter is not completely against the idea of an arranged marriage.

content: 海外旅行をしたい気もないではないが、なかなかその時間がとれない。

content.content: It’s not that I don’t want to go abroad, but I just can’t seem to find the time for it.

Used mainly with nouns that refer to intentions or feelings. Means it would not be true to say that a person has no such intentions/feelings at all. When preceded by N +も, this expression can take the form Nもないではない, as in
【ないでもよい】［V-ないで（も）よい］

content: この欄には何も書かないでもよい。

content.content: You don’t need to write anything in this column.

content: 明日は来ないでいいですか。

content.content: Is it OK if I don’t come tomorrow?

content: そんなことは言わないでもいいじゃありませんか。

content.content: Isn’t something like that better left unsaid?

Means “need not do X” and functions in much the same way as V-なくてもいい. Can also be used in the form ないでいい, without も. In spoken language, なくてもいい is used more often than ないでもよい. -ずともよい is also used (e.g. 行かずともよい “you don’t need to go”), but this sounds old-fashioned.
【ないと】［N／Na　でないと］［A-くないと］［V-ないと］
1. ...ないと+マイナス評価の内容

content: 急がないと遅刻するよ。

content.content: Hurry up, or you’ll be late.

content: 勉強しないと怒られます。

content.content: If I don’t study, they get angry at me.

content: 注意しないと病気になるぞ。

content.content: If you aren’t careful, you’ll get sick, you know.

content: 東大合格はもう少し成績が良くないとむずかしいだろう。

content.content: It’ll be difficult for you to pass the entrance exam for Tokyo University unless your marks are a little better.

content: 早く来てくれないと困るよ。

content.content: I’m going to have a problem if you don’t come soon.

When ないと is combined with an expression in sentence-final position that conveys a negative evaluation, such as 遅刻する (be late) or むずかしい (be difficult), it means that something unfavorable will happen if a certain situation or state of affairs is not realized. Often used when the speaker wants to urge, encourage, or advise the listener to do the action expressed in the ...ないと clause.

content: 平均 70 点以上でないと合格できない。

content.content: You can’t pass without an average score of 70 or above.

content: 世の中の動きに敏感でないとすぐれた政治家にはなれない。

content.content: Unless you are sensitive to changes in society, you cannot be a great politician.

content: 背が高くないとファッションモデルにはなれない。

content.content: You can’t be a fashion model unless you’re tall.

content: 食べないと大きくなれないよ。

content.content: You won’t grow up to be big and strong if you don’t eat.

content: 早く出ないと間に合いませんよ。

content.content: Hurry up and go, or you won’t make it.

content: 気温が高くないとうまく発酵しない。

content.content: It doesn’t ferment well if the temperature isn’t high enough.

Means that if a certain situation or state of affairs is not realized, another situation or state of affairs will not be realized either. It is also possible to say なくては...ない or なければ...ない, but ないと...ない sounds more colloquial.
3. ...ないと　いけない／だめだ

content: 風邪を防ぐには十分な休養を取らないといけません。

content.content: To avoid catching a cold, you should get plenty of rest.

content: レッスンを休むときは、絶対連絡しないといけないよ。

content.content: You must let them know when you aren’t coming to class.

content: 映画はまずおもしろくないといけない。ほかの点は二の次だ。

content.content: Above all, a film must be interesting. Everything else is secondary.

content: こういう仕事は若い人でないとだめだ。山田君にやってもらおう。

content.content: This kind of job has to be done by someone young. Let’s get Yamada-kun to do it.
Means that something is necessary, essential, or obligatory. As shown in the example below, the second half of the clause (いけない or だめだ)  can be omitted.
（例）車はやっぱり頑丈でないとね。
At any rate, a car should be solidly built.
なくてはいけない and なければいけない can also be used, but ないといけない and だめだ sound more colloquial. It is also possible to say なくてはならない and なければならない, but there is no such form as ないとならない.
（×）早く行かないとならない。
It’ll be that I must go soon.
（○）早く行かなければならない。
I must go soon.
【なければ】2
【ないといい】［N／Na　でないといい］［A-くないといい］［V-ないといい］

content: あそこの奥さん、もうちょっとおしゃべりでないといいんだけど。

content.content: If only his wife wouldn’t talk quite so much.

content: 新しく配置される部局の仕事、あまり大変でないといいのだが。

content.content: I hope the job in the department I’ve been newly assigned to won’t be too hard.

content: これほど毎日忙しくないといいのだが。

content.content: I wish I weren’t so busy every day.

content: この世に試験なんかないといいのになあ。

content.content: I wish there were no such thing as exams in this world.

content: 雨にならないといいが。

content.content: I hope it doesn’t rain.

Combines with the negative form of a predicate and expresses the speaker’s hope or wish that a situation will not come about. Usually used when a situation or event has already happened, or when there is a risk or fear that it will happen. It is more natural to use softeners such as いいのに／が／けれど after this expression than it is to use it at the end of a sentence. It is also possible to say なければいい.
【ないともかぎらない】

content: 今日は父の命日だから、誰かが突然訪ねてこないともかぎらない。

content.content: Today is the anniversary of my father’s death, so there’s no guarantee there won’t be anyone stopping by unannounced.

content: 鍵を直しておかないと、また泥棒に入られないともかぎらない。

content.content: There is still a possibility that our house will be broken into again, unless we fix the lock.

content: 間違えないとも限らないので、もう一度確認した方がいい。

content.content: You should check it one more time, because you can never be sure you haven’t made a mistake.

content: 事故じゃないとも限らないし、ちょっと電話を入れてみた方がいいかもしれない。

content.content: It might well have been an accident, so maybe you should try to give them a call.

Means that something is not 100% certain. Often used to say that the listener should not complacently assume that nothing will happen but be prepared to take some kind of countermeasure. Usually attaches to negative-form expressions. However, いつ死ぬともかぎらない (below) is an exception. This is an idiomatic usage that takes an affirmative expression and means “no one knows when s/he is going to die.”
（例）人間いつ死ぬともかぎらないのだから、やりたいことはやりたい時にやった方がいい。
Since we don’t know when we’re going to die, we should do whatever we want, whenever we want.
【ないまでも】［V-ないまでも］

content: 毎日とは言わないまでも、週に2、3度は掃除をしようと思う。

content.content: I’m not saying every day, but I’d like to do the cleaning at least two or three times a week.

content: 絶対とは言えないまでも、成功する確率はかなり高いと思います。

content.content: Even though I cannot say it is definite, I think there is a fairly high probability that it will succeed.

content: 予習はしないまでも、せめて授業には出て来なさい。

content.content: Even if you haven’t prepared for it, you should at least come to class.

content: 授業を休むのなら直接教師に連絡しないまでも友達に伝言を頼むか何かすべきだと思う。

content.content: If you’re going to be absent from class, even if you can’t contact the teacher directly, you should at least ask a friend to give her a message or something.

Used with the negative form of a verb, ないまでも means “such a great extent is not necessarily expected, but at least this lesser extent is expected.” The first clause presents a situation or state of affairs of greater extent in terms of quantity or importance, followed by one of lesser extent in the second clause. As shown in

content: and

above, this expression is often used in the forms ...とは言わない／言えないまでも, in which case it means “one won’t/can’t ask that much, but at least this much is expected.” Expressions of obligation, such as すべきだ and ...た方がよい, or expressions of intention, command, or desire are used at the end of the sentence. V-ぬまでも conveys the same meaning but sounds more literary and formal.

content.content: 【ないものか】［V-ないもの（だろう）か］［V-れないもの（だろう）か］

content: この混雑は何とかならないものか。

content.content: Can’t anything be done about this congestion?

content: この橋が早く完成しないものか。

content.content: If only they would finish this bridge soon.

content: この状況をどうにかして打開できないものか。

content.content: I wish there were some way out of this predicament!

content: 私の力でこの人たちを助けてあげられないものだろうか。

content.content: Isn’t there some way that I could help these people?

Used with the negative form of a verb or the negative potential form V-れない, ないものか expresses the speaker’s strong hope that an action or change s/he wants will somehow be realized. This expression is often used with respect to situations that are difficult to realize. As shown in

content: , it sometimes takes the form ないものだろうか.

content.content: 【なお】
1. なお〈degree〉

content: あなたが来てくれればなお都合がよい。

content.content: If you could come, it would be even better.

content: 薬を飲んだのに、病状はなお悪化した。

content.content: Even though I took the medicine, my condition kept getting worse.

content: 祖父は老いてもなお精力的に仕事を続けている。

content.content: Even though my grandfather is getting old, he is still working energetically.

content: 退院するまでには、なお1週間ぐらい必要だ。

content.content: You still need another week before you can be released from the hospital.

content: 反対されるとなおやってみたくなる。

content.content: The more they oppose me, the more I want to do it.

Means that one thing has a comparatively higher degree of something than another, in which case it is similar to 一層 (all the more), もっと (further), さらに (still more), and そのうえ (on top of that). In other contexts, it means that the same situation continues as before, in which case it is similar to まだ (still/yet), 相変わらず (as usual), and 今もなお (still). When the first and second clauses contrast in meaning, as in

content: , the meaning of なお is close to that of かえって (instead/all the more).

content.content: 2. なお〈provisional clause〉

content: 入学希望者は期日までに、入学金を納入してください。なお、いったん納入された入学金は、いかなる場合にもお返しできませんので、ご了承ください。

content.content: Prospective students should pay the enrollment fee by the due date. Also, please note that once the enrollment fee has been paid, it is not refundable under any circumstances.

content: 毎月の第三水曜日を定例会議の日とします。なお、詳しい時間などは、1週間前までに文書でお知らせすることにします。

content.content: The day for the regular meeting will be the third Wednesday of every month. Note that further details, including the time, will be communicated in writing no later than one week in advance.

content: 参加希望者は葉書で申し込んでください。なお、希望者多数の場合は、先着順とさせていただきます。

content.content: Applicants are requested to register by postcard. Please also note that if the number of applicants exceeds the limit, selection will be made on a first-come-first-served basis.

content: 明日は、2、3年生の授業は休講になります。なお、4年生のみが対象の授業は、通常どおり行いますので注意してください。

content.content: Classes for second- and third-year students will be canceled tomorrow. However, please be aware that classes for fourth-year students will be held as usual.

Used to add a proviso, supplementary explanation, exception, or special case to a topic that has just been concluded, or to present a new topic that is not directly related to the previous sentence. As illustrated in

content: , when the sentence after なお adds information that is not consistent with the expectation created by the previous sentence, the meaning of なお is similar to that of ただし (but/however). なお is not used often in spoken Japanese. However, it is used often in posted notices, written announcements, explanatory notes in academic papers, and other written contexts.

content.content: 【なおす】
1. R-なおす〈volitional〉

content: 出版の際に論文の一部を書き直した。

content.content: I rewrote part of my thesis when I published it.

content: 俳優がセリフを間違えたため、同じ場面を3度も撮り直さなければならなかった。

content.content: Since the actor bungled his lines, we had to re-shoot the same scene three times over.

content: 答案をもう一度見直してください。

content.content: Please check your answers one more time.

content: 顔を洗って出直して来い。

content.content: Don’t come back till you’ve sorted yourself out. (lit. “Wash your face before you come back.”)

content: 一度はこの大学をやめようと思ったが、思い直して卒業まで頑張ることにした。

content.content: I was once tempted to leave this university, but then I thought better of it and decided to hang on till graduation.

When attached to the stem of a verb expressing an intentional action, なおす means to repeat an action that was done before. It is often used when the result of the previous action is considered unfavorable and the action is repeated in order to correct the original result. Except for a few cases such as 出る (leave/go out), なおす usually attaches to transitive verbs. Other examples include 言い直す (correct oneself/restate), 考え直す (think over/reconsider), し直す (do over again/try again), 立て直す (restore/rearrange),　建て直す (rebuild),　作り直す (reconstruct/remake),　練り直す (rework/revise), 飲み直す (go somewhere else for another round of drinks),　焼き直す (reheat/rework), and やり直す (do again/start over again).
2. R-なおす〈non-volitional〉

content: 今年になって景気が持ち直した。

content.content: The economy has rebounded since the beginning of this year.

content: 病人はだいぶ持ち直した。

content.content: The patient has recovered considerably.

content: 勇敢な態度を見て彼にほれ直した。

content.content: I fell in love with him all over again when I saw his courageous attitude.

content: 部長のことを見直した。

content.content: I have come to think better of our department head.

When なおす is attached to the stem of a non-volitional verb, which refers to a situation or state of affairs that does not involve any intentional action on the part of a person, it expresses the meaning of a spontaneous change for the better. For example, 持ち直す means that the economy

content: or a patient’s condition
improves.
and

mean that someone has newly recognized someone else’s merits and reassessed his/her overall value. A limited range of verbs can combine with なおす for this usage, including those in the examples above and also 気を取り直す (take heart/pull oneself together). This usage of なおす is different from Usage 1 (above) in that there is no intention on the part of the subject to amend or redo something.

content.content: 【なか】
1. Nのなか

content: 部屋の中にはだれがいるの。

content.content: Who’s in the room?

content: 他人の心の中は外からは見えない。

content.content: You can’t look inside somebody else’s mind.

content: 箱の中からバネ仕掛けの人形が飛び出した。

content.content: A spring-loaded doll popped out of the box.
Refers to the inside of certain spatial boundaries.
2. Nのなかで

content: 3人兄弟の中では、次男が一番優秀だ。

content.content: Of the three brothers, the second one is the most talented.

content: ワインとビールと日本酒の中で、ワインが一番好きだ。

content.content: Out of wine, beer and Japanese sake, I like wine the best.

content: この中で一番背が高い人はだれですか。

content.content: Who is the tallest person of all of those here?
Indicates the boundaries of comparison for three or more items. In some cases, as in

content: above, specific candidates for choice are listed using the pattern NとNとNの中で.

content.content: 3. ...なかを［Nのなかを］［A-いなかを］［V-るなかを］

content: 激しい雨の中をさまよった。

content.content: I roamed about in the heavy rain.

content: 雪が降る中を5時間もさまよい続けた。

content.content: I wandered around for five hours in the falling snow.

content: お忙しい中をご苦労様です。

content.content: Thank you for taking the time to help out.

content: 本日はお足元の悪い中をわざわざお出でいただき、まことに有り難うございます。

content.content: We really appreciate your coming all the way here today in such terrible weather.

The pattern ...中をexpresses the situation or circumstances in which the action subsequently referred to takes place. The second half of the sentence usually contains a verb of motion, such as 歩く (walk), さまよう (wander/roam) or 来る (come). Since なかを originally means “to move from one place to another,” as in the examples above, this usage is connected to the notion of “spatial boundaries” in Usage
1. Example

content: is interpreted to mean お忙しい中を(お出でくださり) (... (for coming) during such a busy time), but the phrase お出でくださり (for coming) is omitted. In
and
, なかを can be replaced by ところ.

content.content: 【ながす】［R-ながす］

content: このレポートは、何の調査もせずに、思いついたことを適当に書き流しているだけだ。

content.content: In this paper I’m just writing down anything that comes to mind, without doing any research.

content: 彼が着物を軽く着流した姿は、なかなか粋である。

content.content: He cuts a fine figure, wearing his kimono so casually.

content: ざっと読み流しただけですが、なかなか面白い本ですよ。

content.content: I just skimmed through it quickly, but it was really quite an interesting book.

content: 彼のいうことは聞き流しておいてください。

content.content: Please pay no attention to what he says.

content: 老政治家は検察の執拗な追及も軽く受け流している。

content.content: The old politician is effortlessly brushing off the prosecutor’s tenacious cross-examination.

When ながす is attached to a verb stem, it means that the action referred to by the verb is performed in an easy and relaxed manner, without a great deal of effort. If used to indicate a response to another person’s action, ながす means to dodge or evade that action without giving it serious consideration. 着流す in

content: means to wear a kimono casually, without putting on a hakama (a long pleated skirt worn over a kimono). It is often used in the noun form 着流し (casually dressed/in kimono with no hakama).

content.content: 【ながら】
1. R-ながら〈simultaneity〉

content: 音楽を聴きながら勉強や仕事をする人のことを「ながら族」という。

content.content: People who listen to music while studying or working are called nagarazoku.

content: その辺でお茶でも飲みながら話しましょう。

content.content: Let’s talk somewhere over a cup of tea or something.

content: 母は鼻歌を歌いながら夕飯の用意をしている。

content.content: My mother is humming a song while preparing dinner.

content: よそ見をしながら運転するのは危険です。

content.content: It’s dangerous to take your eyes off the road while driving.

content: 飛行機は黒煙をあげながら真っ逆さまに墜落して行った。

content.content: The airplane was trailing thick black smoke as it went into a nosedive.

content: 液体はぶくぶくとガスを発生させながら発酵を続けている。

content.content: The liquid is generating bubbles of gas as it continues to ferment.

Links two verbs in a sentence and expresses that two actions are proceeding concurrently. In this usage, the second verb presents the main action of the sentence, and the first verb (in the nagara clause) presents a secondary action that depicts the circumstances in which the main action is carried out. For instance, in

content: , “studying or working” is the main action, and it is accompanied by the action of “listening to music.” In the same way, the incorrect ながら sentence below means that the action of getting on the train and the action of reading the book were carried out simultaneously. It cannot be interpreted to mean that the subject was reading a book on the train.

content.content: （×）電車に乗りながら本を読んだ。
I read a book while I was boarding the train.
（○）電車に乗って本を読んだ。
I got on the train and read a book.
Both of the verbs must have the same subject (see incorrect example below), and in most cases they refer to the intentional actions of a person. However, as illustrated in

content: and
, in some cases the subject may be an airplane, a natural phenomenon, or something else capable of moving or changing by virtue of its own power.

content.content: （×）私は本を読みながら、彼はウイスキーを飲んだ。
While I was reading a book, he drank whiskey.
2. ...ながら〈appearance, manner〉［Nながら］［R-ながら］

content: いつもながら見事なお手並みですね。

content.content: Your work is marvelous, as always.

content: この清酒メーカーは、昔ながらの製法で日本酒をつくっている。

content.content: This refined sake maker uses the traditional method of manufacture.

content: 被害者は涙ながらに事件の状況を語った。

content.content: In tears, the victim related the circumstances of the incident.

content: 生まれながらのすぐれた才能に恵まれている。

content.content: She is gifted with a great natural talent.

content: この子は生まれながらにして優れた音楽的感性を備えている。

content.content: This child was born with exceptional musical sensibility.

When attached to a noun or the stem of some verbs, ながら expresses a state or situation that continues as it is without change. For instance, 生まれながら and 昔ながら mean “just as it is, ever since a certain time,” and these expressions are similar to 生まれつき (by nature) and 昔のまま (as it was before), respectively. 涙ながらに means “in a tearful state” and can be replaced by 涙を流して (weeping). Expressions that exemplify this usage are relatively fixed, and only a small number of words, including those in the examples above, can precede ながら.
3. ...ながら（も／に）〈adversative connective〉［N／Na　ながら］［A-いながら］［R-ながら］

content: このバイクは小型ながら馬力がある。

content.content: In spite of its small size, this motorbike has impressive horsepower.

content: 敵ながらあっぱれな態度であった。

content.content: Although he was my foe, I must admit he behaved admirably.

content: 子供ながらになかなかしっかりとした挨拶であった。

content.content: That was quite a good speech, for a child.

content: 残念ながら、結婚式には出席できません。

content.content: Unfortunately, I will not be able to attend the wedding.

content: 狭いながらもようやく自分の持ち家を手に入れることができた。

content.content: Cramped as it was, I was finally able to get my own home.

content: 何もかも知っていながら教えてくれない。

content.content: Even though he knows everything, he won’t tell me.

content: すぐ近くまで行きながら、結局実家には寄らずに帰って来た。

content.content: I was in my parents’ neighborhood, but I ended up coming home without dropping by.

content: 学生の身分でありながら、高級車で通学している。

content.content: Even though she’s a student, she travels to school in a luxury car.

content: 細々ながらも商売を続けている。

content.content: We’re continuing to run our business, although we’re just scraping by.

content: ゆっくりながらも作業は少しずつ進んでいる。

content.content: Although it’s going very slowly, the work is progressing little by little.

When ながら is attached to a noun, an i- or na-adjective, a verb stem, or an adverb (without と or に, in the case of adverbs that usually take these particles), it expresses the meaning of contradiction or opposition, similar to ...のに or ...けれども／が. It can also be combined with the particle も and used in the form ながらも. ながらに, as in

content: , sounds old-fashioned and is not normally used in colloquial speech. In this so-called “adversative” usage, ながら is usually preceded by a stative predicate. On the other hand, in Usage 1, which presents “parallel/simultaneous” actions, ながら must be preceded and followed by action verbs.

content.content: 4. ...とはいいながら→
【とはいいながら】
【なきゃ】

content: 早く行かなきゃ間にあわない。

content.content: I’ve got to hurry up or I won’t make it in time.

content: もう帰らなきゃ。

content.content: I have to leave now.
なきゃ is a casual way of saying なければ.
【なければ】
【なくしては】［Nなくしては］

content: 親の援助なくしてはとても一人で生活できない。

content.content: It’s impossible to live on my own without my parents’ support.

content: 無償の愛情なくしては子育ては苦痛でしかない。

content.content: Without unconditional love, raising children is nothing but pain.

content: 彼女のこの長年の努力なくしては全国大会の代表の座を勝ち取ることはできなかっただろう。

content.content: If it had not been for her many years of effort, she wouldn’t have been able to win the position of national conference representative.

content: 当事者同士の率直な意見交換なくしては問題解決への道のりは遠いと言わざるを得ない。

content.content: I have to say that the problem is far from being solved if the parties concerned will not honestly exchange views with each other.

content: 愛なくして何の人生か。

content.content: What is life without love?
Means “if N did not exist.” Expresses that, without N, something is difficult to do. Depending on the context, the particle は may be omitted.

content: is an idiomatic expression that means “if there is no love, then what is the meaning of life?” なくしては is a formal, written expression, and in spoken Japanese Nがなかったら is used instead.

content.content: 【なくちゃ】［N／Na　でなくちゃ］［A-くなくちゃ］［V-なくちゃ］

content: 勉強しなくちゃ怒られる。

content.content: I’ll really get it if I don’t study.

content: 早く帰らなくちゃ。

content.content: I’ve got to go home right away.
なくちゃ is a casual way of saying なくては.
【なくては】
【なくて】［Nがなくて］［N／Na　でなくて］［A-くなくて］［V-なくて］

content: 検査の結果、ガンでなくて安心した。

content.content: I was relieved to find out from the test results that I don’t have cancer.

content: 結婚した頃は、お金がなくて苦労した。

content.content: When we got married, we had no money so we had a really hard time.

content: 子供の体が丈夫でなくて大変だ。

content.content: I’m having a hard time because my child’s health is not very good.

content: 思ったより高くなくてほっとした。

content.content: I can breathe easily now, since it’s less expensive than I had expected.

content: ちっとも雨が降らなくて困っている。

content.content: We are in a bad way because it hasn’t rained a bit.

content: あいつが来なくて助かった。

content.content: I’m glad that guy didn’t come.

Means “since such-and-such did not happen/is not the case.” The clause that ends with なくて indicates the cause or reason for the situation or event described in the subsequent clause. The subsequent clause includes an expression describing the speaker’s emotion or evaluation, such as 安心する (be relieved), 困る (be in trouble/be at a loss), or 助かる (be saved some trouble).

However, なくて essentially indicates that the events or situations in the first and second clauses are realized simultaneously. Its main function is not to specify a cause or reason. Because of this, it often sounds unnatural if なくて is replaced by ないので or ないから (see examples above).
【なくては】［N／Na　でなくては］［A-くなくては］［V-なくては］

content: 我慢強い人でなくては彼女と付き合うのは難しい。

content.content: Unless you have the patience of a saint, it’s hard to get along with her.

content: どんなにお金があっても健康でなくては幸せだとは言えない。

content.content: No matter how much money you have, if you aren’t in good health, you can’t say you’re happy.

content: 成績がもっとよくなくてはこの大学への合格は無理だろう。

content.content: Without better grades, you probably won’t be able to pass the entrance exam for this university.

content: 彼がいなくては生きていけない。

content.content: I can’t live without him.

content: 聞いてみなくては分からない。

content.content: Unless you ask, you’ll never know.

content: もっと食べなくては大きくなれないよ。

content.content: You won’t grow up to be big and strong unless you eat more.

Used with the negative form of a verb or a negative expression such as 無理だ (impossible) or 難しい (difficult) at the end of the sentence. Has the meaning “unless X, Y is impossible.” Used when the speaker wants to say that realization of the situation or event expressed in the first clause is desirable or necessary. In many cases, なくては can be replaced by なかったら, なければ and/or ないと. In casual spoken language, N／Naじゃなくちゃ and A-くなくちゃ／V-なくちゃ are used instead.
【なくてはいけない】［N／Na　でなくてはいけない］［A-くなくてはいけない］［V-なくてはいけない］

content: 履歴書は自筆のものでなくてはいけない。

content.content: Your resume has to be handwritten.

content: 教師はどの生徒に対しても公正でなくてはならない。

content.content: Teachers have to be fair to every single student.

content: 家族が住むにはもう少し広くなくてはだめだ。

content.content: If a family is going to live here, it needs to be a little more spacious.

content: 目上の人と話す時はことばづかいに気をつけなくてはいけない。

content.content: You must be careful with the way you speak when you speak to a superior.

content: 家族のために働かなくてはならない。

content.content: I have to work for the sake of my family.

This expression takes the forms V-なくてはいけない／ならない／だめだ and means that generally it is “obligatory” or “necessary” to do a certain action or to be a certain way. In spoken Japanese, なくては may be contracted to なく(っ)ちゃ and the latter part いけない／ならない／だめだ may be omitted, as below.
（例）もっとまじめに勉強しなくちゃだめだよ。
You’ve got to study harder.
（例）もう行かなくちゃ。
I've gotta go now.
Regarding the difference between なくてはいけない and なくてはならない, see なければ (Usage 2).
【なくてはならない】→
【なければ】2
【なくてもいい】［N／Na　でなくてもいい］［A-くなくてもいい］［V-なくてもいい］

content: 時間はたっぷりあるから、そんなに急がなくてもいいですよ。

content.content: We have plenty of time, so there’s no need to rush.

content: 毎日でなくてもいいから、ときどき運動して下さい。

content.content: You don’t have to do it every day, but please get some exercise once in a while.

content: この染料はお湯で溶かすんだけど、温度はそんなに高くなくてもいいよ。すぐ溶けるから。

content.content: You dissolve this dye in hot water, but the temperature doesn’t have to be that high. It dissolves right away.

content: 仕事が忙しい場合は、無理して来なくてもいいですよ。

content.content: If you’re busy at work, please don’t feel obligated to come.
Means “it is not necessary to do X.” Can be replaced by なくてもかまわない or なくても大丈夫. In formal Japanese, なくともよい, a more formal expression, may be used instead.
【なくともよい】［N／Na　でなくともよい］［A-くなくともよい］［V-なくともよい］

content: 履歴書は自筆でなくともよい。ただし、その場合は最後に押印、署名のこと。

content.content: Your resume does not have to be handwritten. However, if it is not, it must be stamped and signed at the bottom.

content: 入学式には必ずしも父母同伴でなくともよい。

content.content: It is not necessary for parents to accompany students to the entrance ceremony.

content: 支柱の強度はそれほど強くなくともよい。

content.content: The pillar doesn’t have to be that strong.

content: 委任状を提出すれば、必ずしも本人が出席しなくともよい。

content.content: If a letter of proxy is submitted, the person in question does not necessarily have to attend.

Means “it is not necessary to do X.” This is a written expression that means the same as なくてもよい／いい, and in modern Japanese it is seldom used, except in formal situations. When combined with the verb する, it may also be used in the form せずともよい.
【なくもない】Attaches to a verb or an adjective and means that a certain thing is not entirely unfeasible, but sometimes exists or arises. It is also possible to say ないこともない and ないでもない.
1. V-なくもない

content: A:お酒は召し上がらないんですか。

content.content: Won’t you have a drink?
B:飲まなくもないんですが、あまり強くはありません。
It’s not that I never have any alcohol, but I’m not really that much of a drinker.

content: 時には転職することを考えなくもない。

content.content: I won’t deny that I sometimes think about changing jobs.

content: 日本語の会話は、日本に来てから少し上達したと言えなくもない。

content.content: I can say that my spoken Japanese has improved somewhat since I came to Japan.

content: 最近彼女は少し元気がないような気がしなくもない。

content.content: I have to admit that recently she seems to have less energy.

Means that a certain action or awareness may sometimes be realized. When used with verbs of thinking or perception, such as 言う (say), 考える (think), 思う (think/believe), 認める (acknowledge), 感じる (feel), or 気がする (have the sense that), it means that for some reason the speaker has a certain kind of feeling.
2. Nがなくもない

content: 再婚するつもりがなくもない。

content.content: I’m not saying that I won’t get married again.

content: あの人を恨む気持ちがなくもない。

content.content: I can’t say that I hold no grudge against her.

content: A:あの人まだ独身ですが、結婚するつもりがないのでしょうか。

content.content: He’s still single, but does that mean he has no intention of getting married?
B:その気もなくはないようですが、今のところは特にそんな様子はありませんね。
I wouldn’t say that he’s not interested at all, but at the moment there aren’t any indications that anything’s happening.

Used mainly with nouns expressing some kind of intention or feeling. Means it is not the case that the person in subject position has no such intention or feeling at all. When なくもない is preceded by N +も, the form Nもなくはない may be used instead, as in
【なけりゃ】［N／Na　でなけりゃ］［A-くなけりゃ］［V-くなけりゃ］

content: この仕事はあなたでなけりゃ勤まらない。

content.content: No one is equal to this job but you.

content: ころばなけりゃ勝てたのに。

content.content: You could have won if you hadn’t tripped.
なけりゃ is a casual way of saying なければ.
【なければ】
【なければ】［N／Na　でなければ］［A-くなければ］［V-なければ］When the verb する is used with this expression, it may take the form せねば, in addition to the usual form しなければ. In spoken Japanese, なけりゃ and/or なきゃ may also be used.
1. ...なければ...ない

content: この映画は成人でなければ見ることができない。

content.content: You can’t watch this movie unless you’re an adult.

content: 体がじょうぶでなければこの仕事はつとまらない。

content.content: You must have a strong physical constitution to carry out this task.

content: 私はワープロでなければ論文が書けない。

content.content: I can’t write an academic paper without a word processor.

content: 背が高くなければファッションモデルにはなれない。

content.content: You can’t be a fashion model unless you’re tall.

content: 安くなければ買わない。

content.content: I won’t buy it unless it’s inexpensive.

content: 勉強しなければ大学には入れない。

content.content: You can’t get into university unless you study hard.

content: 君が手伝ってくれなければこの仕事は完成しない。

content.content: I won’t be able to finish this job without your help.

なければ is used in combination with the negative form of a verb or a negative expression such as 無理だ (impossible/unreasonable) or むずかしい (difficult) at the end of the sentence. It means that when one situation or event is not realized, another situation or event is not realized either. It is also possible to say なくては...ない.
2. ...なければいけない...なければならない...なければだめだ

content: 教師は生徒に対して公平でなければならない。

content.content: Teachers have to be fair to students.

content: そろそろ帰らなければいけません。

content.content: It’s about time to go home.

content: もっと自分を大切にしなければだめですよ。

content.content: You’ve got to look out for yourself more.
Means that it is necessary, essential, or obligatory to be or do something. The second clause can be omitted, as below.
（例）もう 10 時だから、そろそろ帰らなければ。
It’s already ten o’clock, so I should head home pretty soon.
なければいけない can sometimes be replaced by なくてはいけない, なくてはならない, or なくてはだめだ. However, there are some differences between these expressions, as explained below.

なければならない and なくてはならない mean that it is obligatory or necessary to be or do something, in light of conventional social wisdom or the nature of the thing in question. These expressions are usually used to state widely-held views that all people have the obligation or need to do a certain thing. On the other hand, なければいけない and なくてはいけない are often used when particular circumstances oblige or necessitate a certain action. なければだめだ and なくてはだめだ are similar to なければいけない and なくてはいけない, but the first two are more colloquial in tone.
When なければ is replaced by ねば, and ならない by ならぬ, the result is a more formal expression usually used in written Japanese.
（例）人生には我慢せねばならぬこともある。
In life, there are some things that you must endure.
Also, ならん and いかん are sometimes used instead of ならない and いけない, respectively, but the former are colloquial forms that sound rather old-fashioned.
（例）優勝するには、もっと志気を高めなければならん。
We must boost the morale of the team in order to win.
（例）少しぐらいつらくても、我慢しなければいかんよ。
Even if things are a little difficult, you must be patient.
3. ...なければV-た

content: 彼が助けてくれなければこの本は完成しなかっただろう。

content.content: Without his help, this book would not have been completed.

content: 金目当てでなければ、彼女はあんな老人とは結婚しなかったに違いない。

content.content: I’m sure she wouldn’t have married such an old man if she hadn’t been after his money.

content: あの一言さえなければ別れることにはならなかったのに。

content.content: If I hadn’t said that one thing, I know we wouldn’t have broken up.

content: あのミスさえしていなければ合格できたはずなのに。

content.content: If I hadn’t made that mistake, I could have passed the exam.

content: 体がこんなに弱くなければ仕事が続けられたのに。

content.content: If my health were not so poor, I could have continued working.

Expresses the counter-factual meaning that if the circumstances had been different, there would also have been a different result. This pattern is often used in combination with sentence-final expressions such as だろう (I suppose), にちがいない (there is no doubt that...), はずだ (should be/do), and のに (I wish/if only...).
【なさい】［R-なさい］

content: うるさい。すこし静かにしなさい。

content.content: You’re making too much noise! Quiet down a little.

content: 明日も学校があるんだから、早く寝なさい。

content.content: Tomorrow is another school day, so hurry up and go to bed.

content: A:あいつ、本当に馬鹿なんだから。

content.content: That guy is a real idiot!
B:よしなさいよ。そんな言い方するの。
Cut it out! Don’t talk that way.

content: A:明日のパーティー、どうするの？

content.content: Are you going to the party tomorrow?
B:行こうかな。どうしようかな。
Hmm...I wonder. Should I go, or not?
A:迷ってないで、行きなさいよ。絶対おもしろいから。
Don’t think about it too much, just go! I’m sure it’ll be fun.

content: 《試験の問題》次の文を読んで、記号で答えなさい。

content.content: 《exam question》Read the following passage and answer the questions, using the symbols.

Indicates a command or instruction. Often used by people in supervisory positions. For instance, parents use it to address children, and teachers to address students. However, なさい can also be used between people with close relationships, such as family or friends, as shown in

content: and
is an expression of prohibition used to admonish the addressee regarding his words and actions, and
is a strong suggestion. なさい may also be used in the instructions for exam questions, as in

content.content: ごめんなさい (I’m sorry) is an expression of apology used between people with a close relationship. おやすみなさい (Good night/Sleep well) is a conventionalized expression used before going to bed.
【なさんな】［V-なさんな］

content: 風邪などひきなさんな。

content.content: Now, don’t catch a cold.

content: 大丈夫だから、そんなに心配しなさんな。

content.content: It will be all right, so don’t worry so much.

なさんな is a spoken language expression derived from the phrase なさるな, which consists of なさる, the honorific equivalent of the verb する (do), and the particle な, which expresses prohibition. なさんな means the same as するな (don’t do X).

なさんな can only be used between people with a close relationship. Older people use this expression, but it is seldom used by young people, who usually prefer expressions like 風邪をひくなよ (try not to catch a cold!) or 心配するなよ (don’t worry!). In situations that call for politer language, the pattern ...ないでください and its honorific forms are used, as in 心配しないで／ご心配なさらないで／ご心配にならないでください.
【なしでは...ない】［Nなしでは...ない］

content: あなたなしでは生きていけない。

content.content: I can’t live without you.

content: 辞書なしでは英語の新聞を読めない。

content.content: I can’t read an English newspaper without a dictionary.

content: 議長なしでは会議を始めるわけにはいかない。

content.content: We shouldn’t start the meeting without the chairperson.

content: 背広にネクタイなしではかっこうがつかない。

content.content: A suit without a tie doesn’t look right.

content: この会社で働くのに労働許可証なしでは困る。

content.content: If you want to work for this company, you have to have a labor permit.

なしでは... is followed by an expression of impossibility or negation at the end of the sentence and means “without a certain thing, someone cannot do X/has a big problem” or “N is absolutely necessary.” Variations of this pattern include Nが(い)なくては／(い)なければ...できない／困る.
【なしに】［Nなしに］

content: この山は冬は届け出なしに登山してはいけないことになっている。

content.content: This mountain is not to be climbed in winter without prior notification.

content: 断りなしに外泊したために、寮の規則で一週間ロビーの掃除をさせられた。

content.content: Because I stayed out overnight without permission, I had to clean the main foyer for a week, in accordance with dormitory regulations.

content: 前田さんは忙しい人だから約束なしに人と会ったりしないでしょう。

content.content: Since Maeda-san is a busy man, he probably doesn’t see people without an appointment.

content: 研究会では、前置きなしにいきなり本題に入らないように、皆にわかりやすい発表をこころがけてください。

content.content: At the research conference, don’t jump straight into the main topic without introduction; keep in mind that your presentation should be easy for everyone to follow.

content: 今度事務所に来たアルバイトの高校生はいい子なのだが、いつもあいさつなしに帰るので、いつ帰ったかわからなくて困る。

content.content: The new high school part-timer in our office is a good kid, but she always goes home without saying goodbye, so it’s a bit of a problem because we never know when she has left.

When used with action nouns such as 届け出 (notification) or 断り (permission), なしに means doing something without having done the action expressed by the noun. It is often used in the sense of “do X without doing Y, which should of course have been done in advance.”
When the noun is preceded by 何の, as in the example below, the particle も is inserted after the noun and Nなしに changes to 何のNもなしに.
（例）彼は何の連絡もなしに突然たずねてきて、金の無心をした。
He showed up all of a sudden without contacting me in advance and asked for money.
なしに is mainly a written expression. In spoken Japanese, しないで is used.
【なぜ...かというと】

content: なぜ遅刻したかというと、出かける前に電話がかかったからです。

content.content: The reason I was late is that I got a phone call right before I left home.

content: なぜ偏西風が吹くのかというと、地球が自転しているからだ。

content.content: The reason the westerlies blow is that the earth is rotating on its axis.

content: なぜアメリカに留学したかといえば、親戚がいるからです。

content.content: The reason I studied in the United States is that I have relatives there.

content: なぜあんなに勉強しているのかといえば、彼は弁護士資格をとるつもりなのです。

content.content: The reason he’s studying so hard is that he’s planning to get the qualifications he needs to become a lawyer.

This pattern takes the form なぜ...かというと or なぜ...かといえば and is used to explain the reason for a certain result or a current situation. なぜ is followed by a description of the result or situation, and the reason is stated in the subsequent clause.
This pattern is usually accompanied by the use of からだ (because/since) at the end of the sentence のだ (since/because) can also be used, as shown in
【なぜか】

content: 最近なぜか家族のことが気にかかってしかたがない。

content.content: I don’t know why, but my family has really been on my mind recently.

content: 彼は今日はなぜか元気がないようだ。

content.content: Somehow he just doesn’t seem like himself today.

content: だめだと思ってたのに、なぜか希望していた会社に採用されてしまった。

content.content: Even though I thought it was hopeless, for some reason I got hired by the company of my choice.
Expresses the feeling “I don’t know the cause or reason, but....” Often used when the speaker is describing something that contradicts his/her senses, intentions, or expectations.

なぜかというと...からだ

content.content: 【なぜかというと...からだ】

content: A:宇宙に行くとどうして物が落ちないのですか。

content.content: Why is it that objects don’t fall in outer space?
B:なぜかというと、地球の引力が働かなくなるからです。
It’s because the gravitational pull of the earth doesn’t work there.

content: 彼が犯人であるはずがない。なぜかというと、その時彼は私と一緒にいましたから。

content.content: He can’t be the perpetrator, because he was with me at the time.
Same as なぜかといえば...からだ．
【なぜかといえば...からだ】

なぜかといえば...からだ

content.content: 【なぜかといえば...からだ】

content: A:天気はなぜ西から東に変化して行くのでしょう。

content.content: Why does the weather change from west to east?
B:それはなぜかといえば、地球が自転しているからです。
It’s because the earth is rotating.

content: 彼は背広とネクタイを新調した。なぜかといえば、就職の面接がもうすぐあるからだ。

content.content: He’s gotten himself a brand-new suit and tie. It’s because he has a job interview coming up very soon.

Used to explain the cause or reason for the thing described in the previous sentence. なぜかといえば... is usually followed by からだ (because/since) at the end of the sentence, but ためだ (due to/because) can also be used instead. This pattern is often used to state the cause of a natural phenomenon or the reason for a judgment on the part of the speaker.
【なぜならば...からだ】

content: 原子力発電には反対です。なぜならば、絶対に安全だという保証がないからです。

content.content: I am opposed to nuclear power generation. The reason is that there is no guarantee that it’s absolutely safe.

content: 殿下のご結婚相手はまだ発表するわけにはいかない。なぜならば、正式な会議で決まってないからだ。

content.content: We cannot announce yet that she is going to marry His Imperial Highness. The reason is that it has not been decided at an official meeting.

content: 私は車は持たないで、タクシーを利用することにしている。なぜなら、タクシーなら、駐車場や維持費がかからず、結局安上がりだからである。

content.content: I use taxis rather than owning a car. This is because, with a taxi, there aren’t any parking or maintenance costs, so it’s cheaper in the long run.

なぜならば...からだ is used to explain the underlying circumstances or reason for what has been stated in the previous sentence. ば is sometimes omitted. This pattern tends to be used in written Japanese, or in spoken Japanese for formal situations. In daily conversation, it is more common to use なぜかというと／なぜかといえば...からだ.
【など】In casual speech, なんか is used instead of など.
1. ...などa. Nなど

content: ウェイトレスや皿洗いなどのアルバイトをして学費を貯めた。

content.content: I did part-time jobs like waitressing and dishwashing to save money for my school expenses.

content: A:このスーツに合うブラウスを探しているんですけど...。

content.content: I’m looking for a blouse that goes with this suit, but....
B:これなどいかがでしょうか。お似合いだと思いますよ。
How about something like this? I think it’ll look good on you.

content: デパートやスーパーなどの大きな店ができたために、小さな店は経営が苦しくなった。

content.content: Since large retailers like the department store and the supermarket were built, the small shops have found it hard to stay in business.
Used to present a few main examples out of a larger range of items. Implies that there are other similar items as well.
b. V-るなどする

content: ひげをそるなどして、もうすこし身だしなみに気を付けてほしい。

content.content: I wish you’d pay a little more attention to your personal appearance, including things like shaving.

content: 時には呼びつけて注意するなどしたのですが、あまり効き目はなかったようです。

content.content: Sometimes I did call her in and give her advice and whatever, but it doesn't seem to have been very effective.
Used to present a few main examples out of a larger range of actions. Implies that there are other similar actions as well.

content: 学校をやめるなどと言って、みんなを困らせている。

content.content: It’s a big headache for all of us because he’s saying things like he’s going to leave school.

content: 来年になれば景気が持ち直すから大丈夫などとのんきなことを言っている。

content.content: She’s making these casual comments, like everything will be all right next year since the economy is going to improve.

content: 東京で仕事を探すなどと言って、家を出たきり帰ってこない。

content.content: After he said he was going to find a job in Tokyo or whatever, he left home and hasn’t been back.

などと, followed by a verb of utterance such as 言う, is used to express the gist of something that someone has said. This pattern is used for quotation, but it implies that other similar things may also have been said.

content: あなたの顔など見たくない。

content.content: I don’t even want to look at you.

content: 私は嘘などつきませんよ。

content.content: I would never tell a lie.

content: 賛成するなどと言っていない。

content.content: I never said I would agree.

content: あんな男となどいっしょに働きたくない。

content.content: I don’t want to work with a guy like that.

content: そんなことで驚いたりなどしないさ。

content.content: I just wouldn’t be surprised by such a thing.

content: 別にあなたを非難してなどいませんよ。

content.content: I’m not blaming you or anything, you know.

content: こんな難しい問題が私のようなものになど解けるはずがありません。

content.content: I’m not at all the person to be able to answer such a difficult question.

content: こんな結果になるなどとは考えてもみませんでした。

content.content: I never thought it would come to something like this.

など attaches to a variety of constituents, including nouns, verbs, and noun + particle combinations, and is followed by a negative expression. This pattern expresses not only the negation of a certain thing, situation, or event but also the speaker’s feeling of contempt, modesty, surprise, etc. with respect to whatever is marked by など.
For instance,

content: simultaneously conveys the meaning that there is no way the speaker could ever answer such a difficult question and the sense that the speaker is humble and does not hold too high an opinion of him/herself.

content.content: 4. ...など...V-るものか

content: そんな馬鹿げた話などだれが信じるものか。

content.content: Who would ever swallow such a ridiculous story?

content: お前になど教えてやるものか。

content.content: Why would I ever tell someone like you?

content: あんなやつを助けてなどやるものか。

content.content: He’s the last guy I’d ever help!

content: これくらいの怪我でだれが死になどするものか。

content.content: No one ever died from such a minor injury!

content: 私の気持ちがあなたなどに分かるものですか。

content.content: How on earth would someone like you ever understand my feelings?

May be preceded by a variety of constituents, including nouns, verbs, and noun + particle combinations. Expresses a strong negation, as well as the speaker’s feeling that the person, thing, or situation marked by など is trivial and worthy only of contempt.
【なに...ない】
1. なにひとつ...ない

content: 家が貧しかったので、ほしいものはなにひとつ買ってもらえなかった。

content.content: Since my family was poor, my parents never once bought me anything that I wanted.

content: あの大地震でも、家の中のものはなにひとつ壊れなかった。

content.content: Even in that big earthquake, not a single thing in the house broke.

content: こんなに一生懸命工夫したのに、まともな作品は何一つ作れていない。

content.content: Even though I’ve tried one thing after another, I haven’t been able to create a single decent piece.

content: この店には、私が買いたいと思うものは何一つない。

content.content: There’s nothing I want to buy in this store.

content: 膨大な資料を調査してみたが、彼らの残した記録は何一つ見つからなかった。

content.content: I examined an enormous amount of material, but I couldn’t find even one record they had left behind.

content: みなさんにお伝えしなければならないような面白い事件は何一つ起こりませんでした。

content.content: Not one thing happened that was interesting enough for me to have to tell all of you about.

Expresses the emphatic denial of a certain thing or event, in the sense of “not...in the least” or “not...at all.” When used to refer to people, this expression takes the form だれひとり...ない (no one at all).
2. なに...ない

content: 彼は父から受け継いだ大きな家に住んで、なに不自由なく暮らしている。

content.content: He lives in a big house he inherited from his father, so he’s well-off and lacks for nothing.

content: この会は気のあった人たちの集まりだから、なに気兼ねなく自由に振る舞うことができる。

content.content: Since this is a gathering of people who get along well with each other, I can behave freely and without constraint.

content: 物質的には何不足ない生活をしているのだが、なぜか満たされない気持ちで日々を過ごしている。

content.content: Although I’m materially well-off and lack for nothing in daily life, somehow I spend every day with the feeling that I’m missing out on something.

content: 祖父は孫たちに囲まれて、何不自由ない満たされた老後を送っている。

content.content: My grandfather is living a fulfilling and comfortable retirement, surrounded by his grandchildren.
Used in fixed, idiomatic expressions such as なに不自由なく (in ease and comfort) or なに不自由ない (lacking for nothing). Expresses a condition of absolute satisfaction, with no inconvenience or insufficiency.
【なにか】
1. なにか〈things〉

content: 冷蔵庫に何か入っているから、お腹がすいたら食べなさい。

content.content: There’s something in the fridge, so when you get hungry, eat.

content: この穴は何かでふさいでおいたほうがいいでしょう。

content.content: We should probably cover this hole with something.

content: 何か質問はありませんか。

content.content: Do you have any questions?

content: 壁に何か堅いものがぶつかったようなあとがある。

content.content: There’s a mark on the wall where it looks like something hard hit it.

content: 私に何かお手伝いできることはありませんか。

content.content: Is there anything I can do to help?
Indicates a thing or event that cannot be referred to in definite terms. Often used adverbially, but can also be used with particles, as in なにかで (see

content: above), なにかが, and なにかを. In colloquial Japanese, なんか is used instead.

content.content: 2. なにか〈appearance〉

content: 彼の態度は何か不自然だ。

content.content: There’s something about his behavior that’s a little odd.

content: 彼女のことが何か気になってしかたがない。

content.content: I just can’t get her out of my mind.

content: この景色を見ているといつも何か寂しい気持ちになってくる。

content.content: This scenery always makes me feel a little melancholy.
Implies “I don’t know exactly why I feel this way, but for some reason I do.” In colloquial Japanese, なにか becomes なんか.
3. ...かなにか［N／V　かなにか］

content: コーヒーか何か飲みませんか。

content.content: Would you like some coffee or something?

content: はさみか何かありませんか。

content.content: Do you have scissors or something?

content: 石か何かの堅いもので殴られた。

content.content: I got hit with something hard, like a stone or something.

content: 吉田さんは、風邪をひいたか何かで会社を休んでいます。

content.content: Yoshida-san is off work because he has the flu or something.

...かなにか follows a noun or verb and is used to indicate a thing or event that cannot be referred to in definite terms, but is similar to the one indicated by the preceding noun or verb. Particles that follow Nかなにか, such as が and を, are often omitted. In colloquial Japanese, かなにか is replaced by かなんか.
4. Nやなにか

content: 休みの日は雑誌や何かを読んでのんびり過ごします。

content.content: I take it easy on my days off, reading magazines and other stuff.

content: かばんの中には洗面用具や何かの身の回り品が入っていた。

content.content: Inside the suitcase were toiletries and other personal effects.

content: A:何を盗まれたんですか。

content.content: What was stolen?
B:金庫は荒らされていなかったんですが、たんすの中の宝石や何かがなくなっています。
The safe wasn’t ransacked, but some jewelry and other things that were in my drawers are missing.

...やなにか attaches to a noun and is used to indicate a certain item and other things similar to that item. In contrast to Nかなにか, which means “a thing that is similar to N,” Nやなにか means that there is N and also other things similar to N. Nやなにか is usually followed by a particle. In colloquial Japanese, Nやなんか is used instead.
5. なにか〈cross-examination〉

content: それならなにか。この会社を辞めてもいいんだな。

content.content: And just what does that mean? You’re looking to quit this company, aren’t you?

content: 君はなにか、僕に責任があると言いたいのか。

content.content: So do you mean to say that I’m the one to blame for this?

なにか is uttered with a rising tone and used to press the addressee strongly for an explanation or answer. It often conveys a feeling of criticism or reproach on the part of the speaker. Male speakers use this expression in spoken Japanese to address others of equal or lower status.
【なにかしら】

content: なにかしらアルバイトをしているので、生活には困りません。

content.content: Because I do part-time work of one kind or another, I can make ends meet.

content: いつもなにかしらお噂を聞いております。

content.content: I have been hearing a lot about you.

content: 家のことがなにかしら気にかかったので、急いで帰ってきた。

content.content: Something worried me about my house, so I hurried back home.

content: 息子は最近なにかしら反抗的な態度を取る。

content.content: Recently my son has been rebelling against anything and everything.

Indicates a thing or event that cannot be described in definite terms. Also implies that there is not just a single thing or event, but many others as well. This expression originally comes from なにか知らぬ or なにか知らん (I don’t know what...).
【なにかと】
1. なにかと

content: なにかと雑用が多くてゆっくりできません。

content.content: There are lots of little things that have to be done, so I can’t take time off and relax.

content: 先生にはいつもなにかとお世話になっております。

content.content: Sensei (Professor), I am very grateful for all the things you do for me.

content: 駅の近くだと何かと便利です。

content.content: Living close to a station is convenient in many ways.

content: お引っ越ししたばかりでは何かとお忙しいことと存じます。

content.content: I am sure you must be busy with all sorts of things, since you’ve just moved.

content: 大勢の人間をまとめなければならないので何かと気苦労が多い。

content.content: I have a lot of worries of one kind or another because it’s my job to bring so many people together as a group.
Refers in a general way to a variety of unspecified things. Similar to いろいろと (various kinds of...) and あれやこれやと (this, that, and the other thing).
2. なにかというと

content: あの人はなにかと言うと文句ばかり言っている。

content.content: That person is always complaining about everything.

content: 母は何かと言うとその話を持ちだしてくる。

content.content: My mother drags this issue out whenever possible.

content: その先輩には何かと言うと意地悪をされた。

content.content: That senior student used to take every chance she could to be mean to me.
Means “every time there is an opportunity.” Followed by an expression referring to a person’s action and means that the action is always repeated. It is also possible to say なにかにつけて.
【なにかにつけて】

content: なにかにつけてその時のことが思い出される。

content.content: I always remember what happened at that time.

content: 叔父にはなにかにつけて相談にのってもらっている。

content.content: I always get advice from my uncle about everything.

content: 駅の近くだとなにかにつけて便利です。

content.content: It is convenient in many ways if you live near the station.

content: 彼はなにかにつけて私の悪口を言いふらしている。

content.content: He tells everyone bad things about me whenever he gets the chance.

Means “every time there is an opportunity” or “whenever possible.” Followed by an expression referring to an event or situation and means that the event is always repeated, or the situation always remains the same. It is also possible to say なにかというと.
【なにがなんでも】
1. なにがなんでも〈intensity, enthusiasm〉

content: あの人にはなにがなんでも負けたくない。

content.content: I don’t want to lose to that woman, no matter what.

content: この仕事は、なにがなんでも明日までに終わらせてもらわなければ困ります。

content.content: I need you to finish this work by tomorrow, at any cost; otherwise, it will be a real problem.

content: なにがなんでも彼女を説得して下さい。

content.content: Please persuade her, no matter what.

content: この取引は社運がかかっているんだから、何が何でも成功させなければならない。

content.content: The fortunes of our company are riding on this deal, so we have to make a success of it at any cost.

content: この試合に勝ちさえすればオリンピックに出場できる。何が何でも勝たなければならない。

content.content: If we can just win this game, we can go to the Olympics. No matter what, we’ve got to win!

なにがなんでも is followed by an expression of intention or request on the part of the speaker and indicates his/her eagerness to accomplish something, or to have someone else accomplish something, no matter what the circumstances. Similar to どんなことがあっても (no matter what) and 是非とも (at all costs).
2. なにがなんでも+マイナス評価表現〈criticism〉

content: この記事はなにがなんでもひどすぎる。

content.content: No matter how you look at it, this article is just too awful.

content: なにがなんでもそんな話は信じられない。

content.content: There’s just no way I can believe such a story.

content: なにがなんでもこんな小さな子供にその役は無理だ。

content.content: It’s simply impossible to ask a child this young to take on that role.

content: こんな短期間のうちに工事を終わらせろなんて、何が何でもできない相談です。

content.content: Asking us to finish the construction in such a short period of time is simply out of the question.

なにがなんでも is followed by an expression of criticism or warning and conveys the speaker’s feeling that censure is warranted, even though s/he understands that there are special circumstances involved. Similar to どんな理由があったにしても (no matter what the reason may be) and いくら何でも (whatever the circumstances).
【なにげない】［なにげないN］［なにげなくV］

content: 何気ないその一言が私の心をひどく傷つけた。

content.content: That offhand comment wounded me deeply.

content: 彼は、内心の動揺を隠して何気ない風を装っている。

content.content: He assumes an air of indifference while hiding his inner turmoil.

content: 彼は特に発言もせずに我々の意見に賛同しているように見えるが、実は、何気ない振りをしてこちらの出方をうかがっているだけなんだ。

content.content: He doesn’t voice any particular opinion and seems to support our views, but I know he’s just pretending to be unconcerned as he watches our every move.

content: 彼女は何気ない顔つきで、みんながびっくりするような発言を始めた。

content.content: With a nonchalant expression on her face, she began to make a statement that surprised everyone.

content: なにげなく窓の外を見ると、空に大きな虹が架かっていた。

content.content: When I casually glanced out of the window, I saw a big rainbow stretched across the sky.

content: なにげなく心に浮かんだ風景をキャンバスに描いてみた。

content.content: I painted on the canvas a picture of a scene that happened to come to mind.

content: 何気なく言った言葉が彼をひどく傷つけてしまった。

content.content: My casual remark hurt him deeply.

Describes a way of behaving without careful thought or deliberate intention. Depending on the context, it can mean “without thinking carefully,” “unconsciously,” or “casually.” When this expression is used adverbially, it may take the form なにげなしに, as well as なにげなく.
【なにしろ】

content: なにしろ彼は頭がいいから、私がどんなに頑張っても言い負かされてしまう。

content.content: After all, he is smart, so no matter how hard I try, I lose every argument.

content: なにしろ観光シーズンですからどのホテルも予約は取れないと思います。

content.content: At any rate, this is the tourist season, so I don’t think you’ll be able to get reservations at any hotel.

content: もっと早くお便りしようと思っていたのですが、なにしろ忙しくてゆっくり机に向かう暇もありませんでした。

content.content: I meant to write to you much earlier, but what with my busy schedule, I haven’t even had time to sit down at my desk.

content: どこにも異常はないかもしれないが、なにしろ大至急検査をしてみる必要がある。

content.content: There may be no problem anywhere, but still it’s necessary to do an examination as soon as possible.

Used to emphasize a certain thing, at least for the time being, while leaving various other possibilities aside. Often used to state the reason for something, in patterns such as なにしろ...から and なにしろ...て. Similar to なんにしても (in any case) and とにかく (anyway).
【なににもまして】

content: なににもまして健康が大切です。

content.content: Good health is more important than anything else.

content: あなたにお会いできたことがなににもまして嬉しく思いました。

content.content: What pleased me most was that I could see you.

content: なににもまして必要なのはこのプランを実行に移すことだ。

content.content: What is necessary above all is to put this plan into action.
Means “more than anything else” or “first and foremost.”
【なにも】
1. なにもa. なにも...ない

content: 外は暗くてなにも見えない。

content.content: It’s dark outside, so I can’t see anything.

content: かばんの中にはなにも入っていなかった。

content.content: There was nothing in the bag.

content: そのことについて、私は何も知りませんでした。

content.content: I didn’t know anything about that at all.

content: 作業は順調に進み、心配していたようなことは何も起こりませんでした。

content.content: The work went smoothly, and none of the things we had worried about ever happened.

Followed by an expression of negation or denial and means “not...at all” or “nothing...at all.” Used to talk about things, events, and animals other than human beings. For people, the pattern だれも...ない is used (no one...at all), and for places, it becomesどこも...ない (nowhere...at all).
b. なにも...ない

content: なにもみんなの前でそんなに恥ずかしい話をしなくてもいいでしょう。

content.content: You don’t have to tell such an embarrassing story in front of all of them!

content: 団体旅行で添乗員もいるのだから、なにもそんなに心配する必要はありませんよ。

content.content: It’s a group tour and there’s a guide, so there’s no need to be so concerned.

content: 彼らも悪気があって言ったことじゃないんだから、何もそんなに怒ることはないじゃないですか。

content.content: They didn’t mean to offend you by what they said, so there’s no reason for you to get so angry.

content: ちょっと注意されただけなのに、何もそんなに気にすることはないですよ。

content.content: There’s no reason for you to be so upset over just one little piece of advice.

content: 何もそこまで懇切丁寧に指導してあげる必要はありませんよ。彼らはもう十分に訓練を受けている人たちなんですから。
