content.content: As the key is hidden in a place so high that an adult can barely reach it on tiptoes, it cannot be taken by a child.
Used together with expressions of possibility, means “N which can barely/just narrowly ....” Used to express that “(It) is difficult but, somehow, (it) can just barely be done.”
【よかった】
1. V-てよかった

content: あ、雨だ。かさを持ってきてよかった。

content.content: Oh, it’s raining. I’m glad I brought my umbrella.

content: 財布、見つかってよかったですね。

content.content: I’m pleased that you found your wallet.

content: 今日はお天気になってよかった。おかげで予定どおり遠足に行ける。

content.content: It’s good that the weather turned out nice today. Thanks to that we can go on our trip as planned.

content: 友達もできたしいろんな経験もできたし、本当に日本に来てよかったと思っている。

content.content: Because I made friends and had a variety of experiences, I really am glad that I came to Japan.

content: あの映画、見に行かなくてよかったよ。全然おもしろくなかったんだって。

content.content: It’s good that you didn’t go to see that film. It really wasn’t any good.
Demonstrates the speaker’s positive evaluation that fact that the action denoted by the verb or an event has occurred is a good thing. よかった is in the past form but it demonstrates a current feeling.
2. V-ばよかったa. V-ばよかった

content: しまった。あいつの電話番号をメモしておけばよかった。

content.content: Damn it! I wish I’d made a note of that guy’s telephone number.

content: あの服、買っておけばよかった。もう売り切れてしまったんだって。

content.content: I wish I’d bought those clothes. They say they’ve already sold out.

content: 野菜がしなびている。冷蔵庫に入れておいたらよかった。

content.content: The vegetables are wilting. I should have put them in the refrigerator.

content: 一人で悩んでいないで、もっと早く相談しに来ればよかった。

content.content: Instead of worrying by myself, I wish I had come for consultation sooner.

content: 田中さんも誘ってあげたらよかったね。

content.content: We should have invited Tanaka-san too, shouldn’t we?
In the forms V-ばよかった and V-たらよかった, this expresses a feeling of regret that something which was not done ought to have been.
b. V-なければよかった

content: こんな服、買わなければよかった。派手すぎてとても着られない。

content.content: I shouldn’t have bought these clothes. They’re too gaudy for me to wear.

content: こんなごちそうが出るんなら、さっき間食しなければよかった。

content.content: I shouldn’t have been snacking before such a feast.

content: あいつ、彼女が結婚することを知らなかったのか。それなら言わなかったらよかった。

content.content: Didn’t he know she was getting married? If that’s the case, I wish I hadn’t said anything.

content: きのうはあんなに飲まなければよかった。二日酔いで頭が痛い。

content.content: I wish I hadn’t drunk so much yesterday. My head hurts with the hangover.
In the forms V-なければよかった and V-なかったらよかった, expresses the speaker’s feelings of regret at having done something they didn’t ought to have.
3. V-ばよかったのにa. V-ばよかったのに

content: 昨日のパーティーにあなたも来ればよかったのに。楽しかったよ。

content.content: You should have come to the party yesterday. It was fun.

content: そんなにやりたくないのなら「いやだ」と言えばよかったのに。

content.content: If you didn’t want to do it so much, you should have just said “no.”

content: 今日花子も誘ったらよかったのに。あの人このごろ暇だって言ってたよ。

content.content: You ought to have invited Hanako too today. She said she has been free recently.

content: 田中じゃなくて君が立候補したらよかったのに。田中じゃたぶん勝てないよ。

content.content: You ought to have announced your candidacy, not Tanaka. Tanaka probably won’t win.

content: 行きたくなかったのなら、断ればよかったのに。

content.content: If you didn’t want to go, you should have refused.
In the forms V-ばよかったのに and V-たらよかったのに, expresses the speaker’s feelings of disappointment and criticism at something the listener did not do in reality but ought to have done.
b. V-なければよかったのに

content: そんなこと言わなければよかったのに。

content.content: You didn’t ought to have said such a thing.

content: あんな人に会いに行かなければよかったのに。

content.content: You shouldn’t have gone to meet such a person.

content: 風邪をひいているのなら、スキーなんかしなかったらよかったのに。

content.content: If you had caught a cold, you shouldn’t have gone skiing.
In the forms V-なければよかったのに and V-なかったらよかったのに, expresses the speaker’s feelings of disappointment and criticism at something the listener has done but didn’t ought to have.
【よかろう】

content: のんびりしたいのなら、観光地に行くよりは温泉の方がよかろう。

content.content: If you want to relax, rather than going to a sightseeing area, it would be better to go to a hot spring.

content: どうせみんな時間どおりには集まらないのだから、少しぐらい遅れて行ってもよかろう。

content.content: Anyhow, as everyone will not assemble on time, I suppose it would be okay for us to go a little late.

content: 医者には止められているが、少々ならよかろうと思ってビールを1杯飲んだのが間違いだった。

content.content: I was stopped by the doctor but, thinking just a little would be okay, I made the mistake of drinking a glass of beer.

content: どうせすぐに戻ってくるんだから、車はここに止めておけばよかろう。

content.content: I’ll be back straight away and so I suppose it’s okay to leave the car here.

content: 荷物を運ぶのは若い者に任せたらよかろう。

content.content: It’s better to leave carrying the luggage to the youngsters.

content: どうしても行きたければアマゾンでもどこでも行くがよかろう。ただし、何が起こっても私は知らないぞ。

content.content: If you really want to go, it doesn’t matter if you go to the Amazon or anywhere but, whatever happens, I know nothing about it.
This, like いいだろう and かまわないだろう is a conjectural form of よい. As in example

content: , it can be used to give permission in the form ...がよかろう. In speech it is rarely used by young people.

content.content: 【よぎなくさせる】→
【をよぎなくさせる】
【よぎなくされる】→
【をよぎなくされる】
【よく】
1. よく〈frequency〉

content: 彼はこの店によく来る。

content.content: He often comes to this store.

content: 私は仕事でよく中国へ行くが、まだ一度も万里の長城に行ったことがない。

content.content: I often go to China with my job but I still haven’t been to the Great Wall.

content: 若い頃はよく一人で貧乏旅行をしたものだ。

content.content: I often took cheap trips by myself when I was young.
Shows that the frequency of something is high. Means frequently or incessantly.
2. よく〈degree〉

content: 最近よく眠れなくて困っている。

content.content: Recently I’m being troubled by not sleeping well.

content: おやつは手をよく洗ってから食べるのよ。

content.content: Wash your hands well before you eat your snacks.

content: 次の文章をよく読んで問題に答えなさい。

content.content: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions.

content: 《試合の後で監督が選手に》みんな、よくやった。

content.content: 《a coach to the players after a match》Well done everyone.

content: 《山の頂上まで登った人に》よくがんばったね。

content.content: 《to someone who has climbed to the top of a mountain》Great effort.
Shows that the degree of something is sufficient. Means sufficiently or satisfactorily. Also, as in examples

content: and
, used to praise the satisfactory efforts someone has made in order to achieve a difficult thing.

content.content: 3. よく（ぞ）〈deep emotion〉

content: よくいらっしゃいました。

content.content: I’m glad you could come.

content: そんな大事な秘密をよく私に話してくださいました。

content.content: Thank you for confiding and sharing such an important matter with me.

content: 本当にみんな、こんな夜遅くまでよく働いてくれたね。ありがとう。

content.content: Really, you’ve all worked so hard until late tonight. Thank you.

content: こんなに遠いところまでよくぞいらして下さいました。

content.content: Thank you for coming to such a faraway place.
Expresses the speaker’s deep emotion and happiness that something great has been done especially for them. Often used with てくれる.
4. よく（も）〈surprise〉

content: おじいさんの子供の頃なんて、よくもそんな古い写真が残っていたね。

content.content: How amazing that such an old photo of when grandfather was a child still be around!

content: 田中さん、よくもあんな早い英語を正確に聞き取れるもんだね。

content.content: I don’t know how Tanaka-san can follow such fast English accurately.

content: あんな吹雪の中でよくも無事でいられましたね。どうやって寒さをしのいでいたんですか。

content.content: How did you survive such a snow storm? However did you endure the cold?
Expresses surprise that a difficult thing which was not expected to be done or to happen has been done.
5. よく（も）〈criticism〉

content: よくもみんなの前で私に恥をかかせてくれたな。

content.content: How could you have embarrassed me in front of everyone?

content: あなた、よくそんな人を傷つけるようなことを平気で言えるものですね。

content.content: How could you calmly say such hurtful things?

content: あいつ、みんなにあれだけ迷惑をかけておいて、よくも平気な顔で出社できたものだ。

content.content: How could that guy come to work with such an unconcerned face when he caused so much nuisance to everyone?

content: あの人、よく毎日同じもの食べて飽きませんね。おなかがいっぱいになれば味なんてどうでもいいんでしょうね。

content.content: How does that person not get tired of eating the same thing everyday? As long as she feels full, I guess it doesn’t matter to her what it tastes like.

content: あいつ、ふられた彼女に毎晩電話して「やり直そう」って言ってるらしいよ。あんな情けないこと、よくやるよ。

content.content: I heard that guy calls the girl who jilted him every evening asking her to get back together with him. How could he do such a shameful thing?

content: A:お前、すこし運動でもしてやせた方がいいんじゃないか。

content.content: Wouldn’t it be good if you did exercise or something and lost some weight?
B:よく言うよ。お前だっていつもごろごろして全然体を動かしていないじゃないか。
How can you say that? Isn’t it you who’s always idle and never moves your body?

Expresses the speaker’s feelings of disdain, of criticism and anger, of having had enough of an annoying or cruel thing, or something which lacks common sense and means “why would you do such a thing?” Used together with てくれる, it is an ironic expression. Example

content: , in response to the other person’s utterance, expresses the criticism “you are not qualified to say such things.” Examples
and
are idiomatic expressions and used in conjunction with よく only.

content.content: 【よそに】
1. Nをよそに〈ignore〉

content: 弟は親の心配をよそに毎晩遅くまで遊んでいる。

content.content: Ignoring our parents’ concerns, my brother enjoys himself until late every night.

content: 反則をした選手は、観衆のブーイングをよそに、平然と試合を続けた。

content.content: The player who fouled continued the match calmly, ignoring the booing of the crowds.

content: 密室政治という悪評をよそに、また密室での決定がなされた。

content.content: Regardless of the criticisms of closed-door politics, another decision has been made behind closed doors.

content: 周囲の期待をよそに、彼はせっかく入った一流企業を退職し、小さな店をはじめた。

content.content: Disregarding the expectations of those around him, he retired from the top-rank company he had finally entered and opened a small store.

Using nouns which demonstrate feelings or evaluations of people, such as心配, 噂, 非難, 批判, 期待(concern, rumor, criticism, judgement, expectation), means that such feelings or evaluations are ignored or disregarded. A volitional act comes afterwards.
2. Nをよそに〈unrelated〉

content: 高速道路の渋滞をよそに、私たちはゆうゆうと新幹線で東京に向かった。

content.content: We leisurely headed towards Tokyo on the shinkansen (bullet train), untroubled by the congestion on the highways.

content: 最近結婚した友達は、最近の海外旅行ブームをよそに、奈良へ新婚旅行に出かけた。

content.content: My friend who recently got married, ignoring the recent boom in foreign travel, took his honeymoon in Nara.

content: 昨今の不景気をよそに、デパートのお歳暮コーナーでは高額のお歳暮に人気が集まっている。

content.content: Despite the recent recession, in the corner of the department store for year-end gifts, expensive presents are proving popular.
Using a noun which demonstrates a particular situation, means “with no relation to that” or “untroubled by that.”
【よほど】In speech, this becomes よっぽど for emphasis.
1. よほどa. よほど

content: こんな大邸宅を建てるなんて、よほどの金持ちに違いない。

content.content: She must be wealthy to be building such a mansion like this.

content: よっぽどのことがなければ、彼はここには来ません。

content.content: Unless he was forced by something really important, he won’t come here.

content: あいつはよほど金に困っているらしい。昨日も友達に昼ごはんをおごってもらっていた。

content.content: That guy seems to be having real money troubles. His friend treated him to lunch again yesterday.

content: よっぽど疲れていたんだろう。弟は帰ってくるとご飯も食べずに寝てしまった。

content.content: He must have been really tired. As soon as my younger brother came home he went straight to bed without eating dinner.

content: その映画、続けて3回も観たって？　よっぽどよかったんだね。

content.content: You’ve seen that movie three times? It must be really good.

content: 泣き言を言わない彼女が愚痴をこぼすとは、よほど仕事がつらかったんだろうと思う。

content.content: She never complains and so, if she grumbles, the job must have been really hard.
Shows a condition that, judging from the general standard, is not average. Used to make a conjecture about the extent of something.
b. ...ほうがよほど

content: 真夏の日本よりインドネシアの方がよっぽど涼しかった。

content.content: Indonesia was much cooler than Japan in midsummer.

content: こんなに狭くて家賃の高い部屋に住むくらいなら、今の古い部屋の方がよっぽどましだ。

content.content: I’d much rather live in my old apartment than pay high rent to live in an apartment this small.

content: 姉より弟の方がよっぽどよく家事を手伝ってくれる。

content.content: My younger brother is much better at helping with the housework than my older sister.

content: 入学試験を受ける兄より母の方がよっぽど神経質になっている。

content.content: My mother is much more nervous than my older brother who is taking the university entrance exams.

content: こんなにつらいのなら死んだほうがよほどましだ。

content.content: If it’s this painful, I would rather die.

Followed by adjectives and verbs. In the form (Xより)Yのほうがよほど this compares two things and demonstrates that Y is by far (something) to a greater extent. Often used in cases where Y is preferred. Means “far and away.”
2. よほどV-よう

content: こんなつまらない仕事、よほど辞めようかと思った。

content.content: I thought I would quit such a boring job.

content: あいつに失礼なことを言われて腹が立ったので、よほど言い返してやろうかと思ったが、大人げないので黙っていた。

content.content: Because I got angry when that guy said something rude to me, I thought about answering back but, because that’s immature, I kept my mouth shut.

content: 彼の皿の洗い方があまりにも不器用なので、よっぽど自分でやってしまおうと思ったが、我慢して見ていた。

content.content: Because his way of washing dishes is so ineffective, I thought that I should just do them myself but I forced myself to just watch.

content: その講演はあんまりつまらなかったので、よっぽど途中で帰ろうと思ったが、誰も席を立たないのでしかたなく最後まで聞いていた。

content.content: Because that lecture was so boring I thought about leaving in the middle of it but, as nobody left their seats, I had no choice but to stay to the end.
Often used together with と思った and means “to strongly think one will....” Used in cases where something is only thought and cannot be done and a contradictory clause often comes after.
【よもや】［よもや　...ないだろう／...まい］

content: よもや負けるまいと思われていた選手が予選落ちした。

content.content: The player who it seemed could not lose lost in the preliminary rounds.

content: いくらお金に困っているといっても、よもやサラ金に手を出したりはしていないでしょうね。

content.content: However much financial difficulty you may be in, I hope you are not borrowing money from a loan shark.

content: あんな雪山の遭難ではよもや助かるまいと思っていたが、彼は奇跡的に助かった。

content.content: I thought there was no way he could be rescued from an accident on such a snowy mountain but, miraculously, he was saved.

content: よもやバレることはないだろうと思っていたのに、母は私の嘘を見抜いていた。

content.content: I thought there was no way I would be exposed but my mother saw through my lies.
Used together with conjectural expressions, expresses a strong denial that something is possible.
【より】
1. ...より（も／は）［N／V　より（も／は）］

content: 今年の冬は昨年よりも寒い。

content.content: This winter is colder than last year’s.

content: このシャツの方がさっき見たのより色がきれいだ。

content.content: The color of this shirt is nicer than the one we saw before.

content: 休みの日は外へ出かけるよりうちでごろごろしている方が好きだ。

content.content: On holiday days I like to be idle at home rather than go outside.

content: 田中さんの送別会は予想していたよりずっと多くの人が集まってくれました。

content.content: Many more people than expected gathered for Tanaka-san’s farewell party.

content: やらずに後悔するよりは、無理にでもやってみた方がいい。

content.content: You would be better off having a go at it, however impossible it may seem, than regretting afterwards not having even tried.

content: 仕事は思ったよりも大変だった。

content.content: The job was more difficult than I had thought.

content: 事件の背景は、私が考えていたよりも複雑なようだ。

content.content: It seems that the circumstances of the incident are more complicated than I had thought.
In the forms XよりもYのほうがZ and YはXよりもZ, shows X as the standard for comparison. In casual conversation the forms such as the following can also be used: よりか, それよか.
（例）レストランよりか居酒屋の方がリラックスできていいんじゃないかな。
I think a bar is better than a restaurant because we can relax there.
（例）今から外食しに行くのもいいけど、それよか一緒に買い物に行ってうちで作って食べない？
We could eat out but, rather than do that, why don’t we go shopping together and then cook at home?
2. ...というより

content: 彼は堅実家というよりけちだと言う方が当たっている。

content.content: It’s closer to the mark to see him as stingy rather than prudent.

content: 彼女はきれいというよりはむしろ個性的なタイプで、独特のファッション感覚がある。

content.content: More than just being pretty, she is a unique type; she has her very own sense of fashion.

content: 彼の書いた英文は、できが悪いというより、むしろもう絶望的だと言った方がいいくらいひどい。

content.content: His English composition wasn’t just bad; I’d rather say it was so horrible as to be hopeless.

content: あいつは酒を飲むというより流し込むと言った方がいいような飲み方をする。

content.content: That guy’s way of drinking sake is not so much drinking as it is pouring it down.

content: こんなパーティーは、楽しいというよりも退屈なだけで、一部の人のためのバカ騒ぎとしか思えない。

content.content: This kind of party is actually just boring rather than fun, and I can’t think of it as anything other than horseplay for a small group of people.
Used to compare ways of expressions about or ways of judging a certain thing. Means “You could say X, or see it X way but, in comparison Y is more appropriate.” As in examples

content: and
, it is often used together with むしろ.

content.content: 3. ...よりないa. V-るよりない

content: どうしても大学に通う気が起きないのなら、もう退学するよりないだろう。

content.content: If you can’t bring yourself to attend lectures, there’s nothing to do but drop out of university.

content: 文句を言っても仕方がない。とりあえず今できることを一生懸命やるよりない。

content.content: It’s no use complaining. For now, all we can do is give it our very best effort.

content: こんな不景気なら、どこでもいいから採用してくれるところに就職するよりなさそうだ。

content.content: It seems that, in this kind of recession, all we can do is look for work anywhere they will employ us.
Expresses that, in situations where there is a problem, there is no other way of resolving it. ...しかない and ...以外にない can also be used.
b. V-るよりほか（に／は）ない

content: 今さらあれはうそだったとも言えないし、隠しとおすよりほかにない。

content.content: At this point we can’t say that it was a lie, so we have no choice but to cover it up.

content: 雪はだんだん激しくなってきたが、引き返すこともできないし、とにかく山小屋まで歩くよりほかはなかった。

content.content: The snow gradually became stronger, but as we couldn’t retrace our steps, we had no choice but to walk on to the mountain hut.

content: 放っておけばあの地域のリゾート開発は進む一方だし、こうなったら反対運動を起こすよりほかにないと思った。

content.content: I thought that, if we ignored it, the development of the region’s resorts would proceed, so in that case, I had no choice but to start an opposition movement.
Expresses that, in situations in which there is a problem, there is no other way to resolve it. ...しかない and ...以外にない are also used.
c. ...よりほかに...ない［Nよりほかに...ない］［V-るよりほかに...ない］

content: その部屋は静かで、時計の音よりほかに何の物音も聞こえなかった。

content.content: The room was quiet and, apart from the ticking of the clock, you couldn’t hear a sound.

content: 田中さんよりほかにこの仕事を任せられる人はいない。

content.content: There’s nobody other than Tanaka-san to whom I can entrust this job.

content: あなたよりほかに頼れる人がいないから、忙しいのを承知でお願いしているのです。

content.content: There’s nobody but you I can depend on, so while I know that you’re busy, I’m asking you (this favor).

content: せっかくのお休みで天気もいいのに、うちでテレビを見るよりほかにすることはないのですか。

content.content: It’s finally the holidays and the weather is good, so don’t you have anything other to do than watch television inside?
Used with a negative expression coming afterwards to emphasize that “there is nothing other than that.” ...以外に...ない is also used.
d. V-るよりしかたがない

content: お金がないのなら、旅行はあきらめるよりしかたがないね。

content.content: If you have no money, you have no choice but to give up your trip.

content: 自分の失敗は自分で責任を持って始末するよりしかたがない。

content.content: There is no other option but to deal with your failings by taking responsibility for them yourself.

content: 終電が出てしまったので、タクシーで帰るよりしかたがなかった。

content.content: As the last train had left I had no other option but to go home by taxi.

content: あさってからスキーに行きたいのなら、さっさとレポートを書いてしまうよりしかたがないでしょう。

content.content: If you want to go skiing after tomorrow, you have no choice but to hurry up and finish writing the report, you know.
Expresses that, although with reluctance, there is no other choice in order to resolve a situation. ...ほかしかたがない and ...以外にしかたがない are also used.
【よる】→
【によって】、
【によらず】、
【により】、
【によると】、
【によれば】
【らしい】
1. Nらしいa. NらしいN

content: 最近は子供らしい子供が少なくなった。

content.content: Recently there seem to be fewer truly childlike children.

content: 男らしい男ってどんな人のことですか。

content.content: What kind of person is a manly man?

content: あの人は本当に先生らしい先生ですね。

content.content: That person is very much a teacher’s teacher.

content: このところ雨らしい雨も降っていない。

content.content: There really hasn’t been any measurable rain recently.
Repeating the same noun, conveys the model of the thing denoted by it.
b. Nらしい

content: 今日は春らしい天気だ。

content.content: Today the weather is like spring.

content: 弱音を吐くなんて君らしくないね。

content.content: It’s not like you to be so negative.

content: 彼はいかにも芸術家らしく奇抜なかっこうで現れた。

content.content: He turned up in a striking outfit you would expect an artist to wear.

content: 彼女が選んだ花束はいかにも彼女らしいやさしい色合いだった。

content.content: The bouquet (of flowers) she chose had gentle hues, just like her.
Attaches to a noun, and expresses that the typical properties of that thing are very apparent.
2. ...らしい［N／Na／A／V　らしい］

content: 天気予報によると明日は雨らしい。

content.content: According to the weather forecast, it looks like rain tomorrow.

content: 新しく出たビデオカメラはとても便利らしい。

content.content: The video camera that has just been launched is said to be very handy.

content: みんなの噂では、あの人は国では翻訳家としてかなり有名らしい。

content.content: According to what everyone’s saying, that woman is quite famous as a translator in her country.

content: 彼はどうやら今の会社を辞めて、自分で会社を作るらしい。

content.content: It seems that he’s going to quit the company he’s at now and start his own.

content: 兄はどうも試験がうまくいかなかったらしく、帰ってくるなり部屋に閉じ込もってしまった。

content.content: It seems that my older brother’s exam didn’t go well. As soon as he came home he shut himself in his room.

content: その映画は予想以上におもしろかったらしく、彼は何度もパンフレットを読み返していた。

content.content: That movie must have been more interesting than expected; he reread the flier many times.

content: 料理はいかにも即席で用意したらしく、インスタントのものがそのまま並んでいた。

content.content: It looked as though the dishes were prepared very quickly; many instant food items were lined up as they were.

Attached to the end of a sentence, expresses the speaker’s thinking that the content of the sentence is quite certain to be so. The basis of this judgement stems from external information or observable objective things and not simply the speaker’s impression. For example, the judgement 雨らしい in example

content: is made according to the weather forecast. The judgement made in
, 試験がうまくいかなかったらしい (that the exam did not go well), is based on the fact that the brother shut himself in his room immediately after returning home.

content.content: For the differences between this and みたいだ and そうだ, please refer to Usage 2 in みたいだ.
【られたい】→
【せられたい】

【られる1】This is the passive voice. In cases where the V in V-られる is a Group 1 verb, the dictionary form ending changes to the a-row and れる is added, as in 行く(go)→行かれる and 飲む(drink)→飲まれる. Where Group 2 verbs are used られる is added to the stem, as in 食べる(eat)→食べられる. 来る(come) becomes こられる and する(do) becomes される. V-られる conjugates in the same way as Group 2 verbs.
1. NがV-られる〈direct passive〉

content: この地方ではおもに赤ワインが作られている。

content.content: In this region red wine is primarily made.

content: 木曜日の会議は3時から開かれることになっている。

content.content: Thursday’s meeting will be started at three o’clock.

content: この辞書は昔から使われているいい辞書だが、最近の外来語などはのっていない。

content.content: This is a good dictionary that has been used for a long time but it doesn’t contain recent loan words.

content: 昨夜、駅前のデパートで1億円相当のネックレスや指輪が盗まれた。

content.content: Last night, necklaces and rings worth 100 million yen were stolen from the department store in front of the station.

content: 来月発売される車のカタログを手に入れた。

content.content: I got hold of a catalogue of cars to go on sale from next month.

This is used to give as the subject a thing which is acted upon or which is affected. Often used in factual descriptive sentences and in informative sentences. As the agent cannot be identified, it is usual for it not to appear in the sentence.
2. NがNにV-られるa. NがNに（よって）V-られる〈direct passive〉

content: 漫画週刊誌は若いサラリーマンによく読まれている。

content.content: Weekly manga magazines are often read by young businessmen.

content: その寺院は7世紀に中国から渡来した僧侶によって建てられた。

content.content: That temple was built by a priest who came over from China in the seventh century.

content: このあたりの土地はダイオキシンに汚染されている。

content.content: The soil in this area is contaminated with dioxin.

content: 地震後、その教会は地域の住民によって再建された。

content.content: After the earthquake, that church was rebuilt by the local residents.

content: その展覧会はフォード財団によって支援されている。

content.content: That exhibition is supported by the Ford Foundation.

Used to give as the subject a thing which is acted upon or which is affected. It is often used in factual descriptive sentences and in informative sentences. The agent is indicated by Nに or Nによって. In cases regarding the production of a thing (a work or building), and in formal speech, によって is primarily used.
b. NがN　に／から　V-られる〈direct passive〉

content: おばあさんが犬にかまれた。

content.content: An elderly lady was bitten by a dog.

content: その子は母親にしかられて、泣き出した。

content.content: That child was scolded by his mother and burst out crying.

content: 彼女は皆にかわいがられて育った。

content.content: She was raised being doted on by everyone.

content: 森さんは知らない人から話しかけられた。

content.content: Mori-san was spoken to by a stranger.

content: 彼は正直なので、だれからも信頼されている。

content.content: Because he is honest, he is trusted by everyone.

content: 夜中に騒いだら、近所の人に注意されてしまった。

content.content: When I made a lot of noise late at night, a neighbour admonished me.

Used to give as the subject a person who is acted upon or who is affected. A way of expressing a thing which occurs between two people from the viewpoint of someone other than the agent. The agent is indicated by Nに but when an action showing that a feeling, information or remark is given by the agent Nから is also used. When the speaker is affected by the action, the passive voice is often used to express the speaker’s viewpoint. Furthermore, it is usual for the sentence to convey the point of view of one person.
（×）夜中に騒いだら、近所の人が注意した。
I was noisy in the middle of the night and someone from the neighborhood admonished me.
（○）夜中に騒いだら、近所の人に注意された。
I was noisy in the middle of the night and was admonished by someone from the neighborhood.
c. NがNにV-られる〈indirect passive〉

content: 忙しいときに客に来られて、仕事ができなかった。

content.content: I had a visitor while I was busy and so I couldn’t do my work.

content: A:日曜日はいかがでしたか。

content.content: How was Sunday?
B:家族でハイキングに行ったんですが、途中で雨に降られましてね。
I went hiking with my family but we were rained on while along the way.
A:それは大変でしたね。
Oh, that was too bad.

content: 彼は奥さんに逃げられて、すっかり元気をなくしてしまった。

content.content: He was deserted by his wife and completely lost his will to live.

content: 子どもに死なれた親ほどかわいそうなものはない。

content.content: There is nothing as sad as a parent who has a child die.

Used to relate the standpoint of a person adversely affected by something which has caused their situation. Corresponds with the respective active sentence which uses an intransitive verb such as 客が来る(visitors are coming) and 雨が降る(it rains). The agent is indicated by Nに but Nによって and Nから cannot be used.
3. NがNにNをV-られるa. NがNにNをV-られる〈possessor passive〉

content: 森さんは知らない人に名前をよばれた。

content.content: Mori-san’s name was called by a stranger.

content: わたしは今朝、電車の中で足をふまれた。

content.content: This morning my foot was trodden upon on the train.

content: 犯人は警官に頭を撃たれて重傷を負った。

content.content: The offender was injured after being struck over the head by a police officer.

content: 先生に発音をほめられて英語が好きになった。

content.content: I came to like English after my pronunciation was praised by my teacher.

Used to give as the subject the owner of the thing which is acted upon or affected. Used to show that, through an action which is done to a thing, the owner of that thing is troubled or perplexed. The thing possessed by the owner (such as their name, foot, or head) is indicated in the form Nを. If this possession is taken as the subject, the effect is often unnatural.
（×）私の足がふまれた。
My foot was trodden on.
（○）私は足をふまれた。
I had my foot trodden upon.
When the action is welcome from the point of view of the speaker, expressions which demonstrate gratitude such as V-てもらった are often used but, as in the ほめる of example

content: , when a verb which essentially has a positive meaning is used in the passive voice, the development of feelings such as embarrassment or pride is implied.

content.content: b. NがNにNをV-られる〈indirect passive〉

content: せまい部屋でタバコを吸われると気分が悪くなる。

content.content: When someone smokes in a small room it makes me feel sick.

content: 夜遅くまで会社に残って仕事をされると、電気代がかかって困る。

content.content: If someone stays late working at the company, I worry that it costs electricity.

content: 次々に料理を出されて、とても食べきれなかった。

content.content: One dish after another was brought out and I just couldn’t eat it all.

content: 台所のテーブルの上に宿題を広げられると晩御飯のしたくができないから、はやくどけなさい。

content.content: I want to prepare dinner but can’t if your homework is spread all over the table, so hurry up and move it.

content: 結婚はおめでたいけど、今あなたに会社をやめられるのは痛手だなあ。

content.content: Congratulations on your marriage, but it’s a blow to us that you’re leaving the company.

Used to express the standpoint of a person indirectly bothered by a thing which has happened to cause their situation. It corresponds with the respective active sentence which uses an transitive verb such as (だれかが)タバコを吸う and (だれかが)仕事をする and demonstrates that the speaker is troubled because of that. The agent is indicated by Nに but Nによって and Nから cannot be used. Often the agent is not indicated.
【られる2】

content: 大きすぎて穴から出られなくなった。

content.content: It was too big to get out from the hole.

content: そんなに早くは起きられない。

content.content: I can’t get up that early.
Demonstrates potential.
【れる1】

【れる1】Demonstrates potential. In cases where the V in V-れる is a Group 1 verb, the dictionary form ending changes to the e-row sound and る is added, as in 行く(go)→行ける and 飲む(drink)→飲める. Where Group 2 verbs are used, られる is added to the stem, as in 食べる(eat)→食べられる. 来る(come) becomes こられる or これる and する(do) becomes できる. V-れる conjugates in the same way as Group 2 verbs.

In cases where the V is a Group 1 verb, the potential aspect takes the different form V-れる from the passive voice V-られる (for example the form of possibility becomes 飲める, 書ける (can drink, can write) while the passive form becomes 飲まれる, 書かれる(be drunk (by someone), be written (by someone)). On the other hand, Group 2 verbs take the same form for both the potential and passive voices (both become 食べられる(can eat/be eaten (by someone)), 起きられる(can get up/be gotten up (by someone)), for example). However, in speech nowadays, the more people are omitting the ら from the possible V-れる and so it becomes 食べれる, 起きれる. Also, more people are using NをV-れる rather than NがV-れる.
1. NはNがV-れるGenerally NはNがV-れる is used but a person with an ability or potential is also sometimes indicated with Nに, as in NにNがV-れる.
a. NはNがV-れる〈ability〉

content: リンさんはなっとうが食べられますか。

content.content: Can Lyn-san eat nattoo?

content: かれにできないスポーツはない。

content.content: There is no sport he cannot do.

content: わたしにかれらの指導ができるだろうか。

content.content: I wonder if I can coach them?

content: 読めない漢字があったら、そう言ってください。

content.content: If there are kanji you cannot read, please say so.

content: この本は読み出したら、やめられない。

content.content: Once you start, you won’t be able to stop reading this book.

content: どうしてもあの先生の名前が思い出せなくて冷や汗をかいた。

content.content: I couldn’t remember that teacher’s name no matter what and broke into a cold sweat.

content: 朝6時から練習を開始しますので、起きられたら来てください。

content.content: As practice will commence from six in the morning, please come if you can get up.
This expresses a possibility dependant on ability, skill, or willpower.
b. NはNがV-れる〈possibility〉

content: あの店ではいつも珍しいものが食べられる。

content.content: You can always eat unusual things in that shop.

content: 仕事場の人はだれでもそのファックスが使用できる。

content.content: Everyone at the workplace can use that fax.

content: この動物園では、子供は無料でイルカのショーが見られる。

content.content: At this zoo, children can watch the dolphin show for free.

content: わたしが直接話せたらいいのですが、あいにく都合が悪いんです。

content.content: I would have liked to speak to them directly, but unfortunately it is not convenient.

content: 両親に言えないことでも、友達になら言える。

content.content: I can say things to my friends that I can’t even say to my parents.

content: 辞書は図書館で借り出せないので、ひまなときに調べに行くつもりだ。

content.content: As you can’t take the dictionaries out of the library, I intend to go and look (it) up when I am free.

content: 昨日は答えが聞けなかったので、きょうもう一度たずねてみます。

content.content: As I wasn’t able to get a response yesterday, I’ll pay a visit again today.

Expresses that there is a possibility which is dependent on the situation or on opportunity. 見られる(can see/can be seen) and 見える(can see) are similar expressions but the difference is that 見える is used in cases where a thing spontaneously comes into view while 見られる is used when the possibility of seeing a thing occurs because a particular situation or opportunity arises.
（○）昨夜のスポーツニュースはいそがしくて見られなかった。
I wasn’t able to see last night’s sports news as I was busy.
（×）昨夜のスポーツニュースはいそがしくて見えなかった。
I wasn’t able to see last night’s sports news as I was busy.
（○）ここから白い建物が見えます。
You can see a white building from here.
（×）ここから白い建物が見られます。
You can see a white building appear from here.

聞ける and 聞こえる are the same in the sense that 聞ける shows that a thing spontaneously comes into hearing while 聞こえる is used when the possibility of hearing a thing occurs because a particular situation or opportunity arises.
（○）携帯ラジオをもってきたので、どこでも天気予報が聞ける。
Because I brought a handheld radio, we can hear the weather forecast anywhere.
（×）携帯ラジオをもってきたので、どこでも天気予報が聞こえる。
Because I brought a handheld radio, we can hear the weather forecast anywhere.
（○）どこからか鳥の声が聞こえた。
I could hear the sound of a bird from somewhere.
（×）どこからか鳥の声が聞けた。
I could hear the sound of a bird from somewhere.
For eyesight and hearing 見える and 聞こえる are used.
（例）生まれたばかりの猫の子は目が見えない。
The eyes of a newborn kitten are blind.
（例）補聴器をつけたら、耳がよく聞こえるようになった。
Wearing a hearing aid I could hear much better.
2. Nは V-れる〈characteristic〉

content: この野菜はなまでは食べられない。

content.content: This vegetable cannot be eaten raw.

content: この泉の水は飲めます。

content.content: This fountain’s water can be drunk.

content: 悲しい映画かと思ったが、見てみるとけっこう笑える映画だった。

content.content: I had thought it was a sad movie, but watching it, it was quite funny.

content: この教室は300 人は楽に入れます。

content.content: This classroom can comfortably take 300 people.
Expresses possibility as a property of a thing.
【れる2】

content: 車にはねられて怪我をした。

content.content: I was hit by a car and got injured.

content: 表紙に美しい絵が描かれている。

content.content: There is a beautiful picture depicted on the front cover.
Shows passivity.
【られる1】
【ろく】
1. ろくなN...ない

content: こんな安月給ではろくな家に住めない。

content.content: I can’t live in a decent home on such a low salary.

content: 誰もこの言葉を知らないのか。まったくこの課にはろくな奴がいないな。

content.content: Isn’t there anyone who knows this word? I swear, there really is no one I can count on in this department.

content: 上司には怒られるし、彼女にはふられるし、ろくなことがない。

content.content: My boss is mad at me, my girlfriend’s giving me the cold shoulder—nothing’s any good.

content: A:どうもごちそうさまでした。

content.content: Thank you. That was a feast.
B:いいえ、最近ろくなおかまいもできませんで。
Don’t mention it—I haven’t done anything special for you recently.
Shows an unsatisfactory or worse than average thing.
2. ろくでもないN

content: 花子はろくでもない男に夢中になっている。

content.content: Hanako is infatuated with a good-for-nothing man.

content: そんなろくでもない本ばかり読んでいるから、成績が悪くなるのよ。

content.content: Because you only read such worthless books, your grades are suffering.

content: A:そんなに仕事がいやなら、早いとこお見合いでもして結婚したらどう。

content.content: If you dislike work so much, how about quickly having an arranged marriage?
B:そんなろくでもないこと言わないでよ。
Don’t say such stupid things!
Expresses that a thing is worthless, good-for-nothing, or stupid.
3. ろくに V-ない

content: テストも近いというのに、あの子ったらろくに勉強もしないんだから。

content.content: Even though the test is soon, that child will not study enough.

content: あいつは昼間から酒ばかり飲んでろくに仕事もしないくせに、食べるときは人一倍食べる。

content.content: Even though that guy just only drinks sake from noontime on and hardly does any worthwhile work, when it’s time to eat he puts away as much as anyone.

content: せっかく海に来たというのに、彼女はろくに泳ぎもしないで肌を焼いてばかりいた。

content.content: We finally came to the sea but she hardly swam at all and just sunbathed.

content: ろくに予習しなくたって、あの授業は先生がやさしいから何とかなる。

content.content: I haven’t prepared enough but the teacher of that class is easy-going so I’ll manage somehow.

content: そんな雑誌、ろくに読まなくてもだいたいどんなことが書いてあるかは見当が付くよ。

content.content: Even without reading much of that kind of magazine, I have a general idea of what sort of things are written in it.
Shows that something is not done to one’s satisfaction. Means “almost not...” and “not (done) enough.”
【ろくろく】［ろくろく V-ない］

content: 電気屋さんで新製品のカタログを山ほどくれたが、どれもろくろく見ないで捨ててしまった。

content.content: I got a mountain of new product catalogues from the electrical goods store, but not seeing anything suitable, I threw them away.

content: 兄はろくろく勉強もしないで、すんなり東大に合格してしまった。

content.content: Barely having studied, my older brother easily passed into Tokyo University.

content: 彼女はその手紙をろくろく読みもしないで破り捨ててしまった。

content.content: Having hardly even read the letter, she tore it up and threw it away.

content: 隣に引っ越してきた人は、うちの前で顔を合わせてもろくろく挨拶もしないんだ。いったいどういうつもりなんだろう。

content.content: The person who has moved in next door barely even greets me when we come face to face. What’s that supposed to mean?
Means “to mostly not do...” or “to not do... sufficiently.” Expresses a negative viewpoint in relation to something that is not done. As in examples

content: to
, in the form N-もしない, R-もしない, it is often used to emphasize the negative.
昨日は山登りに行ったが、雨に降られるわ道に迷うわで、散々だった。

content.content: Yesterday I went mountain-climbing but it rained and I got lost; it was terrible.

content: 今週は試験はあるわレポートの締切は近いわで、寝る間もない。

content.content: This week I have an exam and the deadline of my report is close; there’s barely time to sleep.

content: このごろ忙しくて、もう家事はたまるわ、まともな食事はしないわ...。

content.content: I’m so busy these days; the housework is piling up, I’m not eating properly....

content: あいつは高校生のくせにタバコは吸うわお酒は飲むわ無断外泊はするわ、悪いことばかりしていて親を泣かせている。

content.content: That guy’s a senior high school student but he smokes, drinks alcohol and stays out all night without permission; he reduces his parents to tears just doing bad things all the time.

When several bad things occur all at once, this is used to list them as exemplificatory and to emphasize a feeling of annoyance. What follows are details of how (it) was terrible because of those things or that the person was annoyed because of those things.
2. V-るわV-るわ

content: 新しくできた水族館に行ったら、人がいるわいるわ、魚なんか全然見えないぐらいの人出だった。

content.content: When I went to the new aquarium there were people on top of people! It was such a large turnout that I couldn’t see the fish at all.

content: 忙しくて新聞がたまるわたまるわ、もう2週間分も読んでいない。

content.content: I’m really busy and the newspapers keep piling up; I haven’t read them for two weeks already.

content: 部屋を久しぶりに掃除したら、ごみが出るわ出るわ、段ボール箱にいっぱいになった。

content.content: When I cleaned my room for the first time in a long while, there was so much rubbish that it filled a cardboard box.
Repeating the same verb, expresses surprise that the quantity of a thing or the frequency of an occurrence is higher than expected. Often, details of the resulting situation follow.
【わけがない】［N　な／である　わけがない］［Na なわけがない］［A／V　わけがない］

content: あいつが犯人なわけ（が）ないじゃないか。

content.content: There’s no way that guy could be the perpetrator.

content: A:最近元気？

content.content: Have you been well lately?
B:元気なわけ（が）ないでしょ。彼と仲直りできなくて、もう悲惨な状態なのよ。
There’s no way I could be well. I can’t make up with my boyfriend; it’s a miserable state of affairs.

content: 北海道で熱帯の植物が育つわけがない。

content.content: It’s impossible for tropical plants to grow in Hokkaido.

content: こんな忙しい時期にスキーに行けるわけがない。

content.content: It’s impossible for me to go skiing at such a busy time.

content: 勉強もしないで遊んでばかりいて、試験にパスするわけがないじゃないか。

content.content: There’s no way you can pass the exam—not studying and just enjoying yourself all the time.

content: 考えてみれば、彼女が彼に対してそんなひどいことを言うわけがなかった。

content.content: If you think about it, there’s no way she could have said such a horrid thing to him.

Used to strongly insist that there is no reason for such a thing to occur/no possibility of such a thing occurring. In speech, わけない is often said, with the が being omitted. It can be rephrased as はずがない.
【わけだ】

1. ...わけだ〈monologue-type〉［N　な／である　わけだ］［Na なわけだ］［A／V　わけだ］States a logically-derived conclusion from a fact or situation showing a previous utterance or context. Used in cases where the speaker or writer is explaining or elucidating something.
a. ...わけだ〈conclusion〉

content: イギリスとは時差が8時間あるから、日本が 11 時ならイギリスは3時なわけだ。

content.content: As there is an eight hour time difference between the United Kingdom and Japan, if it is eleven o’clock in Japan, it will be three o’clock in the United Kingdom.

content: 体重を測ったら 52 キロになっていた。先週は 49 キロだったから、一週間で3キロも太ってしまったわけだ。

content.content: When I weighed myself I weighed 52 kilograms. I weighed 49 kilograms last week and so it means that I’ve put on three kilograms in one week.

content: 最近円高が進んで、輸入品の値段が下がっている。だから洋書も安くなっているわけだ。

content.content: Recently the value of the yen has been increasing and so the price of imported goods is going down. This means Western books are also getting cheaper.

content: 彼女は中国で3年間働いていたので、中国の事情にかなり詳しいわけである。

content.content: She worked in China for three years and so she’s quite knowledgeable about the Chinese situation.

content: 私は昔から機械類をさわるのが苦手です。だから未だにコンピュータも使えないわけです。

content.content: I’ve always been bad with machines and so, to this day, I can’t even use a computer.
Takes the form X。(だから)Yわけだ. Shows that Y is the natural course of development from X, or is an inevitable conclusion. It is often used together with phrases such as だから, から and ので.
b. ...わけだ〈restatement〉

content: 彼女の父親は私の母の弟だ。つまり彼女と私はいとこ同士なわけだ。

content.content: Her father is my mother’s younger brother. That is to say, we are cousins.

content: 彼女はフランスの有名なレストランで5年間料理の修行をしたそうだ。つまりプロの料理人であるわけだ。

content.content: I hear that she spent five years training in a famous French restaurant. In other words, she’s a professional chef.

content: 彼は大学へ行っても部室でギターの練習ばかりしている。要するに講義にはほとんど出ていないわけだが、それでもなぜか単位はきちんと取れているらしい。

content.content: Even though he goes to school, he just practices his guitar in his room all the time. In other words, he hardly ever goes to his lectures but, even so, somehow he seems to pick up the credits he needs.

content: 父は 20 年前に運転免許を取っていたが車は持っていなかった。つまり長い間ペーパードライバーだったわけだ。

content.content: My father got his driver’s license twenty years ago but didn’t have a car. That is, for a long time he was a driver only on paper.

content: 私はおいしいものを食べている時が一番幸せである。言いかえれば、まずいものを食べることほどいやなことはないわけで、それが強制されたものだとなおさらである。

content.content: I’m happiest when eating something delicious. In other words, there’s nothing I like less than eating something bad, and if I’m forced to, then it’s even worse.
Used in the form X。（つまり）Yわけだ, Shows that X and Y are the same thing and that X can be said in other words as Y.
c. ...わけだ〈reason〉

content: 今年は米のできが良くなかった。冷夏だったわけだ。

content.content: The quality of this year’s rice was poor. It’s because it was a cool summer.

content: 彼女は猫を3匹と犬を1匹飼っている。一人暮らしで寂しいわけだ。

content.content: She keeps three cats and one dog. It’s because she is living alone and is lonely.

content: 姉は休みの度に海外旅行に出かける。日常の空間から脱出したいわけだ。

content.content: When there’s a holiday my older sister goes on a trip abroad. It’s because she wants to escape from her everyday life.

content: 山田君は就職難を乗り越えて大企業に就職したのに、結局3ヶ月でやめてしまった。本当にやりたかった音楽関係の仕事をめざすことにしたわけだが、音楽業界も就職はむずかしそうなので、心配している。

content.content: Even though Yamada-kun overcame the job shortage and was employed by a large company, in the end he quit after three months. He did it because he decided to try to find a music-related job he really wants to do, but it seems that finding work is difficult in the music field too and so he’s worried.
Takes the form X。Yわけだ. Means that Y is the cause of X.
d. ...わけだ〈claim of fact〉

content: 4人とも車で来るわけだから、うちの前にずらっと4台路上駐車することになるね。

content.content: As four people are arriving by car, I suppose there will be four cars parked in a line on the street in front of my house.

content: 私は古本屋めぐりが好きで、暇があると古本屋を回っては掘り出し物を探しているわけですが、このごろはいい古本屋が少なくなってきたので残念に思っています。

content.content: I like to look around second hand bookstores, so when I have free time, I go looking for bargains in them, but unfortunately there are fewer good second hand bookstores nowadays.

content: 私、国際交流関係のボランティア活動はすでに 10 年近くやってきているわけでして、自慢じゃありませんが、みなさんよりもずっと経験はあるわけです。そういう立場の者としてご提案させていただいているわけです。

content.content: I have been doing international exchange-related volunteer work for already ten years. I don’t mean to boast, but it’s from that position of being by far the most experienced that I make this proposal.

content: ねえ、聞いてくれる。昨日駅前に自転車置いて買い物に行ったんだけど、帰ってきたらなくなってるわけ。あちこち見てみたけど見つからなくて、しょうがないから警察に行ったわけよ。そしたら「鍵かけてなかったんじゃないの」なんて言われちゃって...。

content.content: Hey, listen to this. Yesterday, I leave my bike in front of the station and go shopping, but when I come back, it’s gone. I look here and there but can’t find it and so the only thing I can do is to go to the police. And then, they tell me something like “Well, you probably didn’t lock it....”

Used to insist on or emphasize that what one is saying is a fact with a logical foundation. Often used in speech and, especially even in cases where there is no logical basis for what is being said, it is often used as a sentence-ending particle. Frequently used when attempting to persuade another person by telling him what your thinking is.
As in examples

content: and
, used even when the listener does not know the truth, and in such cases can seem pushy, meaning “I think you know it too but....”

content.content: 2. ...わけだ〈dialogue-type〉Used to state the logical conclusion after accepting another person’s utterance. There are two possible situations for this: one is for the speaker to confirm the conclusion with the other person and the other is for the speaker to accept the conclusion as a fact based on the logical substantiation of the discourse of the other person.
a. ...わけだ〈conclusion〉［それなら...わけだ］［それじゃ...わけだ］［じゃ...わけだ］

content: A:森さんは8年もフィンランドに留学していたそうですよ。

content.content: I hear that Mori-san has been to Finland to study for eight years.
B:へえ、そうなんですか。それならフィンランド語は得意なわけですね。
Wow, really? If that’s the case, she must be really good at Finnish.

content: A:明日から2泊3日で熱海の温泉に行くの。

content.content: From tomorrow, I’m going to a hot spring in Atami for two nights, three days.
B:へえ、いいわね。じゃ、その間仕事のストレスからは解放されるわけね。
Wow, that’s great. While you’re there you should get relief from your work stress.
Used in the form それなら／それじゃ／じゃ...わけだ, taking what the other person says, this shows the inevitable conclusion.
b. ...わけだ〈restatement〉［つまり...わけだ］［ようするに...わけだ］

content: A:この間書いた小説、文学賞がもらえたよ。

content.content: The other day, I received a literary prize for the novel which I wrote.
B:あなたもようやく実力が認められたわけね。
At last, your real ability has been acknowledged.

content: A:田中くん、富士山登山に行くのやめるんだって。帰った次の日がゼミの発表だから準備しなくちゃいけないらしいよ。

content.content: Apparently, Tanaka-kun has decided not to climb Fuji-san (Mount Fuji). It seems that he has to prepare for a seminar presentation the next day.
B:ふうん。要するに体力に自信がないわけね。
Humph. In other words, he has no confidence in his physical strength.
Takes the form つまり／要するに...わけだ. Used to rephrase something another person has just said.
c. ...わけだ〈reason〉

content: A:川本さん、車大きいのに買いかえたらしいよ。

content.content: Kawamoto-san seems to have bought a new car even though the old one was so big.
B:へえ。子供が生まれて前のが小さくなったわけだな。
Really? The one he had before his child was born must have gotten too small.
A:いや、そうじゃなくて、単に新車がほしくなっただけのことらしいけど。
No, that’s not it. It seems he just wanted a new car.

content: A:ぼく、今度一軒家に引っ越すことにしたんですよ。

content.content: I’ve decided to move to a detached house this time.
B:いいですね。でも家賃高いんでしょう。ってことは、お給料、けっこうたくさんもらってるわけですね。
That’s good. But the rent must be high. So that means you must get a pretty high salary.
A:いや、それほどでもないですけどね。
No, not so much.
Expresses the reason for or cause of what the other person says.
d. ...わけだ〈understanding〉［だから...わけだ］［それで...わけだ］［なるほど...わけだ］［どうりで...わけだ］

content: A:山本さん、結婚したらしいですよ。

content.content: It seems that Yamamoto-san has gotten married.
B:ああ、そうだったんですか。それで最近いつもきげんがいいわけだな。
Oh, is that so? So that’s why she’s always in a good mood lately.

content: A:彼女は3年もアフリカにフィールドワークに行っていたそうですよ。

content.content: I hear that she went to do fieldwork in Africa for three years.
B:そうですか。道理で日本の状況がよくわかっていないわけですね。
Really? It’s no wonder that she doesn’t know much about what’s going on in Japan.

content: A:隣の鈴木さん、退職したらしいよ。

content.content: It seems that Suzuki-san from next door has retired.
B:そうか。だから平日の昼間でも家にいるわけだ。
Oh. So that’s why he’s at home during the day even on weekdays.

content: あ、鍵が違うじゃないか。なんだ。これじゃ、いくらがんばっても開かないわけだ。

content.content: Oh! This must be the wrong key. What’s up with it? No wonder I couldn’t open it however much I tried.

content: 田中さん、一か月で4キロやせようと思ってるんだって。なるほど、毎日昼ご飯を抜いているわけだわ。

content.content: They say Tanaka-san is trying to lose four kilograms in one month. That’s why he’s skipping lunch every day.

Often used in the form だから／それで／なるほど／どうりで...わけだ. Used in the form X。(だから)Yわけだdemonstrates that, although the speaker thought the reason for Y was mysterious, they have accepted that Y is so because of X after hearing information from another person which acts as the cause or reason.
Since the speaker comes to his/her own conclusion about the situation it is not necessary to use such phrases as ね afterwards but, in the polite form ...わけです, phrases such as ね and な are appended.
In example

content: , the situation is that Yamamoto-san has always been in a good mood lately but the reason for that is not known. It shows that, on hearing the information from A that “It seems Yamamoto-san has got married,” B comes to understand that as the reason for Yamamoto-san’s being in a good mood of late. The situation in

is that one person, speaking to him/herself, does not understand why the door will not open and, discovering that he has the wrong key, comes to understand that as the reason for why the door will not open. As in
and

, this is used by persons to detail something they have discovered for themselves or information they have heard from another. Combining that with facts already known, it is also used to show the speaker’s understanding of the situation.

content.content: 3. ...わけだからa. ...わけだから...はとうぜんだ

content: 小池さんは何年もインドネシア駐在員だったわけだから、インドネシア語が話せるのは当然です。

content.content: As Koike-san was located in Indonesia for some years, he naturally can speak Indonesian.

content: あの議員は履歴を偽って国民をだましていたわけだから、辞職は当然のことだ。

content.content: As that member of the Diet lied about her background and deceived the people, it’s natural that she should resign.

content: A:あの人、クビになったんだってよ。

content.content: I heard that person was fired.
B:当然よ。会社のお金、何百万も使い込んでるのがばれたわけだから。
Of course. It’s because he was caught embezzling millions of the company’s money.
In the form XわけだからYは当然だ, takes X, a reliable fact, as the foundation for asserting that, as X is a fact, Y is the natural outcome.
b. ...わけだから...てもとうぜんだ

content: 彼女は大学を出てからもう8年も経っているわけだから、結婚していても当然だろう。

content.content: As it’s already been eight years since she left university, she’s probably married by now.

content: 彼は大学を卒業しているわけだからパソコンが使えても当然なのに、まったく使えないらしい。

content.content: As he graduated from university, you would think he would be able to use a computer, but it seems he can’t use one at all.

content: これだけ利用者が増えているわけだからもっと安くしても当然なのに、電車やバスの運賃は値上がりする一方だ。

content.content: Because the number of users is increasing, bus and train fares should get cheaper, but they just keep rising.
Takes the form XわけだからYても当然だ. Means “when one accepts X as a reliable fact, it would not be strange if Y were also true.” As in examples

content: and
, it is often used in cases where, in reality, the opposite situation to Y has occurred and runs counter to expectations.

content.content: 4. というわけだ／ってわけだ

content: イギリスとは時差が8時間あるから、日本が 11 時ならイギリスは3時（だ）というわけだ。

content.content: As there is an eight hour time difference with the United Kingdom, when it is eleven o’clock in Japan, that means it is three o’clock in the United Kingdom.

content: 彼女の父親は私の母の弟だ。つまり彼女と私はいとこ同士（だ）というわけだ。

content.content: Her father is my mother’s younger brother. In other words, that means we are cousins.

content: A:あしたから温泉に行くんだ。

content.content: I’m going to a hot spring from tomorrow.
B:へえ、いいね。じゃ、仕事のことを忘れて命の洗濯ができるというわけだ。
Wow, that’s great. It means you can kick back and forget all about work.

content: A:川本さん、車買いかえたらしいよ。

content.content: It seems that Kawamoto-san has changed his car.
B:あ、そう。子供が生まれて前のが小さくなったってわけか。
Oh, really? Had the previous one gotten too small after his child was born?
This form is related to the〈conclusion〉,〈restatement〉and〈reason〉uses of Usage 1 and 2 in わけだ.
【わけても】

content: この山は、わけても5月がうつくしい。

content.content: This mountain is particularly beautiful in May.

content: そのクラスの学生はみんな日本語がうまいが、わけてもAさんは上達がはやかった。

content.content: The students in that class are all good at Japanese but A-san’s progress has been particularly fast.

content: 彼はスポーツ万能だ。わけてもスキーはプロなみだ。

content.content: He’s an all-rounder at sports. In particular, he’s like a professional at skiing.

content: 北風が身を切る季節になったが、給料日前の今夜はわけても寒さが身にしみる。

content.content: It’s the season when the north wind bites but tonight, before payday, I feel as though the cold is particularly penetrating.
Means “among some things, particularly.” Written expression and is not used in spoken language.
【わけではない】
1. ...わけではない

content: このレストランはいつも客がいっぱいだが、だからといって特別においしいわけではない。

content.content: This restaurant is always full of customers but that fact doesn’t necessarily mean that the food is particularly good.

content: 私はふだんあんまり料理をしないが、料理が嫌いなわけではない。忙しくてやる暇がないだけなのだ。

content.content: The reason I don’t often cook is not that I dislike it. It’s just that I’m busy and don’t have the time to do it.

content: 私の部屋は本で埋まっているが、全部を読んだわけではなく、買ってはみたものの開いたことさえないというものも多い。

content.content: My room is full of books but that doesn’t mean I have read them all. There are many which I haven’t even opened since I bought them.

content: 来月から英会話を習うことにした。全然話せないわけではないのだが、日頃英語をしゃべる機会がないので、いざというとき口から出てこないのだ。

content.content: I’ve decided to learn English conversation from next month. It’s not that I can’t speak it at all but, as I don’t have a regular chance to speak English, when it comes to the crunch it won’t come out of my mouth.

content: 娘の外泊をただ黙って見のがしているわけではないが、下手に注意したらかえって反発するので、どうしたものかと考えあぐねている。

content.content: I don’t just silently overlook my daughter staying out overnight but clumsily caution her and, as she responds by rebelling all the more, I am at a loss as to what is to be done.

content: 弁解をするわけではありませんが、昨日は会議が長引いてどうしても抜けられなかったのです。

content.content: It’s no excuse but yesterday’s meeting dragged on and I couldn’t escape no matter what.

content: A:イギリスへ行ってしまうんだそうですね。

content.content: I hear that you’re going to the UK.
B:ええ。でも別に永住するわけじゃありませんし、5年たったらまた帰ってきますよ。
Yes, but it’s not permanent; I’ll be back when five years have passed.

content: A:今度の日曜日に映画に行きませんか。

content.content: Shall we go to see a movie next Sunday?
B:日曜ですか。
Sunday?
A:予定があるんですか。
Do you have plans?
B:いえ、予定があるわけではないのですが、その日はうちでゆっくりしたかったので...。
No, it’s not that I have plans but I wanted to spend that day relaxing at home....
Used to deny that which is thought to be naturally derived from what has just been said or from the current situation. It is often used together with phrases such as だからといって, 別に and 特に.
In example

content: , it can generally be concluded from いつも客がいっぱいだ that “the food is delicious” but this is denied as not being the case. Meaning “It is a mistake to conclude that the food is delicious,” おいしいわけではない, in comparison to the directly negative 料理はおいしくない, becomes a euphemistic, indirectly negative expression. Therefore, as in
, it can be used to make a more indirect refusal than 予定はありませんが. そういうわけではないのですが can also be said. Furthermore, as in
and
, when used with words such as 全部・みんな and 全然・まったく, it becomes a partial denial, meaning for example, “I have read a few” or “I can speak it a little.”

content.content: 2. というわけではないってわけではない

content: このレストランはいつも満員だが、だからといって特においしいというわけではない。

content.content: This restaurant is always full but, be that as it may, it doesn’t mean the food is especially delicious.

content: 私はふだんあまり料理をしないが、料理がきらい（だ）というわけではない。忙しくてやる暇がないだけだ。

content.content: I don’t cook very often but it doesn’t mean I hate cooking. It’s just that I’m busy and don’t have the time to do it.

content: A:あした映画に行かない？

content.content: Coming to the movies tomorrow?
B:あした、か。うーん。
Tomorrow? I’m not sure....
A:私とじゃいやだってこと？
You don’t want to go with me?
B:いや、いや（だ）ってわけじゃないんだけど…。
No, no, that’s not it....

content: 今日は学校へ行く気がしない。雨だから行きたくないというわけではない。ただ何となく今日は何もする気になれないのだ。

content.content: I don’t feel like going to school today. It’s not because it’s raining. It’s just that, for some reason, I don’t feel like doing anything today.
This form connects わけではない with という／って. As in the 雨だから行きたくない of example

content: , in cases where the logic XだからY appears explicitly within the same sentence, it is usual to use というわけではない rather than わけではない.

content.content: 【わけにはいかない】
1. V-るわけに（は）いかない

content: ちょっと熱があるが、今日は大事な会議があるので仕事を休むわけにはいかない。

content.content: I have a bit of a fever but there is an important meeting today and so I can’t take a holiday from work.

content: カラオケに誘われたが、明日から試験なので行くわけにもいかない。

content.content: I was invited to karaoke but I have tests from tomorrow and so I cannot make it.

content: 体調を崩した仲間を残して行くわけにもいかず、登山隊はしかたなくそこから下山することになった。

content.content: They couldn’t leave their unwell friend behind and so the mountaineering party had no choice but to descend the mountain from there.

content: いくらお金をもらっても、お宅の息子さんを不正に入学させるわけにはいきません。

content.content: However much money you give me, I can’t dishonestly allow your son to pass into this school.

content: もう 30 近い娘をいつまでも甘やかしておくわけにもいかないが、かと言って自立できる収入もないのに出て行けと放り出すわけにもいかない。

content.content: I can’t keep spoiling my daughter who is almost thirty but, having said that, as she has no income by which she can be independent, neither can I just throw her out.

content: A:うちで猫を飼っていること、大家さんには内緒にしてもらえませんか。

content.content: Will you keep it a secret from the landlord that we’re keeping a cat in the house?
B:いや、そういうわけにはいきませんよ。契約ではだめなことになっているんですから。それにみんな猫の鳴き声で迷惑しているんですよ。
No, I can’t do that. It’s against the terms of the contract. Besides, everyone is annoyed by its cries.
Means “It is not possible to do so.” It does not simply mean “cannot do” but rather that “thinking from general knowledge, socially accepted ideas or past experience (something) cannot be done.”

私はお酒が飲めない shows that the speaker is constitutionally a weak drinker and, therefore “cannot drink.” However, お酒を飲むわけにはいかない does not mean that constitutionally they are a weak drinker, but rather that, for some reason (for example, they have come by car), they cannot drink. Also, as in the そういうわけにはいかない of example

content: where it refers to the inability to keep the secret, it can also be used in acknowledging the previous sentence.

content.content: 2. V-ないわけに（は）いかない

content: 他の人ならともかく、あの上司に飲みに誘われたら付き合わないわけにはいかない。断ると後でどんなめんどうな仕事を押しつけられるかわからないのだから。

content.content: If it’s somebody else it’s okay, but if that supervisor invites you to go drinking with him, you have to go. If you refuse, you don’t know what kind of drudging job you’ll be made to do.

content: 実際にはもう彼を採用することに決まっていたが、形式上はめんどうでも試験と面接をしないわけにはいかなかった。

content.content: In reality we had already decided to employ him but, formally, even though it’s troublesome, we had to conduct an exam and interview.

content: 今日は車で来ているのでアルコールを飲むわけにはいかないが、もし先輩に飲めと言われたら飲まないわけにもいかないし、どうしたらいいのだろう。

content.content: As I’ve come by car today I can’t drink alcohol, but if my superior tells me to drink I’ll have to. What should I do?

content: A:あんなハードな練習、もうやりたくないよ。疲れるだけじゃないか。

content.content: I don’t want to do that kind of hard exercise any more. It will just make me tired (without any benefit).
B:そういうわけにはいかないだろう。監督に逆らったらレギュラーから降ろされるぞ。
That’s no excuse. If you go against the coach you’ll be dropped as a regular.

Connected to the negative form of a verb, this expresses the obligation that “It is not possible not to carry out that action,” in other words, “must do.” This also takes as its reason generally knowledge, socially accepted ideas or past experience. As in

content: , it can also be used in the form そういうわけ or, in other words, やらないわけ.

content.content: 【わざわざ】

content: 山田さんはわたしの忘れ物をわざわざうちまでとどけてくれた。

content.content: Yamada-san came to my house expressly to deliver something I had forgotten.

content: わざわざとどけてくださって、ほんとうにありがとうございました。

content.content: Thank you so much for taking the trouble to deliver this to me.

content: かぜだというから、わざわざみかんまで買っておみまいに行ったのに、そのともだちはデートにでかけたと言う。

content.content: Because I heard that a friend of mine had caught a cold, I went round to pay her a visit with some oranges I had bought just for that, only to find out that she had gone on a date.

content: そんな集まりのためだけにわざわざ東京まで行くのはめんどうだ。

content.content: Going all the way to Tokyo for that kind of gathering is a pain.

content: 心配してわざわざ来てあげたんだから、もうすこし感謝しなさいよ。

content.content: I was worried and have come especially to visit you, so show a bit more gratitude.

Means to do something especially for some reason, not through obligation but through courtesy, good will or concern, and not just by coincidence or chance. Often used together with phrases such as のだから an のに.
【わずか】

content: さいふの中に残っていたのはわずか 200 円だった。

content.content: I had only 200 yen left in my purse.

content: その会議のその日の出席者はわずか5人だった。

content.content: At that conference, there were only five people present on that day.

content: 社員わずか 300 人たらずのその会社がいま大きな注目を集めている。

content.content: That company with not even 300 employees is getting a lot of attention now.

content: わずかな日数で大きな仕事をなしとげた。

content.content: I got a big job finished in only a few days.

content: 飢饉のため、わずかな食糧で暮らしている。

content.content: Because of the famine they are living on very little food.

content: あの会社もわずかに社員8名を残すだけとなった。

content.content: That company has only eight employees left.
When followed by a statement expressing a quantity, this shows that the speaker feels the quantity is small. Also, in the formわずかに, this shows that the quantity is exceedingly small. It means “only.”
【わたる】→
【にわたって】
【わり】
1. わりと／わりに

content: わりとおいしいね。

content.content: Pretty tasty, huh?

content: きょうの試験はわりとかんたんだった。

content.content: Today’s exam was comparatively easy.

content: ああ、あの映画？　わりにおもしろかったよ。

content.content: Ah, that movie? It was rather interesting.
Means “comparing a certain situation with what is expected.” For example, in

content: means “compared to the usual exams,” “in contrast to how everyone had expected it to be difficult.” Used for both positive and negative evaluations where something is felt not to follow the norm. Not often used in formal sentences.

content.content: 2. わりに（は）［Nのわりに］［Na なわりに］［A-いわりに］［Vわりに］

content: あのレストランは値段のわりにおいしい料理を出す。

content.content: That restaurant serves pretty good food for its prices.

content: このいすは値段が高いわりには、すわりにくい。

content.content: This chair is pretty difficult to sit on (is uncomfortable) despite its high price.

content: あの人は細いわりに力がある。

content.content: That person is quite strong for how slim he is.

content: ひとの作った料理に文句ばっかり言ってるわりにはよく食べるじゃないか。

content.content: You eat a lot for someone who does nothing but complain about the food people have made.

content: あまり勉強しなかったわりにはこの前のテストの成績はまあまあだった。

content.content: The result of the last test wasn’t bad considering that I didn’t study much.

content: 山田さん、よく勉強したわりにはあまりいい成績とは言えないねえ。

content.content: Yamada-san, your test result wasn’t that good considering how much you studied, was it?

Means “compared to what would generally be expected from a certain situation.” Used for both positive and negative evaluations where something is felt not to follow the norm. Not often used in formal sentences.
【を...とする】［NをNとする］

content: その中学はその生徒を退学処分とするという決定をおこなったようだ。

content.content: It seems that the junior high school has taken the decision to expel that pupil.

content: 我々は、ここに、我々の国を本日より共和制とすることを宣言する。

content.content: We hereby declare our country to be a republic from this day forth.
【とする2】2a
【を...にひかえて】［NをNにひかえ（て）］

content: 試験を来週にひかえ、図書館は毎日おそくまで学生でいっぱいである。

content.content: As next week’s exam draws near, the library is full of students until late every day.

content: 出産をまぢかにひかえて、その母親ゾウに対する飼育係の人たちの気の使いようはたいへんなものだった。

content.content: As the delivery drew near, the concern of the mother elephant’s handlers was immense.

content: 首脳会談を5日後にひかえ、事務レベルの協議は最後のツメにはいっている。

content.content: With the summit meeting five days away, the administrative level negotiations were hammering out the final details.

The second N inNをNにひかえ（て）takes a noun which demonstrates time. Shows that a thing is getting closer in time. As in the above examples, often used with things which bring a feeling of tension or nervousness. Written expression.
【をおいて】［Nをおいて］

content: 都市計画について相談するなら、彼をおいて他にはいないだろう。

content.content: If you’re going to talk about town planning, I don’t think there’s anyone but him (to talk to).

content: マスメディアの社会への影響について研究したいのなら、この大学をおいて他にはない。

content.content: If you want to research the influence of the mass media on society, there’s no other university than this one.

content: もし万一母が倒れたら、何をおいてもすぐに病院に駆けつけなければならない。

content.content: If, by some chance, mother should collapse, whatever happens, I have to rush to the hospital immediately.
Means “setting aside...except....” The 何をおいても of

content: is an idiomatic expression meaning “whatever happens.”

content.content: 【をかぎりに】［Nをかぎりに］

content: 今日をかぎりに今までのことはきれいさっぱり忘れよう。

content.content: As of today, let’s forget everything that has happened until now.

content: 明日の大晦日をかぎりにこの店は閉店する。

content.content: As of tomorrow on New Year’s Eve, this store will close.

content: この会は今回をかぎりに解散することとなりました。

content.content: It is decided that this meeting is dissolved as of now.

content: みんなは声を限りに叫んだが、何の返事も返ってこなかった。

content.content: Everyone shouted at the top of their voices but they got no reply.
Attaches to words demonstrating time, such as “today” and “this time,” and means “with that time as the last.” Often used with words which include the time of the utterance. Example

content: is an idiomatic expression meaning “at the top of one’s voice.”

content.content: 【をかわきりとして】→
【をかわきりに】
【をかわきりに】［Nをかわきりに］

content: 彼女は、店長としての成功を皮切りに、どんどん事業を広げ、大実業家になった。

content.content: With her success as store manager as the starting point, she rapidly expanded the business and became a big businesswoman.

content: その歌のヒットを皮切りに、彼らはコマーシャル、映画、ミュージカルなどあらゆる分野へ進出していった。

content.content: After that song became a hit they went on to appear in commercials, movies, musicals, and many other fields.

content: 太鼓の合図を皮切りに、祭りの行列が繰り出した。

content.content: At the taiko’s signal, the festival procession set out.
Means “with that as the starting point.” Usually, a situation in which something prospers or develops rapidly comes afterwards. May also be used in the forms ...をかわきりにして and ...をかわきりとして.
【をかわきりにして】→
【をかわきりに】
【をきんじえない】

content: 思いがけない事故で家族を失った方々には同情を禁じえません。

content.content: I cannot help but sympathize with people who have unexpectedly lost their families in accidents.

content: 戦場から切々と訴えかける手紙に涙を禁じえない人も多いだろう。

content.content: Many people must be moved to tears at the poignant letters of appeal from the battlefield.

content: 母の死を知らず無邪気に遊んでいる子供にあわれみを禁じえなかった。

content.content: I couldn’t help but feel compassion for the children who innocently played, unaware of their mother’s death.

content: この不公平な判決には怒りを禁じえない。

content.content: I cannot help but feel anger at this unfair sentence.

content: 期待はしていなかったが、受賞の知らせにはさすがに喜びを禁じ得なかった。

content.content: I hadn’t expected it but I couldn’t help but be delighted at the notification that I had won a prize.

Means that a person cannot help but feel emotions such as anger and compassion in response to a certain situation. Used where such a feeling is held in spite of attempts to repress it. Formal, written expression.
【をけいきとして】［Nをけいきとして］

content: 彼女は大学入学を契機として親元を出た。

content.content: With entering university as her motivation, she left her parent’s home.

content: 彼は就職を契機として生活スタイルをガラリと変えた。

content.content: He took finding a job as the opportunity to change his lifestyle.

content: 日本は敗戦を契機として国民主権国家へと転換したと言われている。

content.content: It is said that Japan converted to popular sovereignty as a result of being defeated in the war.

content: 今回の合併を契機として、我が社は 21 世紀をリードする企業としてさらに発展してゆかなければならない。

content.content: Taking advantage of this merger, our company must further develop and be a leader in the 21 century.
Attaches to nouns demonstrating actions such as “enter university” and “find employment.” Means “with a particular event as the cue/as the turning point.” ...をけいきに and ...をけいきにして can also be said.
（例）彼女は大学入学を契機に（して）親元を出た。
With entering university as her motivation, she left her parent’s home.
Written expression.
【をこめて】［Nをこめて］

content: 母親のために心をこめてセーターを編んだ。

content.content: I put my whole heart into knitting a sweater for my mother.

content: この花を、永遠に変わらぬ愛を込めてあなたに贈ります。

content.content: I present these flowers to you with my eternally unchanging love.

content: 彼女は、望郷の思いを込めてその歌を作ったそうだ。

content.content: People say that she wrote that song infusing it with her thoughts of her hometown.

content: 彼は、長年の恨みを込めて、痛烈な一撃をその男の顔面に食らわせた。

content.content: Full of long-held resentment, he delivered a severe blow to that guy’s face.
Means “filled with feelings of the heart such as love and affection.” Can be used to modify a noun, as in NをこめたN but NのこもったN is more common.
（例）子供たちが心を込めた贈り物をした。
The children sent a thoughtful gift.
（例）子供たちが心のこもった贈り物をした。
The children sent a thoughtful gift.
There are also the following idiomatic expressions withoutを.
（例）父は丹精込めて育てたその菊をことのほか愛している。
My father is particularly fond of the chrysanthemum that he has been cultivating with great care.
【をして...させる】［NをしてV-させる］

content: あのきびしい先生をして「もう教えることは何もない」と言わせたのだから、あなたはたいしたものだよ。

content.content: For that strict teacher to have said to you “I have nothing more to teach you,” you must really be something.

content: あのわからず屋の親をして「うん」と言わせるには、ちょっとやそっとの作戦ではむりだよ。

content.content: Ordinary tactics and strategies won’t work when it comes to persuading such stubborn parents to say “yes.”

content: あのがんこ者をしてその気にさせたのだから、誠意のたいせつさをわかいあなたに教えられた気がする。

content.content: Since you managed to make that stubborn person change his mind, I feel that at your young age, you’ve learned the importance of being sincere.

In most cases N is a noun which represents a person. Means the same as ...に...させる and ...を...させる. When をして is used, usually means “making an unlikely person to undertake something denoted by V.. It is an old-fashioned, formal expression.
【をぜんていに】［NをぜんていにV］

content: 彼女は記事にしないことを前提にそのことを記者に話した。

content.content: She told it to the reporter on the understanding that it would not appear in the article.

content: では、そのことを前提に（して）、今後のことを話しあっていきたいと思います。

content.content: All right, on that premise, I’d like to move on to discuss what happens from now on.

content: 政府は、その問題の解決を前提に援助交渉にのぞむ方針をかためたもようである。

content.content: With the resolution of that problem as a prerequisite, the government firmed up its plans to attend the aid negotiations.
Means “the conditions necessary for a thing to be achieved,” “If (something) must be done, it is subject to certain conditions.” For example, the 記事にしないこと of

content: , is such a condition. Has the tone of written language. In speech, ...をぜんていにして／として are also used.

content.content: 【をたよりに】［NをたよりにV］

content: あなたがいなければ、これからわたしは何をたよりに（して）生きていけばいいのですか。

content.content: If you are not going to be there for me, what should I look up to as my guide in life?

content: その留学生は、辞書をたよりに、ひとりで「橋のない川」を読みつづけている。

content.content: That exchange student continues reading “The River with no Bridge” by himself with the help of a dictionary.

content: 白いつえだけをたよりに、その人は 70 年生き、そして死んでいった。

content.content: That person lived to seventy relying solely on a white cane and then died.

content: もちまえの行動力だけをたよりに、彼女はバイクで世界中を旅している。

content.content: She is traveling all over the world on a bike relying solely on her own resourcefulness.
Means “with the aid of something,” “depending on something.” In speech ...をたよりにして and ...をたよりとして are also used. Similar expressions are ...をたのみにして and ...をたのみとして.
【をちゅうしんに】［NをちゅうしんにV］

content: そのグループは山田さんを中心に作業を進めている。

content.content: With Yamada-san at the center, that group is advancing their operations.

content: そのチームはキャプテンを中心によくまとまったいいチームだ。

content.content: With the captain at its center, that is a well-organized, good team.

content: 太陽系の惑星は太陽を中心としてまわっている。

content.content: The solar system’s planets revolve around the sun.

content: 台風の影響は、九州地方を中心に西日本全体に広がる見込みです。

content.content: The effects of the typhoon are expected to spread over the whole of western Japan, centering on the Kyushu region.

content: このバスは、朝7時台と夕方6時台を中心に多くの便数がある。

content.content: This bus route has many services, particularly between seven and eight in the morning and six and seven in the evening.

This means “with... at the center.” This is used to show the extent of an action, phenomenon, or situation which is placed at the center/is at the core of something. It is also used in the forms ...をちゅうしんにして and ...をちゅうしんとして. Has the tone of written language.
【をつうじて】
1. NをつうじてV

content: その話は山田さんを通じて相手にもつたわっているはずです。

content.content: I expect that Yamada-san has told that story to the other party, too.

content: A社はB社を通じてC社とも提携関係にある。

content.content: Company A has a joint venture with company C, through company B.

content: 現地の大使館を通じて外務省にはいった情報によると、死者は少なくとも 100 人をこえたもようである。

content.content: According to the information received by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from the local embassy the number of casualties has exceeded at least 100 people.

Means “via....” This is used to detail that information is conveyed, relationships are built etc. via something. The thing which is conveyed is information, stories, messages etc. but cannot be used in reference to means of transportation.
（×）この列車はマドリッドをつうじてパリまで行く。
This train is going to Paris, via Madrid.
（○）この列車はマドリッド｛を通って／を経由して｝パリまで行く。
This train is going to Paris, via Madrid.
Has the tone of written language. ...をとおして is also used.
2. Nをつうじて

content: その国は一年をつうじてあたたかい。

content.content: That country is warm all year round.

content: このあたりは四季をつうじて観光客のたえることがない。

content.content: This region is constantly visited by tourists throughout the year.

content: その作家は、生涯を通じて、さまざまな形で抑圧されてきた人々を描きつづけた。

content.content: Throughout his life, that writer depicted people who had suffered various forms of oppression.
Attaches to nouns which demonstrate time, and means “throughout a fixed time period, without interruption.” Has the tone of written language. ...をとおして is also used.
【をとわず】［Nをとわず］

content: 彼らは昼夜を問わず作業を続けた。

content.content: They kept working day and night.

content: 意欲のある人なら、年齢や学歴を問わず採用する。

content.content: If a person has ambition, we will employ them regardless of age or academic background.

content: 近ごろは男女を問わず大学院に進学する学生が増えている。

content.content: Nowadays, regardless of gender, more students are entering graduate school.

content: 新空港の設計については、国の内外を問わず広く設計案を募集することとなった。

content.content: As for the new airport plans, we are taking planning idea applications regardless of whether they are domestic or foreign.

Means “not connected to...” or “without a problem with....” Often used with opposite nouns, such as 昼夜(day and night) and 男女(man and woman). Can also be used in the form Nはとわず, as in the following example.
（例）《アルバイトの広告で》 販売員募集。性別は問わず。
《Part time job ad》 Salesperson wanted. Gender irrelevant.
Has the tone of written language.
【をのぞいて】［Nをのぞいて（は）］

content: 山田さんをのぞいて、みんな来ています。

content.content: Everyone is coming except Yamada-san.

content: 火曜日をのぞいて（は）だいたいあいています。

content.content: We are generally open apart from on Tuesdays.

content: その国は、真冬の一時期をのぞいて（は）だいたい温暖な気候だ。

content.content: Apart from in midwinter, that country has a generally warm climate.

content: 全体的には、この問題を除いて、ほぼ解決したと言ってよいだろう。

content.content: On the whole, apart from this problem, I think we can say it is settled.
Means “with that as an exception.” It is a written expression. In speech ...をのぞけば or ...のほかは are often used.
【をふまえ】［Nをふまえ（て）V］

content: いまの山田さんの報告をふまえて話し合っていただきたいと思います。

content.content: I’d like to have a discussion based on what Yamada-san has just reported.

content: 前回の議論をふまえて議事を進めます。

content.content: Proceedings will continue bearing in mind our last discussion.

content: そのご提案は、現在我々がおかれている状況をふまえてなされているのでしょうか。

content.content: That proposal will be implemented on the basis of our current situation.

content: 今回の最終答申は、昨年の中間答申をふまえ、さまざまな角度から議論を重ねたうえで出されたものだ。

content.content: The final report, based on last year’s mid-year report, will be made public after it has been discussed from a variety of angles.
Means “taking something as basis of a hypothesis or judgment,” or “after taking it into consideration.” It is a formal, written expression.
【をもとに】［Nをもとに（して）］

content: 実際にあった話をもとにして脚本を書いた。

content.content: I wrote the screenplay based on a true story.

content: 人のうわさだけをもとにして人を判断するのはよくない。

content.content: It is not good to judge people only on the basis of gossip.

content: この地方に伝わる伝説をもとにして、幻想的な映画を作ってみたい。

content.content: I want to make a fantasy movie based on a traditional legend of this area.

content: 調査団からの報告をもとに救援物資の調達が行われた。

content.content: Relief supplies were procured on the basis of the report of the inquiry commission.

content: 史実をもとにした作品を書き上げた。

content.content: I wrote a work based on historical fact.
Means “taking a particular thing as material, a hint, or the basis for (something).” When it modifies a noun, as in example

content: , it becomes NをもとにしたN.

content.content: 【をものともせずに】［Nをものともせずに］

content: 彼らのヨットは、嵐をものともせずに、荒海を渡り切った。

content.content: In defiance of the storm, their yacht finished crossing the rough sea.

content: ばくだいな借金をものともせずに、彼は社長になることを引き受け、事業を立派に立ち直らせた。

content.content: In the face of huge debts, he accepted the position of president, and recovered the company’s position splendidly.

content: 周囲の批判をものともせずに、彼女は自分の信念を貫き通した。

content.content: In the face of criticism from those around her, she stuck to her beliefs.
Means “to face up to severe conditions.” Expressions of problem solving come afterwards. It is a written expression.
【をよぎなくさせる】［Nをよぎなくさせる］

content: 台風の襲来が登山計画の変更を余儀なくさせた。

content.content: We were forced to change our mountain climbing plans because the typhoon came.

content: 思いがけないゲリラの反撃が政府軍の撤退を余儀なくさせた。

content.content: An unexpected guerrilla counteroffensive forced the government troops to withdraw.
Attached to a noun which demonstrates an act, means “to be made to do so forcibly” or “to have no choice but to do so.” Used in cases where an undesirable situation is caused.
【をよぎなくされる】［Nをよぎなくされる］

content: 火事で住まいが焼けたため、家探しを余儀なくされた。

content.content: I was forced into house-hunting as my home was damaged by a fire.

content: 長時間の交渉の結果、妥協を余儀なくされた。

content.content: We were forced to compromise as a result of long negotiations.

content: 事業を拡張したが、売り上げ不振のため、撤退を余儀なくされる結果になった。

content.content: Although we had expanded the company, due to a slump in profits, we were forced to withdraw (from the market).

content: これ以上の争いをさけるために全員が協力を余儀なくされた。

content.content: In order to avoid further dispute, all members were forced to cooperate.
Attaches to nouns which demonstrate an act, and means “reluctantly” or “the situation is such that one has no choice but to....” It is a written expression.
【んじゃ】［N／Na 　（なん）じゃ］［A／V　んじゃ］

content: 雨なんじゃしかたがない。あしたにしよう。

content.content: It’s no use if it’s raining. Let’s do it tomorrow.

content: そんなに臆病なんじゃ、どこにも行けないよ。

content.content: If you’re so cowardly, you can’t go anywhere.

content: こんなに暑いんじゃ、きょうの遠足はたいへんだろうね。

content.content: If it’s this hot, today’s outing will be terrible.

content: こんなにたくさんの人に見られているんじゃ緊張してしまうな。
